Mathieu Van der Poel and Pogacar battled over Montmartre in a thrilling finale

Pogacar is unsure what his next goal will be

1 of 5

The one rider who has broken Pogacar's stranglehold of cycling's biggest race in the past was Denmark's Vingegaard, who won in 2022 and 2023.

But this year the 29-year-old Visma-Lease a Bike rider abandoned after breaking his collarbone on a easy right-hand bend on stage 15.

The mistake was very unlike Vingegaard's near perfect technique and execution as a rider, and attention soon turned to scrutiny of the International Testing Agency (ITA), which had awoken Vingegaard at 2am to carry out an anti-doping test.

Other riders had the same treatment, including Pogacar at 5am, but the ITA said there was "exceptional circumstances" to take the night tests, which are rare and require additional permission.

It is not known when the test results will be published.

Pogacar's only other real rival was the much-improved Belgian Remco Evenepoel of Red Bull-Bora-Hansgohe, who finished six minutes 26 seconds behind overall.

Third place went to Pogacar's Mexican team-mate Isaac del Toro, who won stage two thanks largely to Pogacar's babysitting pace in the lead-up to the line.

It would not be the only time Pogacar would aid Del Toro, 22, sacrificing his own potential victory on Saturday's brutal 'queen' stage to Alpe d'Huez to consolidate Del Toro's place on the podium.

Del Toro's white jersey for the best young rider came at the expense of France's new 19-year-old star Paul Seixas of Decathlon-CMA CGM. Seixas looked stronger than Del Toro at times on the climbs but faded substantially on Saturday.

Many think Seixas will be a rival to Pogacar in the future.

In the year when Britain's four-time Tour winner Chris Froome retired, his former team - now known as Netcompany Ineos Cycling - failed to record a stage victory in 21 attempts.

Ex-Ineos rider Tom Pidcock of Pinarello-Q36.5 won on Alpe d'Huez four years ago and returned to this race having achieved much with a new team built entirely around him.

The 26-year-old did not manage to win a stage, but he and his team will be satisfied with Pidcock's consistent battling riding, which earned him ninth in the general classification to build on third place in last year's Vuelta a Espana.

Fellow Briton Adam Yates, 33, showed great tenacity after falling ill on stage 16 and spending two days riding at the back of the field before helping pace Pogacar up a climb for victory on stage 19.

One of the most entertaining riders in the race was Ecuador's Richard Carapaz of EF Education-Easypost. He toiled earlier in the race before coming into great form to claim the king of the mountains' polka dot jersey.

He won stage 18 and Saturday's stage 20 after topping the race's highest point first and after 5,450km of climbing.

The green points jersey was awarded to Denmark's Mads Pedersen of Lidl-Trek, after tenacious riding on climbs he is not typically strong on to hoover up mid-stage points, alongside winning stage four.

He beat a number of sprinters to the jersey, including Philipsen of Alpecin-Premier Tech. Philipsen won stage 17 and fellow Belgian Tim Merlier of Soudal-Quick Step won three bunch sprint stages.

Berlin Pride attack suspect shot and killed during police operation

BBC News Sun, 26 Jul 2026 19:21:26 GMT

The man suspected of carrying out what authorities say was likely an "Islamist terror attack" at Berlin Pride has been shot and killed by police.

Officers opened fire when Abdul Ballout, a 21-year-old German citizen with Lebanese heritage, rushed at them with a knife in Spandau, a western borough of Berlin.

It brought an end to a massive manhunt that was launched after a white van was driven into a crowd of people near Tiergarten park just before 22:00 (local time) on Saturday evening, killing one woman and injuring at least 29 others.

Police say following the ramming, several people were injured in a stabbing attack.

Speaking to reporters on Sunday, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said evidence pointed to it being an "Islamist terror attack".

"We are dealing with a suspected perpetrator, who had previously drawn attention to himself through a high volume of criminal offences, radicalisation and affiliation with the Islamist scene," Dobrindt said.

A statement released by the Berlin public prosecutor's office revealed further details about Ballout's criminal history.

In May 2025, prosecutors said he travelled via Turkey to Lebanon, with the intention of joining the Islamic State group (IS) in Syria. While in Lebanon he allegedly made contact with several individuals he believed were members of IS.

He was arrested in Lebanon in July 2025 and sentenced to three months in prison for incitement to religious and sectarian conflict.

Then in November 2025 he returned to Germany where he was arrested at Berlin Brandenburg Airport and held in pre-trial detention.

In May this year, he was sentenced to one year and 10 months in prison for "preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state". The decision was deferred for six months and he was placed under the supervision of a parole officer.

He was previously convicted of assault and robbery in 2022, and of robbing a victim of headphones in 2020.

Dobrindt said Germany's threat level would be raised following the attack, while other states were also being briefed about the attack and advised to review their security measures for major events.

On Sunday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the scene of the attack in Tiergarten park.

He later spoke outside a church service that paid tribute to victims, where he pledged to "defend the freedom and openness of our lives".

"These extremists have no place in our society," he said, adding that Germany would not allow the "poison of terrorism" to affect its society.

Berlin police have said people were hit on Ahornsteig street, which is a long path stretching across the Tiergarten park, largely in a forested area.

Meanwhile, German media say those injured in the attack are no longer in a life-threatening condition.

Saturday's attack shattered the joy and revelry of Berlin's Christopher Street Day, where hundreds of thousands spill onto the city streets for one of Europe's most famous Pride events.

Christopher Street Day commemorates the first known uprising among the LGBT community in New York City in 1969 at the Stonewall Inn, which is located on Christopher Street.

A clean-up event due to take place at Tiergarten park and a breakfast market scheduled for Sunday morning were both cancelled following the attack.

Later in the day, some members of the LGBT community returned to the iconic Brandenburg Gate for an impromptu vigil.

Speakers condemned extremism in all its manifestations, but they also criticised the government for a lack of support, singling out recent budget cuts for queer organisations.

Armin Duenhoelter from Wolfsburg, who works as a drag artist, was backstage at the main stage when the attack happened.

He told Agency France-Presse that he was still shocked but vowed to be back for next year's pride celebration.

"We won't let it beat us down," he said.

Norris and McLaren almost perfect as Ferrari flounder

BBC News Sun, 26 Jul 2026 19:19:43 GMT

McLaren's Lando Norris won his first grand prix of the year in Hungary

Lando Norris ended the first half of the Formula 1 season with a victory in the Hungarian Grand Prix that he described as "one of my best performances".

It was a drive that had been a long time coming, after a difficult start to the season for the reigning world champion and his McLaren team.

But when McLaren finally gave him a car of the performance level he had become used to in the past season and a half, he more than made the most of it.

While Ferrari, the pre-race favourites, floundered and made, in the words of their team boss Frederic Vasseur "too many mistakes", Norris and McLaren were almost perfect.

Even in the context of Kimi Antonelli's stellar start to the season for Mercedes, this was one of the most impressive and convincing victories of the season.

Norris' one mistake was on the first lap. He converted his pole position into a lead at the first corner, only to misjudge the grip available at Turn Two, slide wide, and gift his position to team-mate Oscar Piastri.

It looked to have been a potentially fatal error to his victory hopes on a track where overtaking is all but impossible between evenly matched cars on similar strategies, but Norris stayed calm.

Seeing he could easily keep pace with Piastri despite being in the dirty air, he said he always believed the win was on.

"It wasn't my finest Turn Two," Norris said, "but after that, seeing what my pace was like and I was just better in every sense, in terms of degradation and pace, I was convinced I could still win the race."

Trapped, Norris begged for a different strategy to give himself a chance of victory, and eventually circumstances presented it to him.

Around half-distance. McLaren pitted Piastri to cover off Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari, which had just stopped for fresh tyres. That gave Norris clean air and he set a blistering pace.

Piastri might still have held the lead, but for a collision with Carlos Sainz as he lapped his Williams. The Australian was angry after Norris came out ahead from his stop a few laps later - but at the Spaniard, not McLaren.

"The fact I could keep up with Oscar on this kind of track, where it's impossible to follow and impossible to overtake, I was within 0.8 seconds or something for, I don't know, almost 40 laps, the fact I could do this is what gave me confidence that I'd win the race no matter what, whether he boxed early or late or whatever," Norris said.

"The pace advantage I had was huge today. But I don't know why. The cars are identical, and I've just been feeling very strong lately.

"I've worked on many areas from last year. I feel much more confident lately with how to extract performance, and I've worked a lot with my engineers to understand this car because it's certainly not an easy car to understand and figure out how to drive on the limit consistently.

"So, why? Just hard work. Hard work from my engineers and from myself to improve me as a driver and improve my driving. That is the answer."

Norris wins his first grand prix of year in Hungary

Complete weekend for Norris but poor result for Sainz - driver ratings

McLaren's Lando Norris is fifth in the drivers' standings while Oscar Piastri is seventh

Norris believes he is driving better this season than he did in the first half of his championship year in 2025.

Last year, he was struggling for feeling from the McLaren.

Like all his rivals, he does not like this new generation of cars as much as the last - especially their engines and the need for so much energy management, and the way they have compromised the driving experience.

But he has gelled with them, while Piastri - so strong in the first half of last season - is struggling.

Team principal Andrea Stella says this is a continuation of the trajectory Norris has been on since a lot of self-assessment led to his strong second half of last year, and eventually the title.

"Lando is much more confident. He's much more aware of his tools that he has in his driving, how to deploy these tools. And I think he's also, let me say, more in control of his emotions," Stella said.

"Because today, when he was behind Oscar, he said a couple of times that he had pace in hand, but he didn't get overly frustrated. And the fact that he wasn't overly frustrated, I think, then allowed him to use the pace at the right time and lead him to the victory. We've seen a great trajectory of development for Lando."

This performance came after a major upgrade to the McLaren car, and there is another to come at the next race, the Dutch Grand Prix after F1's four-week summer break.

Norris' win moves him up to 98 points behind Antonelli, but he cautioned against expectations of a charge up to the top of the championship of the kind Max Verstappen and Red Bull mounted against him and McLaren last year.

"I'm just happy with today," Norris said. "It doesn't mean if I'm quick here, we're going to be quick everywhere.

"One thing I've learned for sure is just to have no expectations of the future and just to work in the present. I think that's the way we've been doing everything as a team.

"That's why we're back on top today: just working hard on ourselves as individuals and also as a team.

"Of course, I'm optimistic for the future and I think we can win more races, but we have good competition and there are still plenty of races I'm not confident in because the car is not to the standard that it needs to be in certain areas."

Oscar Piastri's parked McLaren after he retired because of a gearbox issue

During the race, it appeared as if Piastri's anger over the radio might have been partly directed at the off-set strategy that led to Norris passing him for the lead.

In fact, he was instead furious with Sainz.

"The timing of my stop was fine," he said. "We wanted to cover off Hamilton, which was perfectly normal. Without getting crashed into, I would have been ahead of Lando still.

"In the moment, I was incredibly annoyed. In fact, annoyed is not the word I would use, but there was a multitude that I would, with Carlos. And, yeah, then obviously, when Lando came out ahead, I knew I had no pace to go and attack him.

"I knew my chances of winning the race were done from there."

Discussing the collision with Sainz, Piastri added: "I don't really care if he didn't see me. The fact that he didn't and no-one told him, or there was a lack of complete awareness, is unacceptable.

"He's quite critical of others, and others have given him some stick before for being frustrating on track."

He was not at all mollified by a problem with the GPS system that shows teams where all the cars are on track.

Sainz said he had "no idea I was trying to get lapped", he "didn't expect" Piastri to be there, and it was "impossible to avoid it".

For Piastri, it was academic in the end, a gearbox failure sending him into retirement and denying McLaren a one-two.

Lewis Hamilton was unable to get past Kimi Antonelli in the closing stages of the race

As for Ferrari, they appeared to have the fastest car in Hungary, but underperformed in qualifying. Then Hamilton, after qualifying second, was dropped to fifth on the grid with a penalty for impeding Piastri.

Norris will have been worried about Charles Leclerc starting alongside him on the front row. But instead of challenging Norris, Leclerc lost out to Piastri, Verstappen and Hamilton.

The seven-time champion got ahead of Verstappen in the first pit stops - only to be overtaken again the next time around, the Dutchman making a brilliant move at Turn One that caught Hamilton napping.

A penalty for pit-lane speeding cost Hamilton a further five seconds, and left him behind Leclerc at the end, the Ferraris finishing fourth and fifth.

Hamilton, who remains second in the championship, 50 points behind Antonelli, said "you can't make these kind of mistakes if you want to challenge for a title".

Vasseur said: "It's difficult to clearly understand the pace, because I think the clean air is key, but first it's not a good Sunday, because when you are one-two on Friday, you expect much more.

"And on the top we made too many mistakes today, starting with the penalty and the fact that Max overtook us, that each time that we were doing a pit stop, we were losing a position for 0.2 or 0.3 seconds.

"And then we spent our lives behind the guys, everything went wrong, but for sure we have to do a much better job on Sunday."

George Russell had a bad start in the Mercedes and climbed up from the back of the grid to seventh

Norris was followed across the line by Verstappen and Antonelli, both of whom drove fine races themselves, the three podium finishers fully deserving their results.

Antonelli's team-mate George Russell, meanwhile, had another day to forget. A problem with his engine at the start, for which the team took the blame, dropped him to the back at the start, and he recovered well to seventh, but still lost points to the Italian, who he now trails by 59 points.

"I'm sort of past the point of disappointment now, because it's just, if I'm continuing to be disappointed with everything that goes on, I'll just be disappointed every day of the week," Russell said.

"Obviously, another technical issue that completely ruined the race, but I can tell you some positives. The pace was very strong.

"So, I'll take positives there, but yeah, it's just unbelievable, the list of things that's happened this season.

"Oscar had his thing today as well. It's not like we're the only one, but it does feel like it is happening substantially more to me than others, and hopefully it swings around.

"I don't wish any bad luck on anyone, but I've never had a season like this in my whole career, let alone my F1 career."

Antonelli, then, goes off on holiday in total control of the championship. But he knows to take nothing for granted, as this time last year the same looked to be the case for Piastri.

"I think Lando still had the upper hand this weekend, even on us," Antonelli said.

"On pure pace, I don't think I would have been able to challenge him, especially with how difficult it was to follow as well, with a lot of tyre overheating.

"I did not expect to find myself in this position. But the car has been extremely good, the team has done an incredible job and, on my side, I try to maximise every opportunity I have.

"Of course, there's still lots of work to do, lots to learn, but it was a good first half of the season. Now I'm looking forward to the second half and we're just going to keep pushing."

Firefighters battle wildfire as tens of thousands evacuated near Bordeaux

BBC News Sun, 26 Jul 2026 18:40:08 GMT

Firefighters are battling to contain wildfires burning near the city of Bordeaux as tens of thousands of people have been evacuated from the surrounding region.

France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the situation in the region remained "very unfavourable" and the fire was "moving erratically towards" Bordeaux, though officials downplayed the possibility of evacuation.

Overnight into Sunday, about 55,000 people were evacuated from villages to the south of the city in the Gironde region, famed for its vineyards.

Wildfires have raged across Europe over the past week, primarily in France and Spain, where more than 330,000 people have been evacuated.

France has been one of worst affected regions, with an area of 42,000 hectares burnt in the south-west, making it one of the largest forest fires since World War Two. About 98,000 hectares have burnt across the country since the start of the year.

In total, more than 220,000 people have been evacuated in the south-west of the country.

Captain Nicolas Braz, one of the leaders of the firefighting operation, said the fire had created "its own winds - complete with whirlwinds", adding it was "erratic and unmanageable".

Residents in Le Porge, one of the coastal towns hit by the fires, have set up an improvised volunteer network to support exhausted firefighters, cooking them meals and offering a place to rest in between shifts.

"I think many of them have never experienced a fire of this magnitude before," volunteer Nathalie Augonnet said.

More than 150 houses have been destroyed in the town of 3,500 inhabitants.

"I'm a little devastated for this beautiful town, for its forests, its wildlife and for the people who have lost so much," Augonnet said.

"Right now, we're focused on taking action, so we don't really have time to think. I think the difficult part will come afterwards, during the reconstruction."

Meanwhile in Spain, fires continue to spread, with more than 90,000 evacuated from the regions around Madrid and Ávila.

Around 77,000 hectares have been affected by the fires in Spain, minister for ecological transition, Sara Aagesen, said on Sunday.

She added that the wildfire burning in the Ávila region is the largest in the country's recent history.

Among the residents evacuating surrounding areas is Olga Congacha, 50, who had to flee her village of Robledo de Chavela west of Madrid in a haste.

She said she felt "panicked" when she was told to leave her home.

"I didn't know whether to cry or what. It was a moment when you feel awful," she added.

Returning to her home briefly on Sunday to get medicine, she said the streets were deserted and her house covered in ash.

Tourists in Madrid have reported seeing the fire and smoke near the airport, with one couple from New Zealand describing also smelling the smoke from their hotel in the city.

Canadian tourist Letisha Lucas said the smell was immediately obvious on arrival in Madrid "and very irritating on the throat".

Overnight into Sunday, a new front also opened up near the coastal city of Valencia.

Speaking to reporters late on Saturday, Valencia's regional President Juanfran Pérez Llorca said: "The fire is beyond our capacity to extinguish."

Pilar Bernabe, the central government's delegate to Valencia, said conditions in the region were likely to worsen throughout Sunday.

Sunday is expected to bring high temperatures and low humidity, potentially allowing the fire to spread further.

On Saturday, one civilian was killed in a smaller fire in the Valencia region - the only civilian death so far reported.

Earlier in the week, two firefighters were killed fighting the blaze near to Bordeaux in France.

Speaking on Sunday during a visit to an area hit by wildfires to the west of Madrid, the country's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said "difficult hours lie ahead" but added there were "positive" indications overnight towards containing the blaze.

He also said there needed to be "a major public pact on the climate emergency".

Madrid's regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso described the situation as the "worst fire in the history of the region".

Rescue efforts in France's Gironde region involve 2,500 firefighters, including a Swiss team, 1,500 military personnel and almost 1,200 police and gendarmes, who are carrying out evacuations and helping with rescue and securing operations.

Dry vegetation and brisk winds are causing the fire to spread, with 60km (37 miles) of the A63 motorway, which leads to Spain, having been closed.

On Sunday afternoon, Bordeaux Airport's departures and arrivals boards were showing delays to every flight from 17:15 onwards.

Some 28 Easyjet flights alone were delayed, many with no new departure or arrival time given, and five cancelled including UK flights.

Bordeaux Airport told BBC News air traffic control restrictions had been put in place "to facilitate the work of the emergency services" in fighting the fires, with all commercial flights affected.

It is unclear how long the delays will last, the airport added.

The final stage of the Tour de France was shortened on Sunday from 133km to 89km (from 82 miles to 55) to allow security forces to be redeployed to the firefighting effort.

President Emmanuel Macron said France would "rebuild" and his government would "be there for as long as is needed".

It's me, Cathy – thousands pay tribute to Kate Bush classic

BBC News Sun, 26 Jul 2026 16:37:16 GMT

The sun may be hiding behind grey clouds, but for hundreds of people in flowing red dresses dancing on Yorkshire moorland it'll take more than a threat of rain to dampen their spirits.

This is Brontë country, after all, so it's fitting that it's also perfect Brontë weather.

The group, swaying in unison, have come together to re-create the music video for Kate Bush's 1978 song Wuthering Heights, inspired by Emily Brontë's novel.

Every year, thousands of people around the world don red robes – and in some cases long black wigs – for The Most Wuthering Heights Day Ever.

Events have previously taken place in places such as Sydney, Copenhagen, Berlin, Folkestone and Preston.

This particular "Mass Wuther" perhaps has an even stronger claim than most – it's held on Penistone Hill, not far from the famous Brontë parsonage in Haworth, in the Pennines.

From the field on a clear day can be seen the ruined farmhouse of Top Withens, believed to be the inspiration for the titular farmhouse of Brontë's novel.

"We're really thrilled to be bringing all these people together. It's such a good-hearted, fun event. It doesn't matter whether you can dance or not," says organiser Lydia McKinnon.

"I just hope that the Kates and Cathys have got their thermals and their rain ponchos because they might need them."

The West Yorkshire event was a sell-out in 2025, and this year the 500 tickets were snapped up within 90 seconds, according to event organisers.

Proceeds are split between regional and national charities. This year, Women's Aid, Haworth and Oxenhope District Bridleways Group, and Friends of Brontë Country have been chosen.

Some participants in the Mass Wuther have travelled great distances to attend – in the case of Frances Murphy and Katherine Egan, all the way from Australia.

They both took part in Brisbane's event last year and said they couldn't miss the opportunity to dance in Brontë Country.

"It's wonderful. So many people have turned out, and we're so lucky to have got tickets to get in," Katherine says, adding: "We love you, England."

Martine and Christine are English teachers from Oslo and "are here to dance" as fans of both the singer and the writer.

"We were a bit scared about choreography," Christine admits.

"We're trying to channel Kate Bush and have a lot of attitude and fun."

Wearing a red rose around his neck, Scott Kerman has jumped on a flight from Portland, Oregon, to join in the revelry.

"It's something I've wanted to do for years," he says.

"I'm such a fan of Kate Bush and this song. When I saw that this event was held here on the moors last year, I said, 'Well, where else would I want to do it?'

"It's such a beautiful place, so it's just extraordinary to be here."

Cathy Stoyko said she was "dancing for her sisters" back home in Vancouver Island, Canada.

"I've been a Kate Bush fan since I was a teenager. It's very special to be doing this here. I love the connection to space and community."

Across the UK, other groups of Kate Bush lookalikes gathered to perform the iconic dance.

Twelve years ago, wee Reuben Ward watched wide-eyed as Dan Keatings won gymnastics gold for Scotland in Glasgow.

That was the day he began dreaming.

In his nine-year-old mind, the notion of competing in the Commonwealth Games for Scotland began to form. Not winning gold. Not even being on a podium. Just pulling on the vest and getting out there.

So when the 21-year-old took the acclaim of an ecstatic Emirates Arena crowd after being announced as the Glasgow 2026 all-around champion, it was all he had ever dreamed of and so much more.

Ward - whose parents Brendan and Lisa left East Kilbride for Bury before he was born - had just become the country's third gold medallist on day three of the Games.

"I remember seeing him win and seeing how it was a big deal to people and I thought 'I want to do that'," Ward told BBC Sport Scotland, recalling Keating's success while in the afterglow of his own.

"So to be here now, having done it myself, is spectacular. It's such a full-circle moment. Glasgow and East Kilbride have been like second homes to me my entire life so to do it here is incredibly special."

Scott overcomes pressure and big pal Dean to give Scotland golden start

Why is it so special to be part of Team Scotland?

All the latest news from Scotland at the Games

There was a sense beforehand that Ward could contend here. A bronze maybe. Perhaps even a silver depending how things go.

His team-mates privately made noises that, should everything fall in his favour, gold could be within reach. They had seen him in training, and performed alongside him in the team event on Friday, where Scotland finished fourth.

They knew he was in a good place.

Ward sat seventh after the floor exercise, but streaked into the lead after a splendid performance on the pommel - routinely his strongest event.

He retained that advantage after the rings - by which point assorted Team Scotland officials and members of the Scottish media had arrived in dribs and drabs, with the sniff of a gold in the air.

Ward's vault had been compromised in the team event by a slight issue in his run up - he had to adapt it on the fly and could only execute two twists - but he nailed it this time, performing three to go into the final two rotations top of the standings.

A strong showing in the parallel bars - and a judicious Team Scotland appeal to add an extra 0.100 - maintained his lead at 0.550, meaning he needed to keep his shape in the horizontal bar to clinch gold.

Ward did that and more.

"It kept me awake a little bit because I was picturing it and feeling the emotions. But this beat the expectations by a mile.

"Falling short on Friday was heartbreaking and I'm just so overwhelmed, man. I can barely put words together."

It could get even better. He goes on the floor and pommel on Monday, and is a real medal contender in the later.

My entire family went on a boat trip that they never returned from

BBC News Sun, 26 Jul 2026 14:14:52 GMT

"It's something you don't get over - you learn to live with it."

Sixty years ago, Peter Watts' entire family was killed in a boating tragedy that shocked the nation.

His nine-year-old sister Angela, 10-year-old brother David, mother Doreen and father Frederick George, along with 11 others, died when the Prince of Wales pleasure boat sank on the Mawddach Estuary in Gwynedd on 22 July, 1966.

Now, a memorial recalling the names of the 15 people who lost their lives has been unveiled.

It was another chance for Peter to travel from the village he grew up in, near Milton Keynes, to the picturesque estuary where the catastrophe unfolded.

"We'd been on holidays in previous years and I'd been on this boat trip [before] and I didn't want to go again," Peter recalled.

Peter was 14 at the time, old enough to be allowed to spend the day on his own in the seaside town of Barmouth, where his family were staying in a boarding house.

The rest of his family joined the queue to board the Prince of Wales for the eight mile (13km) trip down the estuary to the George III Hotel at Penmaenpool.

But the tide pushed the ferry boat into the Penmaenpool toll bridge across the estuary, flinging the 42 passengers into the water as the vessel was wrecked on the bridge.

Local people, including the hotel owner and staff and the toll bridge keeper, ran to the aid of those in the water, managing to pull 27 to safety.

But along with Peter's brother and sister, two other children were among the 15 who could not be saved.

"This happened in the morning, at about 11 in the morning, and I was just waiting hours and hours for them to come back - and they didn't come back," said Peter.

"I went down to the harbour and I heard two people talking about a boat that had sunk. I asked them what was going on, and they said what it was, and I said 'My family is on it' - and they said 'Go to the police station'.

"I sat in there for what seemed ever and a day, and they took the details."

The guest house owners came to take him back, while his aunt and uncle drove up to be with him.

"The next morning we went to Dolgellau to the hospital, where they had found three of them - my mother was still missing," he said.

"My father could swim, but my uncle who identified him said he had had a nasty blow on his head."

It would be another three days before his mother's body was found.

An official inquiry found the boat was carrying six more passengers than the maximum 36 permitted under its certification.

There should also have been two crew members - one on the engine and one on the rudder.

But there was only skipper Edward Llewelyn, 73 at the time, who was found to have acted negligently by a Board of Trade inquiry.

The boat was also short of lifebelts and buoyancy apparatus was stowed away.

Llewelyn was ordered to pay £100 towards the inquiry costs, but no prosecutions were ever brought.

However, the inquiry did lead to changes in the law governing insurance and the number of passengers boats could carry.

The events have left a deep mark on Peter, and the urge to return to Barmouth and the estuary as often as he could.

"If I've ever been anywhere near Wales, even when I've been going to Holyhead, when we went to Ireland, I'd come round this way," he said.

"Just to spend a few minutes."

Returning this time on the 60th anniversary of the tragedy, it was marked with a special memorial and the plaque to remember those who died, unveiled by Dolgellau Town Council.

"Those 15 people - I didn't want them to be forgotten. Having their names there - that's what I wanted," said Peter.

I thought the Lockerbie bombing was a closed case until I started asking questions

BBC News Sun, 26 Jul 2026 08:48:18 GMT

I was only a year old when the UK's deadliest terror attack shocked the world.

In December 1988, Pan Am flight 103 exploded - killing all 259 people on board as well as 11 on the ground in the Scottish town of Lockerbie.

I was a teenager by the time Libyan intelligence officer Abdelbaset al-Megrahi was convicted of the bombing in 2001 and, when he later died, I thought that was largely the end of the story.

It wasn't.

The case still rumbles on and, later this year, a man suspected of making the bomb which blew up the plane, Abu Agila Masud, goes on trial in Washington DC.

As part of a Radio 4 Intrigue podcast series, I had an opportunity to delve into this complex case with fresh eyes.

The deeper I dug, the more complicated Lockerbie became and there have been times that I don't know what to believe.

Jim Swire, on the other hand, is sure what he believes - and it is not the official story.

His daughter Flora died in the bombing, but he is convinced that whoever killed her got away with mass murder.

Swire believes Megrahi is innocent, even befriending the convicted bomber up until his death in 2012.

"The burning issue was to get to the truth," he says.

"Always has been, always will be and I will not shut up about what I know to be true."

Swire's doggedness has made him a prominent voice but most of the Lockerbie victims' families don't agree that Megrahi's conviction was a miscarriage of justice - and the bomber’s own appeals against the verdict either failed or were abandoned.

For Swire, the simplest explanation is that Iran was behind the attack - not Libya.

The Lockerbie bombing came five months after 290 people were killed when an Iranian commercial airliner was shot down by a US battleship.

Iran swore revenge and months later Pan Am flight 103 exploded on its way to New York.

And there's more.

Iran - much like they do now - used proxy militant groups to pursue their ends.

Before the Lockerbie bombing, a militant cell based in Frankfurt, part of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine - General Command (PFLP-GC), was foiled by German police.

Police arrested suspects and seized explosive devices, concealed in radio cassette players, that were designed to trigger at altitude.

The bomb that brought down Pan Am 103 was in a radio cassette player hidden inside a samsonite briefcase.

Because of this, Swire believes the device that brought down Pan Am 103 was loaded at Frankfurt, and not Malta as the court had concluded.

And, for Swire, this is only the tip of the iceberg.

He also questions much of the evidence presented at the 2001 trial, discredits witnesses, and is extremely suspicious of the involvement of intelligence agencies - like MI5, MI6 and the CIA - in the aftermath of the bombing.

Combine these suspicions with his all-consuming grief and you can see why Swire is such a force to be reckoned with on his quest for a truth he believes has been denied to him.

"Discovering the truth became my way of handling the consequences of the grief reaction," Swire says.

"And it was very tough for other people to understand that but that's just the way I'm made, I suppose."

Dick Marquise, who led the FBI's Lockerbie task force, says that in the early days of the case he too believed the PFLP-GC were the "number one suspect", but years of investigation found nothing to prove it.

"There was not one shred of evidence that could be taken to court and get a conviction," he says. "You couldn't do it. There was nothing."

However, there are others, besides Swire, who still question the "official narrative" - including former CIA agent John Holt who also believes Iran was behind the bombing.

Holt worked with Libyan intelligence assets in the 1980s and was the handler of double agent Abdul Majid Giaka, whose information became central to the investigation into the Lockerbie bombing.

Holt now believes Giaka was a "BS artist" who was out for money and was feeding the CIA fake stories to get paid.

"I didn't think much of him at all," he says.

"He gave us some little tidbits about what was going on, but he never knew anything about the Pan Am bombing. And he knew a lot about Megrahi," Holt says.

Holt believes the fact the CIA bankrolled Giaka devalues him as an informant.

"It makes it easier for somebody to say whatever the person who's giving them money wants them to say," Holt says.

I managed to get a hold of the CIA papers - known as cables - from the time, which showed what Giaka had told the Americans.

The cables date back to the months before Lockerbie and include notes of conversations between Giaka and Holt and two earlier CIA handlers.

Within the cables, Giaka places Megrahi in Malta - where the bomb was said to have been planted - at a key time in the Lockerbie plot.

Megrahi is also said to have visited a Maltese clothes shop, buying shirts and baby grows - which were placed in the suitcase with the bomb and later found at the plane crash site.

Giaka had even talked to the CIA about eight kilos of orange-coloured explosives stored at the Malta airport offices. Semtex, the explosive used in Lockerbie, is orange.

In the 2001 trial, Giaka was to be a "key" witness in the prosecution's case but the four judges de­scribed some of his evidence as "at best grossly ex­ag­ger­ated and at worst sim­ply un­true".

Decades on from Megrahi's conviction, new intelligence documents have been recovered allegedly from the heart of Libyan intelligence.

They are believed to have come from Libyan leader Colonel Gaddafi's notorious intelligence network run by his spy chief Abdullah Senussi.

These leaked Libyan intelligence documents contain information that could potentially put an end to the doubt, theories and countertheories that have tied so many, including me, in knots.

The original 'Senussi Files', as they are now known, were shown to French journalists who later published a book, The Murderer Who Must Be Saved.

I travelled to Paris to meet one of the authors, investigative journalist Vincent Nouzille.

He brought piles of documents, enough to cover the whole bed and the hotel room desk.

You can tell he loves his work and despite having pored over these documents for years, he's still awestruck by their content.

Some of the Senussi files date back to autumn 1988, in the months before Lockerbie, and contain documents apparently detailing plans to target aircraft on multi-stop flights using a 11-hour long-delay timer bomb concealed in luggage much like the Lockerbie bombing.

It even mentions tests on concealing a device inside a tape recorder.

As we go through each document, my head is spinning.

There are references to dry runs, apparent weaknesses in airport security, and enough detail about the movements of Megrahi and others for Nouzille to crosscheck dates and places against other sources.

Nouzille says he spent three years carefully verifying everything in the files.

He shows me another file which details the apparent movements of Megrahi and Masud, coming in and out of Malta.

This account lines up with the information provided in the CIA cables from the previously discredited Giaka.

"We know from the CIA cables that Giaka reported the same people, the same dates, the same false passport, at the same date," Nouzille says.

"So two sources, independent, which match."

The Senussi Files seem to corroborate several details first mentioned in the cables, including the presence of semtex at Luqa Airport in Malta.

Nouzille shows me a translated document, signed by Megrahi, dated January 87, which mentions "10 kilos of explosive material" stored at the airport by Lamin Khalif Fhimah, the man who stood trial alongside Megrahi in 2001 but was acquitted.

I tried to contact Fhimah via his trial lawyer to put these allegations to him, but I was unable to reach him.

Nouzille concedes that these documents are not "final proof" that Libya was targeting Pan Am 103 flight, but he believes this is evidence of their modus operandi.

"We have a preparation of a multi-stop flight and a suitcase - and after 11 hours the bomb will explode," Nouzille says.

The Senussi Files that Nouzille has are copies, not originals, so they cannot be forensically tested.

It remains to be seen whether they will be admissible in the upcoming trial.

If they're authentic, these files may prove once and for all that Megrahi was guilty.

As Nouzille packed away the documents, I thought of Jim Swire and what this could all mean for him.

He's devoted his life to this case - even befriending Megrahi during his quest to find answers.

However, despite the years spent by Nouzille to authenticate the documents, the Senussi Files have failed to convince him that Libya was responsible.

Swire says: "I don't think that you should, with your eyes open, go into believing that any documents, however perfect they may seem to be, are genuine which prove conveniently that this was a Libyan job."

He said the CIA had the ability to forge any documents they wanted.

Despite several delays, Masud is due to go on trial in August this year.

Whether this will be pushed back again remains to be seen.

It's very likely that historical evidence from the original Lockerbie trial will be brought under the microscope once again - opening up old wounds and catalysing a new era of questioning.

Or, if admissible and verified, the Senussi Files might prove once and for all what Dick Marquise and other investigators have been saying all along.

He's skydived, eaten raw fish eyes on I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! and now Aitch has reached new heights - literally - by climbing Mount Kilimanjaro.

The Manchester rapper has been pursuing some of these tasks to raise awareness and money for the Down's Syndrome Association in honour of his younger sister Gracie, who has the condition.

Aitch tells BBC Newsbeat the 16-year-old is an "absolute legend in the streets of Manchester" and beyond.

"Everyone loves her. She's just a big bottle of light in every room," he says.

"She's everyone's best friend and she's just got such a positive outlook on the world.

"I just feel like everyone should be more like her."

The musician's journey up Kilimanjaro has been captured in an upcoming Netflix documentary, Aitch: Don't Be Afraid.

But he says the whole point of it was to share how having someone in his life with Down's syndrome is "one of the best things in the world".

However, the 26-year-old admits he does feel "a little bit of pressure" to up the scale and fundraising targets of his challenges.

"You've just got to think about the end goal, which is trying to raise the most money and make the most difference to what's going on," he says.

He has "smashed" his target this time by bringing in more than £160,000 so far from his climb of the highest peak in Africa.

The rapper says he was able to handle the altitude and physical elements of the hike, which others in his group struggled with.

But the "big mental challenge" was the biggest obstacle for him, he says.

Between the early mornings, late nights and the change of climate from rainforest conditions one minute to a blizzard the next, Aitch says it was "just all a lot".

He confesses the group would probably have turned around if they hadn't been doing the climb for "such a good cause".

Down's syndrome is when you're born with an extra chromosome - and people with the condition are likely to have some level of learning disability.

Aitch's fundraising efforts have been inspired by Gracie, who was also the subject of My G, a viral song he released in 2022.

He thinks it was so popular because it showed the bond between the siblings.

"People love genuine things," he says.

"And that relationship there between me and my sister, both of my sisters, is just undeniable. Do you know what I'm saying? So I feel like that's why people loved it."

Having grown up as a sibling carer, Aitch has faced challenges, and seen Gracie overcome obstacles.

Reflecting on how he would advise others in his position who are struggling, he says "you've got to see the blessing in it every time".

"I suppose if you ask yourself the question, 'would you change it for the world?', there's probably not a chance," he says.

"So it's always going to be a bit of a challenge, but sometimes you've got to just take it on the chin, keep it stepping and it'll all be all right."

He also feels there is "always more that can be done" to support young carers and improve understanding around various conditions and learning disabilities.

"Where I stand, I'm trying to do what I do to raise awareness," he says.

"And hopefully that brings people in.

"Hopefully that makes people want to get a little bit more involved in the whole thing and just spread more awareness than ever."

Andy Burnham says he would be prepared to call out Donald Trump to defend Britain's "national interest before anything else" if it is the right thing to do, in his first major interview as prime minister.

Speaking exclusively to the BBC, Burnham said he had had a good first exchange with Trump, finding him to be "really warm".

But asked twice if he would trust the US president, he did not say, answering, "it's a changing world isn't it, and you just obviously have to call things as they develop".

In the interview, to be broadcast in full on Monday, he said: "I can't at any point say that I won't take a different opinion from him [Trump], that I will need to voice a different idea that is right for Britain."

Burnham said: "My strength is remaining close to people, close to the public, that will not change as prime minister."

Asked if he would call out Trump if it was the right thing, he said, "of course", going on to say: "You have to defend your own national interest before anything else. That's what you're required to do if you're to do this job properly."

Burnham also said he had had "concern" about the president starting the conflict with Iran, and he "wouldn't hold back from saying what I think is right".

Responding to Burnham's comments, Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said: "Clearly, the US is a long standing ally. We need to have good relations with them but if they do something we disagree with, we should honestly say so."

The prime minister would not commit to a date when the government would spend 3% of GDP on defence. His Chancellor John Healey resigned from the previous government saying that unless a commitment was made to spend that amount by 2030, the country would not be safe.

But Burnham said: "I appointed my new chancellor very aware of what he had said about the critical importance of defence spending and the position that he had taken about that.

"The first challenge facing us both is to ensure that the defence investment plan is fully funded and that's the thing that's right in front of us and we need to work that through as we go towards the budget later this year."

Asked again specifically about the commitment to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP, he said: "We've got to work out the way of doing that."

Burnham, for the first time, explicitly dismissed the idea of an early general election before 2029, saying: "I'm going to rule it out... I don't think people want it." He said his focus instead was on "getting the country back where it should be".

Philp said the Conservatives were ready to fight an election whenever it happens.

"It pretty clear to me we are back in business and that the polls suggest that we are pretty much neck and neck with other parties" he said.

Primark's new 'supermarket tactic' to woo customers in online price war

BBC News Sun, 26 Jul 2026 00:17:50 GMT

It is something I keep hearing shoppers say when I ask them whether they shop at the fast-fashion giant.

"It's definitely got more expensive," says 19-year-old student Eshal Malik as she browses the jewellery at Primark with a friend.

But that might be about to change. Primark said on Monday that it was lowering prices on hundreds of clothing items, including jeans, jumpers and socks.

"It's the kind of headline you'd expect from M&S or Next," says retail analyst Natalie Berg, explaining that price cuts like this from such a low-cost retailer are surprising.

"You don't want to join a race to the bottom," she says. "But when Shein is selling dresses for £3, you've got to respond, right?"

Primark, which has more than 190 UK stores, has been experiencing a drop in like-for-like sales, a key measure in the retail industry.

Increases to the price of fabric, minimum wages, shipping and energy costs and a focus on higher standards overall has contributed to the rising price of clothes for the likes of Primark in recent years.

The announcement of price cuts comes ahead of parent company Associated British Foods' plan to spin off the business onto the London stock market next year.

The level of competition among fashion retailers has "evolved dramatically" over the past few years, and Chinese online marketplaces Shein and Temu are now competing for Primark's customers, says Berg.

But there is also competition from other online retailers like TikTok Shop and Vinted, she says.

By slashing prices on some core items, Primark is likely hoping to woo shoppers with low-cost staples, in the same way that supermarkets attract customers with cheap milk and bananas, Berg says.

When Tasneem Jafar wants to buy new clothes, the first place she looks is Primark.

The 32-year-old from Salford has been shopping at the fashion retailer since she was 16, picking up jeans, T-shirts and beauty products.

But for the past few years, Tasneem has also been buying clothes from Temu.

Roughly every six weeks, she orders three or four new pieces of clothing from the retailer, she says.

For student Eshal, part of the reason Primark feels more expensive is because she knows how low prices are at Shein. She says she buys going-out tops for less than £10.

Temu and Shein have been able to undercut traditional retailers like Primark because they do not pay for physical locations, most of their packages are exempt from import duties – though this exemption is set to end in October 2028 - and they have an efficient operating model that leaves them with little unsold stock, says Berg.

Currently low Shein prices are seen as the new baseline, Berg says. And they are luring in younger shoppers.

According to Mintel research from July 2025, 32% of women aged 16-34 who buy clothes online said they had shopped at Shein during the previous year.

Low prices, abundant discount codes and seemingly endless pages of products all feed into its attraction.

Primark, in contrast, has a click and collect service but does not offer delivery - a decision it has previously said was a "deliberate choice to streamline operations and pass the savings directly to customers".

Fast fashion is a term coined to describe the rapid turnover of fashion trends with cheap, mass-produced clothing. The practice has an environmental impact, using a lot of natural resources and creating greenhouse gases which are responsible for climate change.

Overall, the fashion industry is responsible for around 8% of global emissions, according to the United Nations, which is more than aviation and shipping combined.

Critics of Shein have called for a boycott of the global behemoth over the environmental impact of fast fashion, working conditions in its Chinese factories, and the sale of childlike sex dolls on its website.

Allegations surrounding the sale of the dolls first came to light from France's anti-fraud office in November 2025. Shein at the time promised to co-operate fully.

Some shoppers think better value for money can be found elsewhere on the High Street.

Isobel Guffick, 30, from Staffordshire, feels Sainsbury's Tu range has greater quality clothes for similar prices. It is "really good for basics", she says.

To save money, she also buys clothes secondhand where possible, from charity shops, car boot sales and sites like Vinted.

She visits charity shops every week and loves the "treasure hunt" feel of finding a bargain.

As well as lowering prices, Primark says it is making improvements to the quality, fit and style of clothes.

The cost-of-living crisis is also affecting how much people spend on clothes, says Mintel analyst Bridget McCusker.

About a third of clothing shoppers say they have bought clothes less frequently compared with the previous 12 months, according to a Mintel survey.

Shoppers are more focused on getting value from their purchases, such as thinking about cost per wear, McCusker says. In Primark's latest trading update, it referred to a "challenging consumer environment".

Getting a couple of pounds off a jumper or a pair of jeans might not seem like a lot to a customer, but for a shop with tight margins like Primark, how might this affect the business?

"Our business model and focus on buying at scale and keeping costs low helps us to offer the prices we do, but we don't compromise on quality or ethics to do that," a Primark spokesperson told BBC News.

In its latest annual report, it said that about 85% of its products are £10 or less.

Crucially, the new lower prices do not cover everything Primark sells. McCusker describes the price reductions as a marketing exercise designed to bring in more shoppers - and says that even if they are drawn in by the lower prices of jeans or jumpers, they'll probably end up putting other items in their basket, too.

"Primark is known for that impulse nature," she explains.

One big issue for some fashion retailers is having big piles of leftover stock that has to be discounted heavily so they can shift it. Primark will be expecting that the price changes "will help them shift stock, meaning they don't have to discount too much any further," says AJ Bell analyst Russ Mould.

Ultimately analysts think Primark's new pricing is in response to a highly competitive retail environment.

"When it comes to staying relevant to customers today, you have to offer value for money," Berg says.

"Especially if you are meant to be the value fashion retailer in the UK, you have to deliver on that promise."

What Love Island tells us about the changing face of dating

BBC News Sat, 25 Jul 2026 23:31:49 GMT

On the fourth series of Love Island UK in 2018, Megan Barton-Hanson pulled fellow Islander, Wes Nelson, for a chat.

Just moments earlier, she had ended her relationship with Eyal Booker after admitting the pair had little more than physical chemistry. Now, sitting opposite Wes, who had been coupled up with Laura Anderson since the start of the competition, she decided not to wait for him to make the first move.

"I think it's pretty obvious that I do really fancy you," she told him. "And I just felt like, if I didn't say something, I'd regret it massively."

By the end of the episode, viewers had a new nickname for her: "Muggy Megan". Critics accused her of moving too quickly between relationships and breaking "girl code". Others admired her honesty.

At the time, Barton-Hanson argued that she had been treated differently to her male counterparts. "People definitely do give girls a harder time than men… It's sexist."

But eight years later, scenes like Barton-Hanson's no longer feel quite so out of the ordinary. Until this series, the opening coupling had always seen the men choose first. This year, the show's rules were changed, with the women making the first choice.

Alicia Denby, a sociologist at Manchester Metropolitan University, argues the show's tweak is reflective of a broader societal change where "women may now be more likely to approach someone first".

At its peak, around five million people tuned in to Love Island every night. Live audiences are not what they were, but it remains ITV's biggest programme among 16 to 34-year-olds.

For Prof Kitty Nichols, who researches relationships and popular culture at the University of Sheffield, Love Island has become "an important cultural vehicle" allowing us to "reflect on the dating scene and culture at the moment".

Former PE teacher Kai Fagan met his now wife, Sanam Harrinanan, when he won the 2023 series, an experience he says transformed his life.

"My life ever since then has been a fairytale. The whole show is about love. That's the point of it. You're put in a situation to fall in love."

For Fagan, the show delivered exactly what it promised: love. Meanwhile, for thousands watching at home, it has become a window into how modern relationships are formed, tested and understood.

As another series of Love Island approaches its end, what do Love Island's changing dynamics tell us about dating culture beyond the villa? And does women making the first move really represent genuine progress towards equality?

For much of the 20th Century, heterosexual dating followed a script that would have felt familiar to the characters in Pride and Prejudice. Men were largely expected to make the first move. They asked women out, paid for dates and, in many cases, took the lead in deciding when the relationship moved forward.

By the 1960s, the women's liberation movement began challenging many of those norms. As Aretha Franklin's Respect became an anthem for a generation demanding greater equality, the widespread availability of contraception changed the ideas about sex. Then with the rise of online dating in the 2000s, millions of people began meeting through websites and, later, dating apps.

But whether these changes have really done anything to shift gender expectations is unclear.

As recently as 2021, sociologist Ellen Lamont reviewed more than 100 studies on heterosexual dating and found traditional dating scripts still remained, with men still expected to make the first move.

For cultural commentator Coco, who goes by her first name and has amassed more than 100,000 followers on TikTok analysing Love Island, this reflects an important distinction.

She argues women aren't replacing men as the pursuers, they simply have greater freedom to act on what they want.

"Women haven't flipped the roles," she says. "Women have just been allowed to exist." She believes women now have "more choice, freedom and opportunity than we've ever had in history".

But even if women are becoming more comfortable making the first move, Denby argues that this does not mean gendered power relations have disappeared.

She argues that women on Love Island are often praised for their patience and loyalty while male contestants explore connections with other contestants. But she says when women take a more active role in pursuing relationships, they are judged differently.

"It's almost as if women are praised for being submissive in the villa, because when they do take on more of an active or expressive role, they are criticised for it."

On this year's Love Island, in a move that may have reflected the growing trend of women on the show taking the lead, Elicia Bailey took both Aidan Murphy and Finley Maddock to the Hideaway, the villa's private romantic room.

But she faced criticism for it and Denby points to what she sees as a sexual double standard around women's sexuality. Another female contestant on this year's show, Priya Jaswal, was labelled a "sexual person" by a male contestant and accused of "pouncing" on Murphy, comments that Denby argues, suggest "women are judged for taking an active role" in dating.

Nichols sees similar patterns.

She believes Love Island has what she describes as "pockets of diversity" and "little moments of change", where contestants challenge conventional gender roles.

Yet she argues those moments are often temporary, with Islanders reverting "back to the expected gender roles".

According to Nichols, double standards persist. "If a woman behaves in the same way that a man behaves, they get reprimanded."

That reaction can be seen in the programme's history.

For example, Ekin-Su Cülcüloğlu's pursuit of Jay Younger divided viewers during the 2022 series. Some accused her of betraying Davide Sanclimenti, who she later won the show with, while others praised her confidence.

For Nichols, those responses reveal something about British attitudes to dating.

"I think audience members receive more positively men diverging from their expected roles," she says.

She said it may be because viewers "don't anticipate" behaviour like that, but adds that, "sometimes women doing so is sort of seen less positively."

For Tareq Ferguson, a long-time Love Island viewer and TikTok commentator with more than 50,000 followers, one of the biggest changes in recent series has been watching male contestants become more passive.

"The men want to be passenger princesses," he says. "They want to sit back, kick up their feet, while the women do the grafting and do the work."

On this year's show, Lorenzo Alessi was reluctant to make Julia Majchrzak a morning coffee, something many contestants see as an act of care for the person they're coupled up with. It become a flashpoint on the show and sparked debate among viewers.

For Ferguson, moments like those reflect a wider shift in modern dating, with some men appearing increasingly hesitant to take the lead.

But some research suggest that men's reluctance may stem less from disinterest and more from uncertainty about how to navigate dating today.

In a recent Cosmopolitan survey, men said online dating had made them feel judged on their appearance. Ohers said repeated rejection and lack of matches had damaged their confidence.

Research like this echoes what Coco believes is happening both inside and outside the villa.

"Society has rightly expanded what's possible for women," she says. "But we haven't spent the same amount of time helping young men understand what their role looks like in this landscape. The cultural conversation hasn't kept pace with the social change."

She also believes online conversations have contributed to that uncertainty.

"I think the manosphere content we're seeing has done something to women," she says. "It's put their guard up."

But she is keen to stress that does not mean there are "no good men out there".

Instead, she believes men seem to be taking a more cautious approach to dating as expectations around relationships continue to change. "They don't want to be perceived as a creep. They don't want to be seen as trying too hard in front of their peers. They want to come across as relaxed and cool."

So does Love Island simply mirror the UK's evolving dating culture or actively shape it?

For Prof Nichols, the two are closely connected. She believes the programme doesn't simply entertain audiences. Watched by millions each summer and discussed constantly across social media, it has become part of the conversation around modern relationships.

"I think for young people who are still the biggest viewers of Love Island, it probably creates these norms for them in terms of how they would expect to be treated or how dating functions."

Fagan believes some younger viewers take lessons from what they see on screen.

"Younger people probably get dating tips from a show like Love Island," he says.

But he adds: "In real life, you have a bit more control of how you pursue and what happens and the obstructions.

"On Love Island, you could be with someone for three weeks and then suddenly you're put into a challenge where your relationship is made vulnerable just for the entertainment of the public.

"If that's happening on the outside, you don't necessarily know about it. On the show, you have to confront it head on."

Yet despite those differences, some viewers still believe Love Island influences how people think about dating.

Ferguson believes many young people watch the programme not just as entertainment but as a reflection of what dating now looks like.

"People will look at this, especially the younger audiences, and think, 'if this is how people are being treated, then obviously I can expect this on the outside.'"

One study by researchers at Liverpool John Moores University examining Love Island and relationship education, found some young people do look to reality dating programmes for ideas about romance and relationship behaviour. But it also found most viewers described the programme as entertainment and were aware that what they watched did not necessarily reflect real life.

For Nichols, the influence is undeniable.

"It plays into features of the current dating culture, where we see this propensity towards disposability and a lack of exclusivity," she says.

"It's like a chicken and an egg. I think it normalises that massively."

Every generation has tended to challenge the dating expectations that came before it. From the move away from formal courtship to the arrival of dating apps and now a generation asking more questions about who should make the first move.

But while analysts argue that Love Island is far from a perfect mirror of society, it nonetheless operates as a cultural stage where shifting gender norms and emerging challenges are publicly rehearsed.

For Denby, that is precisely what makes the show significant.

"Recouplings, comparisons between potential partners and the idea that there is always someone better around the corner can mirror some of the less positive aspects of app-based dating culture", she says.

But she is equally clear that viewers are not watching the programme without question.

"I don't think viewers are simply passive consumers. Many people watch Love Island critically and debate issues like sexism, classism and racism, so the programme both reflects and shapes contemporary dating culture."

Pizza, pasta, potatoes, protein - how Italian children became so overweight

BBC News Sat, 25 Jul 2026 23:30:07 GMT

Daily life is not easy for Salvatore. At 17, he weighs 170kg (26st 10lb) and struggles to walk.

He can't tie his own shoelaces and his Vespa scooter strains to bear his weight - in one week, its wheels broke seven times.

"He eats constantly," says his mother Anna.

Salvatore is among a growing number of Italian children and teenagers living with obesity. The problem is particularly acute in the south: in parts of the Campania region, more than 40% of eight and nine-year-olds are overweight. The town of Ponticelli, on the outskirts of Naples, has earned the unenviable reputation as one of the world's child obesity capitals.

It is a striking development in a country long regarded as the spiritual home of the Mediterranean diet. Yet today, Italian children are among the most overweight in Europe, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

Salvatore is waiting for life-changing surgery at the Betania Hospital in Ponticelli, where Dr Sonja Chiappetta has spent 15 years treating patients with severe obesity.

Until recently, she says, most of her patients were in their fifties. "Now I see those same patients when they're teenagers, as young as 16. They are getting younger, and it's frightening."

The surgery she carries out removes up to 90% of the stomach - meaning people are unable to eat large quantities of food. Demand has risen sharply in this part of Italy.

But Salvatore has been told he cannot get the operation. His weight is so excessive it makes the surgery too dangerous.

Instead, Dr Chiappetta has prescribed him a GLP-1 weight-loss injection to reduce his appetite and help him lose enough weight for the operation.

For decades, Italy was held up as a model of healthy eating.

The Mediterranean diet - rich in vegetables, legumes, olive oil, whole grains and fish - became famous after US physiologist Ancel Keys and his wife, biochemist Margaret Keys, studied communities in southern Italy in the 1950s and linked their habits to remarkably low rates of heart disease.

Their research transformed a regional way of eating into one of the world's best-known diets; a blueprint for healthy living.

But the Italy that inspired those studies no longer exists.

"The traditional Mediterranean diet has been lost," says Doctor Valter Longo, director of the Longevity Institute at the University of Southern California. "Only 10% of Italians really follow it."

Dr Longo sums up the modern Italian diet with what he calls the "five Ps": pizza, pasta, potatoes, protein and pane - the Italian word for bread.

The transformation is visible everywhere: from supermarket shelves stocked with ultra-processed foods to pizzerias selling slices piled high with chips, sausages and fried snacks.

Doctor Roberto Berni Canani, a paediatrician and obesity specialist at the Federico II University in Naples, sees the consequences every day.

"I've treated children who are just two or three years old and already weigh 25kg," he says.

He says most parents don't recognise their children are overweight. "They come to see me because of other problems - a cough, stomach pain, diarrhoea. They don't realise their child's weight is what's causing it."

Ten-year-old Francesca has a persistent cough and struggles to swallow. Doctors suspect an inflammatory condition of the oesophagus.

She weighs 60kg (9st 6lb) - but that's not why her parents have sought medical help.

Francesca says she eats bread with Nutella for breakfast, a chocolate-filled sponge cake as a snack, pasta with lentils for lunch and usually chicken for dinner.

"But she doesn't eat vegetables," her mother, Carmen, interjects. "I put them in front of her, but she won't touch them."

Francesca's parents insist she is active. She does artistic gymnastics and Latin dance, and doesn't get tired. They have never considered her weight as a problem.

Dr Berni Canani reaches a different conclusion.

The problem, he explains, is the overall pattern rather than any single meal. Small, calorie-dense foods consumed throughout the day, sugary drinks, too few fruit and vegetables and little understanding of how these habits accumulate over time.

"This is a very good mother," he says. "A very good father. They simply don't recognise the importance of diet quality and body weight."

By the time many families arrive at his clinic, unhealthy habits have already become deeply ingrained. They begin at home and are reinforced at school.

And in Italy, encouraging children to be more active can be surprisingly difficult.

Many schools are housed in beautiful old palazzi - they were never designed with modern physical education in mind.

The Ugo Foscolo primary school is no exception. Its gym has barely enough space for a class of children to move around.

"I have one pupil I'm particularly concerned about," says Francesca Pecce, who teaches at the school. "He's 10 years old and weighs around 60 kilograms."

She has tried raising the issue with his mother.

"But she is not worried," Pecce says. "In Neapolitan culture, if a child is a little chubby with rosy cheeks, people often think they're healthy."

Schools, she believes, can help change that, especially if children "take home" lessons about healthy eating.

"Sometimes it's easier to educate the parents through their children than the other way round."

At a secondary school in Naples, students file into a classroom for a nutrition workshop run by the Valter Longo Foundation.

The programme is part of a regional initiative to tackle childhood obesity. Over the coming months, more than 17,000 students across 25 schools will take part. Families will receive support to help change eating habits at home.

But not all of the students are convinced.

Eighteen-year-old Ciro doubts that information alone will change behaviour.

"My classmates already know what's healthy," he says. "They just don't care."

Carmen, 19, is more optimistic.

"I thought it was actually really helpful because teenagers today are really big into junk food, and don't exercise as much."

She says the problem is that temptation is everywhere. Even foods traditionally associated with Italy have changed.

"When we go out for pizza, people don't just order a Margherita. They put chips, sausages and fried food on top."

Add to that the centuries-old cliches of Italian mothers and grandmothers showing their love through food, and it's a perfect storm.

Obesity is an "escalating global epidemic", says the WHO. More than one billion people worldwide are now obese, and childhood obesity has quadrupled since 1990.

In 2025, Italy became the first country to pass a national law recognising obesity as a chronic, progressive and relapsing disease.

Rather than treating obesity simply as the result of poor choices, the country's new law recognises it as a chronic disease influenced by biology, environment and social circumstances.

The Campania region has become a testing ground for putting that philosophy into practice, implementing a series of ambitious interventions - including a controversial trial of a "fast-mimicking diet".

Researchers are recruiting 300 overweight adolescents who will spend five days every three months on a controlled diet of 1,100 calories on day one and 770 calories on following four days - so restrictive it resembles a fast.

The goal is to trigger a "metabolic reset".

"Fasting, or controlled deprivation of food, is linked to a longer and healthier lifespan," says Dr Longo, who has spent three decades studying the effects of fasting.

But not all obesity specialists are persuaded that fasting is the right approach for children.

Paediatrician Berni Canani believes the evidence for fasting-mimicking diets in children is still too limited to be recommended in Italy's clinical guidelines.

He also worries restrictive diets could carry psychological risks for adolescents, whose relationship with food is still developing.

"I fear that imposing food restrictions on teenagers could increase the risk of eating disorders, anorexia and body dysmorphia," he says.

Meanwhile, Salvatore hopes to have surgery in the summer, so that, for the first time in years, he can wear a swimming costume without feeling self-conscious.

But he is not alone. Across Italy, a generation of children is growing up increasingly removed from the Mediterranean diet that once made the country famous.

Additional reporting by Bob Howard.

Another UK heatwave looms after cooler end to weekend

BBC News Sat, 25 Jul 2026 23:29:25 GMT

Another UK heatwave could be declared next week as temperatures are once again forecast to intensify across England and parts of Wales.

Following some much-needed rain in the north and north-west of the UK this weekend, temperatures will rise back to heatwave threshold levels in many locations.

Maximum temperatures are forecast to climb as high as 35C (95F) in the hottest areas.

Yellow heat health alerts have already been issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) for several regions from 9:00 BST on 28 July until 9:00 BST on 31 July.

Sunday will be a cooler day for the whole of the UK as temperatures fall widely by a couple of degrees.

A few locations will finally mark the end to their third heatwave of the year, including Usk in Monmouthshire and Exeter in Devon.

Both places are forecast to see temperatures drop beneath the heatwave threshold for the first time in 21 consecutive days.

Temperatures will largely be in the mid-20s Celsius for the south-east of the UK and in the mid-teens Celsius further north.

For many, the relief from the heat will be short-lived as high pressure is set to build close to the south of the UK next week.

This will stall rain-bearing weather fronts and any wet weather will become confined to northern and western areas - especially north-west Scotland.

In southern parts of the UK, temperatures look set to climb once again.

Tapping into the heat over the near continent, the UK is likely to enter another heatwave, with temperatures in England and Wales forecast to peak around 25-32C for much of next week.

Yellow heat health alerts will come into effect for Yorkshire and Humber, the West and East Midlands, the East of England, London, south-east and south-west, at 9:00 BST on 28 July 2026 and last until 9:00 BST on 31 July.

The UKHSA warns that heat is expected to cause minor impacts for health and social care services, with an increased risk to life for vulnerable people.

Wednesday is likely to be the hottest day

The hottest weather will initially be focused on central and eastern England by Tuesday before spreading northwards and westwards.

Scotland and Northern Ireland will remain cooler with temperatures generally in the high teens or low to mid-twenties Celsius.

Wednesday is likely to be the hottest day of the week.

East Wales and most of England could see temperatures between 30-35C.

It will also become warmer in Scotland and Northern Ireland with temperatures reaching the mid twenties.

Some computer models suggest an even more intense surge of heat could arrive by midweek.

By next weekend, the forecast suggests a return to cooler weather with Atlantic systems bringing some rain and westerly winds.

Unfortunately for southern areas, where the rain is needed most, it may remain dry.

How long the heat lasts depend on whether a southerly or westerly wind develops.

A westerly wind will bring an end to heatwave conditions, while southerly winds could signal a return to intense heat.

You can check the latest forecast for your area on the BBC Weather website and app.

Boiling Point: The Week of Extreme Heat

The last week of June 2026 saw record-breaking temperatures across parts of the UK and Europe. While some enjoyed the sunshine, the heat caused trains, schools and emergency services to buckle.
