This El Niño will be the hottest by a huge margin

New Scientist July 23, 2026

The planet-warming super El Niño now developing will almost certainly be the strongest ever, breaking the record by an unprecedented margin.

Out of hundreds of simulations by 14 forecast models, 90 per cent predict the tropical Pacific will reach a sea surface temperature anomaly that hasn’t been seen in 150 years of observations, according to the California non-profit organisation Berkeley Earth. It is expected to peak at 3.6°C above average, far above the 2.75°C record set in 2015-16.

Zeke Hausfather at Berkeley Earth says this is one of the few times a climate forecast has truly shocked him.

Advertisement

“Even the median of all the models expects we beat the record by 0.8°C,” he said at a media briefing on 23 July. “If this does end up occurring, it really would be record-shattering and unprecedented.”

El Niño happens when easterly winds weaken in the tropics, allowing water they’ve pushed into the Western Pacific Warm Pool to wash back towards the eastern Pacific. Rainfall shifts eastward, weakening easterly winds further in a self-reinforcing feedback loop. Although it’s a natural cycle, it delivers a jolt of heat on top of 1.4°C of global warming, setting off extreme weather around the world, according to Berkeley Earth.

Already, this El Niño is revving up faster than any previous event. Sea surface temperatures in the central-eastern Pacific have reached 2.1°C above average, vastly outpacing the 1.6°C increase seen at this time of year during the 1997-98 El Niño, the previous record-holder for speedy development.

Why El Niño’s impacts on the UK are hard to predict

This “explosive onset” has already put the event in very strong or “super” El Niño territory, only a month after it started. And once you consider that El Niño doesn’t peak until late autumn or winter, it really does look like the world is facing a “Godzilla” El Niño, the name given to those that increase temperatures past a rise of 3°C.

Within a few months, the huge swathe of warm water across the Pacific will heat up the rest of the world. Global temperatures in 2027 are likely to reach 1.7°C above the pre-industrial average, smashing the record set in 2024, when temperatures were 1.5°C above the average. The El Niño is coming on so fast that there’s even a chance 2026 will break that global temperature record first, as some have predicted.

As a result, the 20-year temperature average will likely exceed 1.5°C by 2029, failing the goal set by the Paris Agreement, said Robert Rohde at Berkeley Earth in the briefing.

“We’re already over 1.4°C, so there’s very little margin left,” Rhode said.

Free newsletter

Different regions will see different extreme weather. Densely populated southern China could experience heavy rainfall in the spring and summer, raising the risk of flooding on the Yangtze river, forecasters have warned. The 1997-98 super El Niño caused flooding on the Yangtze that killed more than 3000 people.

The north-eastern US tends to face drier conditions during El Niño, while the southern US gets wetter, which can unleash mudslides in places like California. Australia tends to dry out, raising the threat of bushfires like those seen during the “Black Summer” of 2018-19.

India, southern and central Africa and parts of Central and South America all face drought risks, which could push up the price of commodities like rice, coffee and chocolate even in less-exposed countries like the UK.

How extreme heat affects the body – and the best ways to cope

“We might get lucky and have smaller reduction in rainfall in Africa or India, but generally… the damages scale with the strength of the El Niño,” said Hausfather.

Strong El Niño events also cause harm to ecosystems, such as widespread coral bleaching, which is expected this year as well.

While some research suggests El Niño events are getting stronger, other studies disagree. What is clear is that the impacts will get worse as global warming accelerates.

“It’s something we need to start preparing for today and make sure we have systems in place to deal with drought conditions,” said Hausfather.

Extremely basic AI prompt cracks decades-old maths problem

New Scientist July 23, 2026

A long-standing mathematical conundrum has been solved by ChatGPT in a few hours, with only a few simple prompts.

The Dinitz-Garg-Goemans conjecture is a 30-year-old question in graph theory, but a counterexample posted on X by Dmitry Rybin, co-founder at AI start-up Autokernel, has shown that it is false.

A golden age of maths is dawning and mathematicians are freaking out

Rybin entered just four prompts into ChatGPT 5.6 Pro: an initial one instructing the AI to “do a breakthrough and find a structured counterexample”, followed by three others simply urging it to continue searching. All four prompts added up to fewer than 60 words, and the AI took a total of 5.5 hours to crack the problem.

Advertisement

Graph theory is the study of networks made up of nodes, or vertices. The Dinitz-Garg-Goemans conjecture can be thought of as a logistical challenge: imagine shipments from a warehouse to multiple locations can be split into much smaller deliveries that can be sent on different routes. The conjecture states that this scenario can be converted into another where shipments cannot be split, and that the total cost of shipping will not increase.

Rybin didn’t respond to a request for comment, but said on X: “I know counterexamples to old conjectures are becoming a meme at this point. But I really cared about this problem and spent many weeks thinking about it.”

Chris Bowman-Scargill at the University of York, UK, says there’s a running joke in mathematics that every conjecture in graph theory is false, just as the Dinitz-Garg-Goemans conjecture has now been proved to be.

“In fields like number theory or algebra, patterns that hold for small rank [simple situations] often hold for a long time,” says Bownman-Scargill. “Whereas in graph theory, structural behaviour can shift dramatically once you add just one or two vertices… which is how these conjectures continue to be made. You can see how people miss these things.”

AI has made rapid advances in mathematics in recent months. In May, an OpenAI model cracked a decades-old conjecture by Paul Erdős, causing a stir in mathematical circles. Earlier this week, an AI found a counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture, which had stood for nearly a century. Today, other AI users claim to have solved a Graffiti conjecture and a second graph theory problem. A website has even sprung up to catalogue the AI findings and list them by the model that was used.

Mathematics is undergoing the biggest change in its history

Abhishek Saha at Queen Mary University of London says current AI models seem particularly well-suited to problems like the Dinitz-Garg-Goemans conjecture, but there are limits to what is currently possible – and the problems solved by AI so far are of limited complexity.

“AI is really good, and at least at some mathematical tasks, already superhuman,” says Saha. “There is a fair bit of low-hanging fruit out there. Some conjectures can now be proved or disproved by AI with very little human input; the main challenge is simply pointing the system in the right direction. On the other hand, I don’t think AI is yet at a place where it can build the theory needed to prove some of the deepest open conjectures people care about.”

But there are signs that AI is here to stay and will become a vital tool for mathematicians. Alexander Yong at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign says AI’s growing role in mathematics will empower researchers to discard dead ends and instead push in promising directions.

“Counterexamples to old conjectures are never quite as impressive as finding a sequence of interlocking arguments that constitute a proof,” says Yong. “However, I’d expect that AI will soon prove many conjectures by a combination of their inherent superhuman energy in knowing the literature and trying many things at a prompt. Those conjectures that survive AI scrutiny will be the genuine goals for human innovation.”

Damage to the dishes in Spain could be disastrous for NASA. The DSN is already drastically oversubscribed, which slows down the process of getting commands to spacecraft and data back down from them. If the oversubscription gets severe enough, it’s possible that some data will never make it back to Earth.

The other problem comes from the way the three stations of the DSN are set up. “These stations are designed to cover about a third of the sky, such that at any given time we can use two to track and communicate with spacecraft way out beyond Earth’s orbit,” says Paul Byrne at Washington University in Missouri. “As a function of geometry, there will now be times of the day when certain spacecraft are out of touch when they otherwise wouldn’t have been.” That is particularly a problem for extremely distant spacecraft, such as Voyager 1 and 2.

A parasitic fungus that grows on caterpillars has been turned into a dress designed to be able to repair itself if damaged.

In the video game and TV series The Last of Us, Cordyceps fungi evolve to infect humans and turn them into zombies, but in reality they are harmless to humans.

How our ancestors used mushrooms to change the course of human history

Using the fungus Cordyceps militaris as a base, Ke Li at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and her colleagues created a living textile that can be “programmed” with different properties using various microbial components.

Advertisement

It feels denser and less fibrous than cotton, says Li, and is closer to a soft, non-woven sheet or a flexible leather-like material.

“After washing and processing, the material does not have a strong mushroom-like smell,” she says. “A slight biological or fermentation-related odour may be detectable in freshly prepared samples, but this can be greatly reduced through cleaning, drying and post-treatment.”

Free newsletter

The fungus is made up of thin filaments known as hyphae. Li and her colleagues first grew the fungus as small, spherical pellets in liquid culture, then washed them and placed them into moulds where they formed a sheet.

To prevent the resulting textile from becoming brittle, it was soaked in glycerol, which acts as a “plasticiser”, making the naturally rigid fungal structure softer and more flexible.

“We do not use a conventional fabric, polymer mesh or other external supporting scaffold,” says Li. “The Cordyceps militaris mycelial pellets themselves serve as the structural building blocks, and their intertwined hyphae form a continuous, self-supporting sheet.”

To add colour to the material, the team introduced yeast cells that were engineered to produce orange, blue and purple pigments. “These cells can be applied to the fungal textile so that the colour is generated biologically, rather than through conventional synthetic dyes,” says Li.

The researchers also showed they could change the properties of the textile by adding other fungi, for example making it clean itself by repelling water droplets. For UV protection, they added Aspergillus niger, a mould that commonly grows on fruit and vegetables. This forms a dark layer on the surface of the material containing melanin pigment, which absorbs ultraviolet radiation.

How our ancestors invented clothing and transformed it into fashion

If the textile is damaged, then fresh, wet fungal pellets can be applied to the area that needs repair and the fungus simply grows over the breach.

Under dry conditions, most biological activity is greatly reduced, and the cells may remain inactive or dormant, says Li.

But under humid conditions with nutrients present, some cells can become active again. This latent biological capacity is what enables functions such as regrowth and repair, and also means that the material is readily biodegradable, showing near-complete visible degradation in soil after just over 40 days.

Li and her colleagues created a dress out of their fungal material, but so far no one has worn it. “We’ve treated it as a rather precious display piece, and it was made in a small size,” she says. “Perhaps next time we should find a few petite and adventurous volunteers to try it on and see how it looks in motion.”

Justin Beardsley at the University of Sydney, Australia, says the biodegradability of the dress is amazing compared with what we currently have in terms of getting rid of waste from fast fashion.

But that is also a drawback because you don’t really want to be wearing something that is too easily biodegradable, as “it’ll break down while you’re wearing it”, he says.

As the textile is alive, Beardsley envisages one day being able to change its qualities in real time. “If there was some way that you can make it water-repellent for a while, becoming less breathable during rain, that would be fantastic, and then you can revert to the more breathable, less water-repellent version afterward,” he says.

Earth is heating up faster than at any time in its history

New Scientist July 24, 2026

As Europe bakes in what could be its hottest and driest summer on record, the rapid transformation of our climate is harder than ever to ignore. But how much hotter will it get, and what will that mean for life on Earth?

To get a picture of our future, we can either use computer models or look to episodes of rapid climate change in the geological record. While models are invaluable in terms of tracking where our world may be heading, peering back into deep time provides unrivalled information about cause and effect; about how the climate has changed in the past and what the consequences were. There is no guesswork involved, as the evidence is all laid out for us in the sediments and rocks, in the ice sheets and in the remains of ancient life.

Europe’s heatwave is the hottest and most humid ever

Looking back in time also helps us to put human-caused global heating in context by making comparisons with past episodes of rapid temperature increase, and when we do this, the news isn’t good. It isn’t so much the degree of heat that is the issue – our world has been much hotter than it is today for much of its 4.6-billion-year history – but the speed of change.

Advertisement

Perhaps barring the immediate aftermath of the dinosaur-obliterating asteroid impact 66 million years ago, atmospheric carbon dioxide levels have never risen as quickly as they have in the last couple of centuries. Even worse, nowhere in the geological record is there evidence for the average temperature of our world climbing as quickly as it is now. This means 10 times faster than during the Palaeocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum, which marked extreme hothouse conditions 56 million years ago, and at least 20 times faster than at the end of the last glacial period.

Judicious analysis of past climates also permits us to recognise potential analogues for where our world is heading in the decades and centuries to come. Over the last 50 million years or so, the planet’s climate has followed a broadly cooling trend, which we are now rapidly rewinding – a process, if you like, of prehistorification. Deciding how far back we will end up is still within our gift, but it is a given that our grandchildren will grow up in a climate different to any experienced during the tenure of human civilisation.

Free newsletter

Modelling studies suggest that if – and it’s still a big if – emissions peak by 2040 and then fall quickly, we will rewind the climate clock 3 million years and bequeath to our descendants a Late Pliocene climate. Then, atmospheric CO2 levels were much lower than today, at 330 to 400 parts per million (ppm), but the temperature was between 2.5ºC and 4ºC above the pre-industrial average, and sea level 15 to 25 metres higher. Pliocene conditions could start to appear in the continental heartlands as soon as the 2030s and spread out from there.

If we fail to rein in emissions fast enough, or if natural feedback effects drive more heating than expected, then a further rewinding of the climate clock back to the Miocene becomes more likely; to a time 15 million to 17 million years ago, when CO2 concentrations, at 400 to 600 ppm, were a bit lower to moderately higher than they are today. At 6ºC to 8ºC above the 1800s, however, the temperature was far higher than expected for such CO2 levels, suggesting the involvement of other heating factors that we don’t yet fully understand. Sea level was maybe 50 metres higher than it is today.

Collapse of AMOC ocean current may already be locked in

But this may not be the end of it. The current high rate of heating documented by satellite observations and borne out by Earth’s rapidly escalating energy imbalance implies that rewinding the climate clock back fully 50 million years remains within the bounds of possibility, eventually reprising the blistering heat of the early Eocene hothouse. Such conditions would make most of our world uninhabitable for humans, and severely test the capacity of our species to prevail.

As the Persian poet and mathematician Omar Khayyam observed almost 1000 years ago: “When I want to understand what is happening today, or try to decide what will happen tomorrow, I look back.” They are words that serve us well as we contemplate our future climate, and that we ignore at our peril.

Bill McGuire is professor emeritus of geophysical and climate hazards at University College London. His book, The Fate of the World: A history and future of the climate crisis, is published by HarperNorth.

But fasting can also involve eating no, or very little, food for a single, continuous stretch of time, which is sometimes done for religious reasons.

There are only a few anti-ageing supplements that actually work

Focusing on this type of fasting, Steve Horvath at the University of California, Los Angeles, and his colleagues recruited 32 volunteers with no known health conditions, who consumed just 200 to 250 calories a day in the form of fruit juice, vegetable broths and honey for 12 days. “This is not something to try at home,” says Horvath. “It was a medically supervised inpatient programme at a specialist clinic, with clinical monitoring throughout.”

Advertisement

These calories were consumed in three windows: 7am to 9am, 11.30am to 1pm and 6.30pm to 8pm. This put the participants – who were aged between 25 and 72 – in a fasting metabolic state, says team member Robin Mesnage at King’s College London, which occurs when the body shifts from burning energy from food to energy stored in the body.

The team used 12 different epigenetic clocks to estimate and track the volunteers’ biological ages over the course of the study. These mostly work by looking at patterns of chemical tags on DNA, which change in predictable ways with age, but can also be altered by our lifestyle, such as how much we exercise.

Free newsletter

The clocks varied in their responses to the fast. Some ticked upwards to an older age, suggesting that the extreme fast put negative stress on the body. But one clock, which was built to detect changes in body mass index, went down.

Incongruous results are a known issue between different epigenetic clocks. But one finding was fairly consistent: the participants who were generally deemed to have a young biological age, relative to their chronological age, at the start of the study lost more weight than those who were biologically older.

The researchers weren’t expecting this result, according to Hovarth. “Honestly, we don’t know the mechanism,” he says. But he thinks the most likely explanation is that biologically younger people have better metabolic adaptability, which means they can swiftly switch from using food for energy to stored fat when calories are scarce.

This is plausible, because biologically younger people tend to have more efficient mitochondria, which leads to faster switching to fat burning, says Paulina Correa-Burrows at the University of Chile.

A clinical trial to reverse age-related vision conditions using stem cell treatment could finally deliver on the promise of a major discovery in ageing and regeneration made 20 years ago, says columnist Graham Lawton

Biologically younger people may also have better pathways for sensing nutrients in cells, which could also enable more efficient switching between fuel sources to burn fat. But Correa-Burrows cautions that the group of volunteers was small, so the results are inconclusive.

Horvath now wants to see investigations into whether biologically younger people also lose more weight under less restrictive diets. “A 12-day medically supervised fast is not a long-term diet and it isn’t meant to be one,” he says.

In the meantime, a healthy lifestyle can help lower our biological age. “The habits with the strongest evidence for healthy epigenetic aging are the familiar ones: do not smoke, [do] physical exercise, keep a healthy body weight and maintain good relationships,” says Hovarth.

Do not change your diet without first speaking to a doctor.

10 of the best pictures of solar eclipses throughout history

New Scientist July 24, 2026

A total eclipse occurs somewhere in the world about once every 18 months on average, and that has been the case for all of human history. For millennia, humans have been documenting their views as the moon moved between Earth and the sun, blocking out the sun’s light and revealing its swirling outer layers.

The earliest confirmed written record of a solar eclipse comes from the 13th century BC, when scribes in China wrote that the sun had been “eaten”. Scientific and religious texts continued to document eclipses up until the present day, and researchers now use these texts to study both how eclipses have changed in the intervening centuries and how human views of them have evolved throughout time. This particular petroglyph, carved into stone by the early Pueblo people in New Mexico, is thought to represent a total solar eclipse that occurred on 11 July 1097. The swirls around its perimeter bear a resemblance to the corona of the sun, which is only visible when the moon hides the rest of the solar disc.

More recent art depicts religious and scientific figures observing eclipses directly. This watercolour from the late 17th century shows a group of French missionaries observing a solar eclipse with King Narai of Siam and his court in April 1688. They can be seen using the projection method to avoid looking directly at the sun: the light passes through a telescope and projects the shape of the eclipse on a screen beneath it. This technique is still commonly used today, with pinhole cameras or even just the gaps between shadows cast by leaves on the ground.

Advertisement

Scientific sketches of eclipses proliferated as science became more of a formal, professionalised pursuit. This drawing, by astronomer José Joaquín de Ferrer, depicts an eclipse that occurred over New York on 16 June 1806. Watching this event led de Ferrer to give the outermost layer of the sun, the corona, its name. He was among the first people reported to have hypothesised that the corona must be part of the sun, not the moon, because of its incredible size – it can stretch to as much as 20 times the width of the main disc of the sun, as he sketched here.

The first photograph of a total solar eclipse with enough detail on the corona to be scientifically useful was taken on 28 July 1851 by Julius Berkowski at the Royal Observatory in Königsberg, Prussia. With help from the astronomers at the observatory, he attached a small telescope to a device called a heliometer, a specialised instrument for measuring the sun. This daguerreotype was an 84-second exposure taken through the telescope. Not only is the corona visible, but several eruptions can be seen blasting from the sides of the sun over the edge of the moon.

After Berkowski’s image, the ability to take photographs of eclipses became more widespread around the world. These images were taken by William and Frederick Langenheim on 26 May 1854 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Without access to the scientific tools Berkowski used to magnify the light from the eclipse, they were forced to use small cameras to create these miniature daguerreotypes, the largest of which is just 7.2 centimetres tall and the smallest less than half that size.

The total solar eclipse that swept over parts of Africa and South America on 29 May 1919 proved to be one of the most important eclipses ever observed. This image comes from the expedition that astronomer Arthur Eddington made to the African island of Principe. He and his team photographed several stars located close to the sun to compare their apparent positions in the sky before and then during the eclipse. In this image, the stars are marked with horizontal lines. The comparison proved that the gravity of the sun bent the light coming from those stars, providing some of the first evidence for Albert Einstein’s theory of general relativity and creating a new understanding of the workings of the universe.

Eclipses became popular photographic targets for scientists and non-scientific photographers alike. This image, taken by Frederick Goetz on 24 January 1925, shows an effect called the diamond ring, or Baily’s beads. This effect occurs just at the beginning and end of totality, when the edge of the moon is nearly, but not quite, covering the entire disc of the sun. Ridges and craters on the moon’s surface let through only a few rays of sunlight, creating the glare that earned Goetz’s inscription of “Signs and Wonders”.

Modern images of solar eclipses, such as this one taken in California on 11 July 1991, display the corona in much more detail than has ever been achievable before. Past observations revealed an astonishing mystery: the corona is about 300 times hotter than the sun’s surface. Eclipses provide prime opportunities to try to figure out how and why it gets so hot, plus research how we might be able to predict solar activity someday to mitigate its potential effects on satellites, astronauts and even electrical grids on Earth.

The sun itself is, of course, not the only thing that researchers study during eclipses. As seen in this image taken in Chile on 2 July 2019, during a total solar eclipse the sky darkens almost completely. Temperatures drop precipitously. Birdsong ceases almost entirely. Through studying how animals react, researchers try to decipher what they may be feeling and thinking, and how they perceive the unexpected darkness.

When viewing an eclipse from the ground, it can be hard to imagine the scale of it. These images of an 8 April 2024 eclipse, taken by NASA’s Deep Space Climate Observatory (DSCOVR) satellite, show that handily. The dark spot moving across the planet in these pictures is the shadow of the moon. People standing within that spot witness totality, and those along the edges see only partial eclipses.

Our ability to image and understand these phenomena has come a long way since petroglyphs in stone walls – imagine what we’ll be able to see in another few thousand years.

For decades, scientists have been discovering neurons with seemingly unique jobs. There are place cells that fire in response to a particular location, mirror neurons that may help us interpret behaviours and even neurons that respond to all things Jennifer Aniston. But a new discovery suggests that most neurons are actually jacks-of-all-trades. “These [earlier] neurons are really the exception, not the rule,” says Stefano Fusi at Columbia University in New York. And the more abundant, generalised cells “can be as important or more important than the good-looking [specialist] neurons we isolated in the past”, he says.

In a 2013 study, Fusi noticed “mixed selectivity” neurons – cells that respond to multiple different task-related inputs at the same time – in the brains of monkeys. But it was unclear how widespread they are in the mammalian brain.

Advertisement

Now, Fusi and his team have turned to the International Brain Laboratory. This holds information on the activity of individual neurons throughout the brains of more than 100 mice while they did a decision-making task. The task involved the mice looking for an image on the left or right side of a screen and moving it to the centre by quickly turning a wheel.

The researchers found that the only areas with specialised neurons were those in dedicated sensory cortices, such as the primary visual cortex. Instead, the neurons in most areas of the brain responded to various aspects of the task. For instance, those outside of the visual cortex also seemed to be involved in processing the image, as well as deciding which side of the screen it was on and generating the movement to turn the wheel. “The important thing to stress is that there are specialised neurons [such as place cells],” says Fusi. But these are not the norm, he adds.

Free newsletter

The researchers also found that most neurons didn’t respond in the same way to the same stimulus. For example, the somatomotor areas, which are regions associated with planning movements, responded strongly to licks and whisker movements. Other areas still responded, but not as strongly. This suggests that while specialism exists, individual neurons generally aren’t myopically focused on one type of information.

“The problem is if you’re arguing there’s no [specialisation], somebody can always say: ‘You just needed [to study] a few more neurons [to uncover it],’” says Ben Hayden at Baylor College of Medicine in Texas. “This [study] is a giant smack in the face saying: ‘Fine, we got 14,000 neurons and we still didn’t find it [for the most part].’”

Having a collection of neurons that respond to the same stimulus in slightly different ways may maximise the amount of information the brain can process. This may mean that these generalised neurons contribute to a plethora of tasks, including memory, cognition, decision-making and perception.

Around a third of people are able to almost fully rebuild their brains after a stroke and uncovering why is pointing the way to better treatments for everyone

The researchers point out that the mice’s task wasn’t particularly complex. A complicated, multidimensional set of tasks could shed light on when individual neurons focus their responses on one aspect of such tasks versus another, says Fusi.

He and his team are now collaborating with researchers who study non-human primates and patients who are conscious during open brain surgeries, such as those treating epilepsy, to see if the findings in mice apply to people.

With all these projects, Fusi hopes to shift the emphasis from looking at the role of individual neurons to patterns of activity across many cells in the brain. “It’s very difficult to draw conclusions by looking at one neuron at the time,” he says. “Instead, we [should] look at all the neurons together. That’s the perspective of the brain because each neuron in the brain doesn’t [get input from] one single [other] neuron. Each neuron in the brain looks at 10,000 other neurons that are connected on its dendritic tree.”

Advertisement

This physicist is hunting for the biggest black hole in the universe

Informed by observations and large-scale simulations of the universe, the team built a mathematical model that could take the idea and properties of a runaway black hole (RBH) and reveal its origin story. “It’s similar to fossil analysis, we are working backwards to see what the past looked like,” says team member Digvijay Wadekar at the University of Texas at Austin.

The team found that an RBH like the one posited by van Dokkum and his colleagues would have had two parent supermassive black holes, where one was spinning quickly and was six times more massive than the other. These would have violently merged about 70 million years ago, creating a recoiling RBH.

The team estimated that a large enough recoil to match the proposed RBH could happen in fewer than 10 per cent of black hole mergers.

“As a mathematical exercise, it’s very interesting, because the physical mechanism to produce a runaway supermassive black hole is there. Now, the chances that this happens in reality are very low,” says Jorge Sánchez Almeida at the Institute of Astrophysics of the Canary Islands in Spain.

There are only a few anti-ageing supplements that actually work

New Scientist July 24, 2026

I’m a big fan of the New Scientist podcast Change Your Mind, on which my erstwhile colleagues Cat de Lange and Helen Thomson discuss “all the brain health advice you really need to know”. One recent episode is well worth a listen if you’re interested in keeping your brain healthy. Cat and Helen invited JoAnn Manson, who is head of preventive medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Massachusetts, to the podcast to discuss her research on multivitamin supplements and brain health. She described how she and her colleagues found that people over 60 who take a daily multivitamin show significantly slower cognitive decline and age-related memory loss over two to three years.

The only four skincare ingredients that have been proven to work

For me, that was a marmalade dropper. On the issue of supplements, I’m a hardened sceptic. Based on a New Scientist feature I edited many years ago, as well as a recent update by another ex-colleague, Alison George, my informed opinion is that very few supplements work and some are positively harmful. I make an exception for vitamin D because I live too far north to make enough on my own from the feeble winter sunshine. But once the clocks have gone forward, I stop taking it. I would also take folic acid if I were female and trying for a baby (I’m neither), long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids if I didn’t eat oily fish weekly and vitamin B12 if I were a vegan. But as for the rest, I don’t waste my money.

For people who are willing to shell out for supplements, there are myriad opportunities. One of the thriving markets is in anti-ageing. Although very few if any have been scientifically validated, I’m slightly less sceptical. A few years ago, I took an anti-ageing supplement called alpha-ketoglutarate for six months for a story I was doing. I had my biological age measured before and after, and it went down. But that is hardly solid data of the sort you get from a clinical trial.

Advertisement

Of that, there is plenty, and it doesn’t cast anti-ageing supplements in a good light. I found a gold mine of information in an academic book published earlier this year called Supplements and Drugs for Healthy Longevity. Under the guidance of the eminent biogerontologist Suresh Rattan at Aarhus University in Denmark, an expert panel rated the evidence for more than 250 compounds with supposed anti-ageing effects. These ranged from vitamins and minerals to plant extracts, traditional medicines, probiotics and hormone supplements, plus some much-hyped compounds I often hear bigged up in anti-ageing circles: NAD+, coenzyme Q10, spermidine and D&Q, or dasatinib and quercetin. Interestingly, they didn’t look at the evidence for alpha-ketoglutarate.

Suffice to say that none of them met the highest standard of evidence, which Rattan defines as “solid, reproducible and trustworthy”. A few reached a secondary level, but, on the whole, the authors recommend obtaining these compounds from food. “At present using one or more nutritional and other supplements… is mostly an act of faith and hope”, rather than being based on strong scientific evidence-based data, the book concludes.

Suddenly feeling old? Evidence now suggests that rather than a long, steady decline, we dramatically age around three specific times in our lives. Might it be possible to stay younger for longer?

But it also says that more research is needed. So, I had a look at Manson’s. Her results come from a clinical trial she and her colleagues ran between 2015 and 2023 called COSMOS (Cocoa Supplement and Multivitamin Outcomes Study). The trial recruited more than 21,000 people aged over 60 and gave one group of them a daily multivitamin plus cocoa extract, which contains flavonoid compounds thought to be beneficial for some age-related conditions. Other groups received just a multivitamin, just cocoa extract or nothing. The principal goal of the trial was to test whether the multivitamin/cocoa cocktail would reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease and cancer. It didn’t, but the researchers still found nuggets of useful information in the data.

One of these was the effect on brain health, as discussed on the podcast. Another, which was published earlier this year, looked at the effect on ageing in general. A subgroup of 958 participants had their biological age measured at the start of the trial and then again two years later. Those who received the daily multivitamin aged, on average, more slowly than those who did not (the cocoa extract had no effect). The effect was relatively modest – a month or two over the two years – but over the course of longer periods that could really add up.

Free newsletter

Another study adds weight to the idea that supplements can slow down ageing. Last year, a team including researchers at the University of Zurich in Switzerland published a study on omega-3 fatty acid supplementation in people aged 70 to 91. The traditional verdict on these supplements has been that they aren’t worth taking unless your diet is deficient in the main sources of omega-3, which are oily fish, flaxseed, chia seeds and walnuts. The Zurich research challenges that. Over the course of three years, the people who took the supplement aged biologically three months less, on average, than those who took a placebo. Adding vitamin D and strength training increased the benefit to four months.

So, have I changed my mind about supplements? Not yet. Both studies rely on biological age measurements, which are notoriously unreliable. Neither found any meaningful change in the health of their participants, and slowing down biological ageing doesn’t necessarily correspond to what really matters: an increase in healthspan. It is also possible, Manson told the podcast, that the participants in her study were deficient in one or more vitamins, and the multivitamin supplement merely corrected for that.

But it’s a start. As Daniel Belsky and Calen Ryan at Columbia University in New York wrote in response to the multivitamin study, “Evidence that simple multi-vitamin supplementation can slow aging, even slightly, would have substantial implications, including for public health guidelines.” We’re not quite there yet, but if and when we are, I’m heading to the pharmacy.

Magnesium has been called the “super mineral of the moment”, hailed for its supposed benefits for the brain and body. But columnist Alice Klein finds that the evidence is lacking for many of these claims

The last test of the Wools of New Zealand UK Shearing Tour, at Corwen, commentator Huw Condon (left) and the New Zealand team of shearers Jack Fagan and Hemi Baddick and manager Digger Balme.

New Zealand shearers Jack Fagan and Hemi Braddick have been beaten by just 0.9 points in Wales, ending New Zealand’s chances of winning the four-test series.

The outcome, a 3-1 series win to Wales on the New Zealand team’s 2026 Wools of New Zealand UK Tour, was decided at the Corwen Shears in North Wales on Saturday, and followed Welsh wins at Epynt and Cothi, and New Zealand’s midweek win at the Royal Welsh Show.

Gethin Lewis claimed best time points, shearing the 20 lambs in 11m 53s, beating Fagan by nine seconds, and teammate Gwion Lloyd Evans had the best quality points in the pens.

Braddick had the best job on the board, the only shearer to average less than one penalty per lamb, finishing with a time-and-quality total just 0.55 points shy of Lewis, the top individual on the day.

Lewis also won the Corwen Shears open final in which Fagan was fourth and Braddick fifth.

A field of 47 lined up in the open heats, including six from New Zealand.

Earlier this year, the Wools of New Zealand team of Fagan and Toa Henderson claimed a 3-0 series win over a Welsh team of Evans and Llyr Jones in New Zealand, with matches at Aria, Pukekohe, and Taumarunui.

An open-class machine shearer for 13 years, Fagan won both the national shearing circuit final at the Golden Shears in Masterton and the New Zealand Shears open final earlier this year.

He was also top individual in the Cothi and Royal Welsh tests, and proved to be a jack of all trades by winning the Corwen Shears junior blades shearing title on Friday.

Fagan beat five other hopefuls comfortably, finishing 4m 25s ahead of the next shearer and winning by 5.362 points.

He cleaned the two sheep in 10m 9s.

By comparison, Welsh World Championships representative Elfed Jackson took 16m 2s to shear six sheep when winning the Corwen Shears Open Blades title. Fagan’s winning time in the New Zealand Shears open final in April was 19m 0.06sec for 25 sheep with the machine handpiece.

It was his fifth blades shearing competition, and he plans to take them up again in intermediate events at the Waimate Shears in October and the Canterbury Shears in November.

“I want to be fast with the blades,” he said.

“Machine shearing is the No.1 discipline for the moment, but I’m keen to keep learning.

“I will need years of practice to even come near the top level of the open [blades] shearers.”

Parents believe now-anorexic child’s obesity misdiagnosis triggered eating disorder

New Zealand Herald July 26, 2026

Lucas' BMI was incorrectly calculated as one that was off the charts for a child.

Content warning: This article references self-harm and eating disorders. Helplines can be found at the bottom of the page.

A now-anorexic boy was incorrectly told by a doctor to lose weight after they miscalculated his BMI, which his parents believe may have contributed to him developing his eating disorder.

His father, Robert, said he was “absolutely disturbed” at what he found when he recently asked for a copy of his son’s medical records.

The Herald previously reported the 14-year-old Wellington teenager Lucas* was repeatedly denied re-admission to Wellington Hospital’s children’s ward because he was not deemed unwell enough, despite his parents saying they could not keep him safe at home.

His mother, Jennifer, described him as a “dangerously” underweight boy who was prone to self-harming.

The parents earlier said they did not know what had brought on Lucas’ eating disorder as he would not open up to them about it. The Herald agreed not to use their surname to protect their son’s privacy.

Lucas’ medical records, which have been released to the family since the Herald’s article, showed he was observed as having a “significantly raised BMI” a year before his eating disorder began to manifest.

In April 2024, Lucas went to the paediatric clinic at Wellington Hospital for allergy testing.

The clinic recorded him as weighing 58.4kg and being 131cm tall, which led to his body mass index (BMI) being miscalculated as 34.

He was actually 151cm at the time, which meant his correct BMI would have been 25.

BMI is a screening tool that uses height and weight measurements to estimate a person’s body size.

It has been widely criticised for being an imperfect tool that cannot accurately calculate a person’s body fat because it does not take into account things like muscle mass.

The World Health Organisation BMI charts for boys ranges from 10 to 32.

For a 12-year-old boy, it shows a BMI of 25 is just over the obesity line.

A BMI of 34 goes off the chart.

The clinic’s records showed Lucas was diagnosed with “high BMI” and told to exercise more and improve his diet, which included reducing sugary foods and drinks.

“Medical professionals should know better than to tell a kid that age they need to lose weight,” Robert said.

He felt doctors should have known Lucas’ height was off just by looking at him.

Lucas’ anorexia emerged a year ago, when he went from refusing to take lunch to school, to skipping dinner, to not eating anything for several days at a time.

In November 2025, his GP clinic sent a referral letter to the Central Regional Eating Disorder Service (CREDS) for a suspected eating disorder.

The GP’s notes said he was “preoccupied with weight and food” and “thinks he is overweight”.

The notes specifically questioned whether the “obesity diagnosis” and subsequent “lifestyle advice” Lucas got from the hospital “might have had an impact on [him]”.

In December, he was admitted to hospital for a fortnight for a medical refeeding treatment, where his condition improved, but he relapsed post-discharge.

“We watched his eating disorder morph from no food intake to food intake but extreme exercise,” Robert said.

Subsequent medical notes from the hospital’s paediatric clinic stated: “Unfortunately during the paediatric outpatient clinic he was counselled on eating more healthily and needing to lose weight due to this incorrect calculation.”

“It would appear his BMI was actually 25 at this time”.

Health New Zealand did not respond to the Herald’s questions about Lucas’ BMI being miscalculated, or the potential impacts this had on him.

In a statement, it said: “Health New Zealand will reach out to [Lucas’] family to discuss any outstanding concerns if they wish.

“We acknowledge the significant stress that eating disorders place on young people and their families throughout treatment and recovery.”

In June, Lucas was taken to hospital after his second fainting episode.

Doctors found self-harm marks on his body which led to him being admitted for four days under a mental health hold.

Since then, a multi-service plan had been created to help Lucas, according to Robert.

He said Lucas’ eating and mood had “dramatically improved” and he was no longer isolating himself in his room.

Robert said it was hard to articulate how he and Jennifer felt after reading the notes and concluding the health system they trusted to help Lucas with his anorexia may also have been part of the cause of it.

“We are angry and upset, we don’t want this to happen to other families.”

Email janhavi. gosavi@nzme. co. nz

*To maintain the family’s privacy, the name of the teenage boy has been changed and the family’s last name has been omitted.

Janhavi Gosavi is a Wellington-based journalist for the New Zealand Herald who covers news in the capital.

Kiwis heading out the door early today will be wise to pull on their beanies, scarves and gloves as shiversome frosts blanket the nation - with one South Island town plunging to -8C overnight.

The calmer conditions come after a turbulent weekend that saw thunderstorms, heavy rain and 100km/h wind gusts batter parts of the country, while slips forced highway closures.

MetService meteorologist Michael Pawley told the Herald that a ridge of high pressure settling over the country would now bring clear skies and light winds, allowing temperatures to plummet.

“The first half of the week will be about those colder temperatures and crisp, sunny afternoons ... settled winter,” he said.

“We’re seeing the chance of frosts for anywhere south of Auckland, and maybe even including some sheltered places within Auckland.

“Places like the Central Plateau, Tokoroa and Taumarunui ... are looking pretty chilly.”

The coldest temperature overnight was at Mt Cook Village, where the mercury fell to a teeth-chattering -8C overnight.

Nearby Pūkaki got as low as -7C, while Christchurch reached -4C, not far off its coldest morning this month of -4.3C, recorded yesterday.

In the North Island Waiōuru also fell to -7C, while Masterton got down to -3.9C and Rotorua was shivering at -2C around 6am.

Even sheltered parts of Tāmaki Makaurau/Auckland, where dense morning fog dominated last week, could wake to frost. MetService’s website showed the central city on 5C early this morning, while temperatures in West Auckland were as low as 2C.

As of 8am, the entire country was in single-digit temperatures, with Twizel the coldest at -7C and the Chatham Islands the warmest with 8.4C. On the mainland, Kaitāia was the hottest city or town at 7.7C.

While much of today will be fine, Auckland could see cloudy periods and the chance of an afternoon shower after a frosty start in sheltered areas, Pawley said.

Wellington is expected to have cloudy periods and the chance of a shower, while Christchurch is forecast to enjoy fine weather once its icy morning gives way.

Pawley said the chilly mornings were less the result of a cold snap than ideal conditions for overnight cooling.

“You haven’t got that blanket of cloud which essentially traps some of that heat in,” he said.

“So with the wind not stirring up the air and mixing it with warmer air aloft, you end up with this really cold layer next to the surface and that’s what causes the frost.”

Pawley urged motorists to take extra care during the morning commute, with frost increasing the risk of black ice, particularly on shaded roads that receive little early sunshine.

He said it would be “a week of two halves”, with a Tasman front expected to arrive from Wednesday, bringing rain to the South Island and the chance of heavy falls and strong northwest winds later in the week.

Mt Cook Village had been forecast to drop even lower, to -9C, which would be among the colder mornings of the winter - though not the coldest.

Earlier this month, Lake Tekapo plunged to -12.5C, the lowest air temperature recorded nationwide this year, while Mount Cook Airport fell to -11.5C.

The policy would be implemented in stages, reaching 30 weeks’ paid leave by 2029.

Nash’s text called National’s Katie Nimon “the laziest MP I’ve ever come across”, and wrongly claimed she took nine months of maternity leave while an MP.

National’s policy would also allow parents who were sharing the leave entitlement to take some or all of it at the same time.

Sunday also saw the Green Party releasing its manifesto at its annual meeting, and unveiling its election slogan, “For all of us”. Co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick also announced the Greens wanted a one-year pause on any new AI data centres being consented, to allow time for regulation to be developed.

Speaking at the parental leave announcement, Luxon called the Greens’ policy “alarmist”, saying he and Willis were “thinking very deeply about an AI strategy”.

“Data centres would need to bring additionality to our energy system and electricity system and we also need to have a conversation about use of water,” he said.

Patient fell trying to kill cockroaches at Auckland Hospital, fleas hit wards

New Zealand Herald July 26, 2026

The Nurses Organisation told RNZ there had been a recent rise in reports of insects at Auckland Hospital. Photo / RNZ, Marika Khabazi

By Kate Green of RNZ

Staff at Auckland Hospital have made hundreds of reports about fleas and other insects, and one patient there slipped and fell trying to stomp on a cluster of cockroaches in the shower.

The patient, Claudia Elliot, was staying in the hospital’s cardiology ward last month after having open heart surgery.

She praised the clinical care she received but told RNZ she had serious concerns about the hospital’s condition and resourcing.

“I have spent 10 years working for the UN in the hot spots of Afghanistan and Somalia,” she said. “So I’m sort of used to a bit of Third World colour. But I was very surprised when I went in for a shower in the cardiology recovery ward to see that there were a number of small cockroaches in the shower.”

Elliott said she tried to stomp on the three small bugs, but slipped and fell.

“I yelled out, and there were about 10 staff members who came racing, picked me up and took me down for an MRI scan to make sure I hadn’t done any damage to my head when I fell.”

She hadn’t – but the cockroaches were not the only concerning observation.

“When I had a heart monitor on, the heart monitor didn’t work, so they had to change it for another one. The second thing that didn’t work was the drip, and they had to change that for another one.”

Staff were also in short supply, she said, with one staff member for five post-surgical patients on her ward. A physiotherapist told her there were two of them on shift, with a caseload of 36 patients that day.

A Nurses Organisation delegate told RNZ there had been a recent increase in reports of fleas, cockroaches and other insects within the wards.

Many wards still had carpet flooring, which was the perfect breeding ground for fleas, they said.

The Health NZ website says cockroaches can spread diseases like dysentery, salmonella and diarrhoea, and they “thrive in unhealthy environments”.

The delegate understood some wards were going to be refloored with vinyl in the coming months, although the work had been delayed by budget restrictions.

“In my wards that I work in, we’ve got two toilets that don’t have the toilet seat lid,” the delegate said.

“It’s quite common for bathrooms to not have hot water running. It’s quite common for showers to have very low water pressure.

“So patients have to then go and find another room to have a shower in, which causes more struggle in terms of logistics.”

They said it was also common for observation equipment to malfunction, or not collect accurate data.

“So we send the equipment off for maintenance checks and to get repaired or get new ones.

“But because there’s quite a strict, tight budget within the hospital at the moment, nurses are having to stretch two or three throughout the whole ward.”

Patients and staff had reported flea bites, with some staff even reporting accidentally passing them on to their own homes and families.

“Our patients shouldn’t have to have to deal with this in the hospital,” the delegate said.

“And it’s quite embarrassing as a healthcare worker in the hospital knowing that our standards should be really high, but we’re not given the resources or the safe environment to be able to provide our care.”

Health NZ’s group director of operations for Auckland, Dr Michael Shepherd, told RNZ in a statement: “Like many large campuses, we have experienced flea activity from time to time.”

He said 142 flea-related incidents had been reported across Health NZ’s Auckland sites in the past year.

“These reports are actively managed through our pest management programme and have reduced significantly in recent years.”

Shepherd said there were comprehensive cleaning, facilities and equipment maintenance programmes operating 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

He said work to replace carpeted areas with vinyl flooring was underway across Health NZ facilities, but had to be carefully planned to minimise disruption as it often required clinical services to be temporarily relocated.

Moral distress: For primary care doctors, ‘doing the right thing’ can feel impossible

New Zealand Herald July 26, 2026

Primary care doctors face moral distress amid growing healthcare pressures. Photo / Getty Images

Modern healthcare systems ask much of primary care doctors. They are expected to diagnose, reassure, coordinate care, manage chronic illness and increasingly fill the gaps when other parts of the system come under strain.

In New Zealand, general practitioners (GPs) deal with around 90% of all medical problems. Research consistently shows that strong relationships with a GP improve patient health outcomes while saving money, with every $1 invested in primary care returning up to $13 elsewhere in the health system.

Yet primary care is facing a mounting workforce crisis. New Zealand is already short by almost 500 fulltime GPs, with that deficit expected to grow in the coming years.

Our newly published research sheds new light on a psychological factor adding to this pressure – and one that tells us much about the taxing environment doctors work in today.

As part of our study, we interviewed 26 GPs in New Zealand and 24 family physicians in the United States about the joys and challenges of their work.

Beneath many of the structural pressures doctors face each day – from heavy caseloads to underpaid administrative work – we found widespread instances of what is known as “moral distress”.

This arises when people know the right thing to do but are unable to do it because of circumstances beyond their control. As one doctor told us: “A lot of my work felt harmful and in conflict with what I knew to be best for my patients.”

It typically leads to feelings of guilt, inadequacy and a deep emotional fatigue that can be confused with burnout. The most common source was cost barriers preventing patients from receiving the care they needed.

In the United States, these barriers largely stem from the profit-driven, insurance-based health system. In New Zealand, they more often reflect under-resourced services and difficulties accessing specialist hospital care.

For example, when patients are declined operations such as hip or knee replacements, they return to their GP, who must continue managing their pain despite having few treatment options. GPs are left carrying the moral burden of decisions over which they have no control.

Doctors described how such scenarios left them in an impossible position that was harmful for both parties. Patients continued to live with severe pain and a reduced quality of life, while GPs could do little to help after hospitals had declined treatment.

Our interviews pointed to three common ways doctors respond to moral distress. One is “moral self-differentiation”, or going above and beyond for patients despite the health system’s constraints.

For example, doctors described frequently working beyond paid hours because, as they put it, doing so felt like “the right thing to do”.

Over time, however, these efforts can become self-sacrificing. Because doctors cannot overcome systemic barriers on their own, continually going above and beyond leaves many physically and emotionally exhausted, contributes to burnout and depression, and may ultimately drive them out of medicine.

Another strategy is moral dissociation, or emotionally distancing oneself. As one doctor put it: “I’ve mentally told myself it’s the system’s fault, not my fault. So I’ve disconnected.”

A third strategy is what we call “extra-role moral engagement”. Rather than trying to push back against the system from inside the consulting room, doctors sought to address underlying issues outside the clinic by advocating for wider reforms.

This also highlights the central role primary care doctors play in healthcare systems. When they experience moral distress, it is a sign the system is asking them to shoulder responsibility for problems they cannot fix on their own.

Just how widespread moral distress is among primary care doctors remains uncertain, and larger studies are needed to understand its prevalence.

But our research made one point clear. Moral distress is much more than a symptom of doctors’ “bleeding hearts”.

The purpose of any healthcare system is, ultimately, to care for patients. That responsibility must, of course, be balanced against financial constraints.

But if those constraints leave doctors unable to provide the care they believe patients need – and drive experienced clinicians from the profession – moral distress becomes more than a subjective wellbeing issue.

It becomes a warning sign that the system is operating at odds with its own fundamental purpose.

James Greenslade-Yeats, Research Fellow in Management, Auckland University of Technology and Tago Mharapara, Senior Lecturer, Department of Management, Auckland University of Technology

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 21:30:44 GMT

Littler sets the tournament’s highest average in 18-9 win

Beau Greaves beats Fallon Sherrock to lift women’s title

Luke Littler bulldozed his way to a second consecutive World Matchplay title as he crushed Gerwyn Price 18-9 in Blackpool. The 19-year-old averaged 111.53 in the final, setting an average for the tournament as a whole of 111.04 to break Phil Taylor’s record of 106.31.

Littler also broke his own competition record for 180s as he hit 12 in the final to reach 66 for the week, as he became only the third man to successfully defend the Matchplay final after Taylor and Michael van Gerwen, who did it most recently in 2016.

It keeps Littler on course for a clean sweep of trophies in 2026, having already won the World Championship, UK Open, Premier League and the Masters, while he will defend the Grand Slam, Grand Prix and Players Championship Finals.

Littler was on a charge from the start, taking a 3-1 lead with a 167 checkout to leave Price feeding on crumbs. A third bullseye finish of the night made it 11-3, but he twice missed double 10 to allow Price a brief moment of hope, as the Welshman cut the deficit to 14-7. Price hit a 11-darter to get to 15-9 but Littler responded with a 148 before finishing it off in short order.

“It’s been a crazy week, one of the best weeks of my life with the darts I’ve played,” Littler said. “It’s not been easy, it’s been tough. The stats make it look easy but when you’re on this stage with how hot it is, I’ve definitely played some of the best darts of my life. I feel like it’s the best version of myself. I have just played so well.”

Littler is eyeing a clean sweep of the majors, and will now turn his attention to the Pro Tour in order to qualify for the Player Championship Finals. “I don’t think my dad is too happy because we were meant to be going to Spain but now we will be going to Leicester for some Pro Tours!” he said.

Price, appearing in his first final since 2022 having never won the trophy, had said earlier in the week that if he brought his best to the final he could beat Littler, but it was not the case as, even averaging 104.97, the Welshman was blown away.

“Luke is one in a million,” Price said. “I think I played pretty decent. “In that game I missed a couple of opportunities but the bull checkouts, the 167, it was a big turning point even though it was early in the game. I didn’t play brilliant, but I played decent.”

Earlier, Beau Greaves claimed her third Women’s World Matchplay title in four years as she edged out Fallon Sherrock 6-5.

Burnham to meet Zelenskyy at UK naval base in show of ‘unwavering’ support

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 21:30:22 GMT

Ukrainian president will be first overseas visitor for new British prime minister

Volodymyr Zelenskyy will become Andy Burnham’s first overseas visitor as prime minister, in a visit that Burnham said underlined Britain’s “unwavering” backing for Ukraine.

Less than two weeks after Keir Starmer travelled to Kyiv for the final foreign visit of his prime ministership, the Ukrainian president will on Monday join Burnham at a naval base where Ukrainian forces have been receiving training.

Zelenskyy was one of the first world leaders Burnham spoke to when he entered No 10 last week, and the prime minister has promised to maintain Starmer’s strong support for the country in pushing back against Russia’s invasion.

On the visit to the base, the pair will speak to Ukrainian and British military personnel who have taken part in Exercise Sea Breeze, a 15-country training deployment based on mine exercises and other maritime operations in the Black Sea.

The second part of this year’s exercise, which took place in Portland, Dorset, finished on Friday and involved more than 200 Ukrainian personnel.

Burnham and Zelenskyy are also due to discuss joint projects including Stone Cloak, an electronic jammer for which the UK has shared the intellectual property, allowing Ukraine to use the system immediately.

Thousands of the jammers, each about the size of a tablet computer, have been sent to Ukraine to be fitted to drones, with the aim of stopping Russian air defence systems from tracking and targeting them.

Ukraine is now able to mass produce the devices itself. After being initially used there, the jammers are due to be fitted to new UK weaponry, including cruise missiles.

Burnham, in a comment released by Downing Street before the visit, said: “Britain stands with Ukraine, shoulder to shoulder, and our support remains unwavering. Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve, and we will not back down until we achieve a long-lasting and just peace for Ukraine.

“Stone Cloak is the best of homegrown British innovation and proven on the frontline, and it will be vital to protecting our security in both our countries.”

The Rapture review – this apocalyptic drama couldn’t be here at a better time

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 21:00:21 GMT

It’s set in a UK racked by an unbearable heatwave and the rise of extremism – this adaptation of the 2010 novel feels horrifyingly apt

When The Rapture by Liz Jensen was first published, in 2010, it was set in a near-future when temperatures in the UK are rising to unbearable heights, culty-Christian groups with apocalyptic bents are springing up all over the place and there is a growing sense that the world is going mad. Swap out “culty-Christian” for “political extremists bent on embracing the apocalypse rather than trying to save us from it” and it would be a deluded soul indeed who wouldn’t place it among fiction’s more prescient offerings.

The adaptation that has arrived on our screens 16 years later – a study in physical and mental discomfort – is the perfect accompaniment to our current record-breaking, fear-inducing heatwave, and gains a lot of power from our growing collective awareness that the future is finally here.

Clinical psychotherapist Dr Gabrielle Fox (Ruth Madeley) is still coming to terms with an apocalyptic event in her own life: a car accident that killed her husband and left her paralysed from the waist down. She was the driver and is pursued by guilt, which she discusses in weekly sessions with her own psychotherapist (Ruth Jones) – because physicians are the worst at healing themselves. But after two years, she must go back to work.

Her first case, at the adolescent secure psychiatric unit at Oxsmith hospital, is a humdinger. Seventeen-year-old Bethany Krall (India Amarteifio) was convicted of killing her mother Carys (screwdriver, eye) when she was 15, and has been locked up on the unit, pretending to take her anti-psychotic meds, ever since. She has no memory of attacking her mother and denies doing it. There were no witnesses but she was the only one in the house at the time, definitely the only one covered in blood immediately afterwards and certainly the only one who had drawn a picture of her mother with a screwdriver poking out of her face a week before it happened.

Bethany claims her drawings are of her visions, not plans. She does them with her eyes closed and they usually involve death or destruction. Her nurse Rafiq (Naby Dakhli) says that the scenes they depict come true and is convinced she is a prophet. Gabs, as a woman of science and observer of human complexities rather than supernatural forces, suspects that Bethany is at best disturbed and at worst mentally ill – and, in either case, in need of treatment rather than obeisance. But then Bethany reveals knowledge of some private details of Gabs’ life, and seems to have drawn a picture of her long before anyone knew she would be assigned her case.

Bethany’s father, Leonard (Sam Hazeldine), just wants to help his daughter. “I’m desperate to see and support her,” he assures Gabs when she visits him at the well-appointed Faith Way centre, where he leads a sect united under the exhortation “Choose hope”. Leonard broadcasts sermons online and preaches against environmental activist groups such as the increasingly militant Climate Front, who, he believes, are frightening people with their doom-mongering ways. We do not like Leonard. In this we are joined by his daughter, who has been refusing visits from her unsettling papa ever since she was arrested. She is unwilling to be used – as she believes her mother was – as a pawn in his game of “playing the good Christian”.

There is an awful lot going on in The Rapture. To all the above we must add an investigative journalist, alternately clarifying and muddying waters; a charming (possibly too charming) new love interest for Gabs; and a mystery woman who might be able to tell them more about Carys’ death, if Gabs can identify her from one of Bethany’s vision-sketches. And that’s just the first two episodes, which were all that were available for review of the total five.

It is clearly aiming for a lot thematically, too. How do we account for the destabilising forces of grief and guilt? How do guilt and grief manifest at a collective rather than individual level? Where do the lines between madness and sanity, impassioned but rational belief (in the climate crisis, say) and religious fervour lie? The overall effect is chaotic. Much is gestured at, and the story has some promising leads, but unless the remaining three episodes become much leaner and clearer, we are probably doomed to frustration.

Nevertheless, the Rapture has smaller-scale scenes and moments that work incredibly well. One is the first crack in Bethany’s wall of denial regarding her part in Carys’s death. Another is Gabs negotiating the new mental and physical territory that comes with her first potential relationship – with Frasier (Jack Farthing) – since she became a widow and a wheelchair (and catheter, it is unobtrusively noted) user. Yet another is journalist Dick (Iwan Rheon) drinking but trying to keep bitterness and collapse at bay. A little less all round could have made The Rapture into a lot more than it – so far – is.

The Rapture aired on BBC One and is on iPlayer now.

Benjamin Netanyahu said on Sunday that Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, is “fomenting hate” by calling the Israeli prime minister a war criminal who should be arrested over Israel’s war in Gaza if he visits the city for the United Nations general assembly.

Netanyahu said he intends to be in New York in September to address the annual UN gathering of world leaders, despite the mayor’s suggestion that he is not welcome. Mamdani said on Wednesday that while New York City does not have legal authority to execute an arrest warrant issued by the world’s top war crimes court, he encouraged the federal government to do so.

“He’s supposed to be the mayor of all New Yorkers – Jews, Christians, Muslims, everyone,” Netanyahu said on the Fox News channel’s Sunday Morning Futures with Maria Bartiromo. “But he’s trying to turn one group against the other.”

The prime minister has become an increasingly polarizing figure over Israel’s war in Gaza, which was ignited by the 7 October 2023 deadly attack on southern Israel by Hamas militants. Israel also joined the US in starting the war against Iran on 28 February before launching a ground invasion in southern Lebanon in response to fire from the Iranian-backed Hezbollah group.

Netanyahu on Sunday dismissed the international criminal court (ICC)’s war crimes charges against him as “bogus”. He pointed to sexual misconduct allegations against the ICC’s top prosecutor, who was removed from that post on Friday, and said the warrant was an attempt to divert attention.

Mamdani’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Sunday.

Netanyahu on Sunday also said he was concerned that once-bipartisan political support for Israel in the US is at risk, particularly as progressive and far-left Democrats aligned with the Mamdani wing of the party splinter.

He also warned against rising antisemitism in the US and other western countries, saying that when he talks to people in New York City, home to the second-largest Jewish population in the world, “Jews feel very uncomfortable”.

“And I think it’s wrong,” he said. “The whole thing is wrong.”

Throughout his 2025 mayoral election campaign, Mamdani said he would seek to order the city’s police to execute the ICC’s arrest warrant over Netanyahu’s role in the war in Gaza.

“I want to be equally clear, Benjamin Netanyahu is not welcome in New York City, nor is any other war criminal at large,” he said in his video message on Wednesday.

He told New Yorkers that he understood their frustration and that expressions of protest is something the city would “always respect”.

The Hague-based court has accused Netanyahu, his former defense minister and the late leader of Hamas of crimes against humanity. The Palestinian territory’s health ministry says more than 73,000 people have been killed in Israel’s offensive – roughly half of them women and children. About 1,200 people, most of them civilians, were killed in the initial Hamas attack on Israel.

Trump on Monday told Netanyahu in a social media post that he “will not be arrested, in any way, shape, or form, while in the United States of America”.

Netanyahu is expected in Washington DC on Monday to meet with Trump and attend funeral services for Lindsey Graham, the late Republican senator.

Graham, a leading defense hawk and strong supporter of Israel, died suddenly on 11 July of a likely torn aorta. Netanyahu called him a “great patriot” and one of Israel’s “greatest friends”.

Adam Ramsay-Peaty armed with ‘battle plan’ for golden revival in 50m breaststroke

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 19:54:39 GMT

Briton ready to bounce back after 100m bronze

‘The last 24 hours have been a bit of a whirlwind’

Adam Ramsay-Peaty has never been one to hide his emotions. He wears them proudly on his sleeve, next to the striking tattoos of a huge lion and Poseidon, the Greek god of the sea.

After his shock defeat in the 100m breaststroke final at these Commonwealth Games, the 31-year-old was back pouring his heart out on Sunday – and insisting he had a “battle plan” to win gold in Monday’s 50m breaststroke final.

Ramsay-Peaty certainly looked smoother in qualifying third fastest from the semi-finals in 26.82sec. However, he still has a couple of tenths to find on the South African Michael Houlie, who was fastest in 26.61.

The Australian Sam Williamson, who is hoping to add the 50m to his 100m crown, also looked good as he won his semi-final in 26.79. Yet Peaty pronounced himself happy with how he had bounced back from Saturday’s shock loss.

“It felt much better,” he said. “The last 24 hours have been a bit of a whirlwind, but I’m really happy with that. We’re on a great trajectory for tomorrow.

“For me, the best way to ever get anything out of my head is just to write it out. When I write down what’s going wrong, what’s going right, what kind of change? What can’t change? Then I’ve got a battle plan.”

He added: “People forget that I haven’t done this for two years. And even I forget that. So as you go through heats, semis and finals, it’s quite difficult if you’re not used to it. So I think that perspective is a good thing.”

Peaty has stood on the top of the podium 32 times in global championships across his glittering career. Yet he has not won a gold medal since the Birmingham 2022 Commonwealth Games. That record was extended on Saturday when he could take only bronze in the 100m breaststroke in 59.65, behind Williamson, who won in 59.3, and the brilliant 18-year-old Filip Nowicki from Jersey.

Afterwards Ramsay-Peaty was strikingly honest about “all the shit I have been through” to get ready for the Commonwealth Games, including the 5.30am starts, missing family gatherings because of training, and also the amount of abuse he and his family has received on social media.

On Sunday he added more context to his struggles, pointing out that he battled with burnout and a broken foot over the past four years, as well as hinting at the much-publicised estrangement with his family.

“There have been a multitude of things at play over the last few years – burnout, breaking my foot, fighting against something that you love. It’s been hard,” he said. “Some of it has been quite painful, particularly from that foot injury onwards.

“Coming back to where I am now and making the decision to go for LA, I think this is going to be the hardest climb I’ve ever faced and the hardest test. It’s really hard to see the summit because it’s so hard. I don’t think anyone understands.”

What was perhaps most striking about that 59.65 was that it was nearly three seconds behind his world record – and slower even than he swam at the British trials in the spring.
