Force of Nature review – this nature show turns the climate crisis into a pompom-shaking spectacle

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 19:00:19 GMT

Cheetahs forced to cross roiling rivers, owls battered by storms … the tone of this look at how extreme weather affects animals is all a bit disaster movie. Subtle, it is not

You have a thick neck and poorly defined calf muscles and you live in South Dakota with your feckless partner and your five expressionless children. You are an owl. Your days consist of lengthy stretches of nothing, punctuated by sudden bursts of unimaginable terror. Coyotes, badgers and snakes are all bent on reducing your beak to marmalade.

But it’s the weather that poses the biggest threat. Specifically, shouts Force of Nature, it’s the “MONSTER STORMS” that rumble ominously across the prairies, each of which forces you and your family to scurry into your burrow, whereupon you will stand with your trembling backs to the wall, legs wide apart and fluffy britches a-flap, like anxious viscounts in the court of Charles II. Will you survive? Or will you be eviscerated by the “cluster bombs of tornadoes” that churn with increasing frequency through the midwest?

Three years in the making, this six-part documentary focuses on the impact of such “extreme weather events” on the planet’s animals. The gist? They’re stuffed. Or are at the very least in terrible trouble. What to do?

“When nature turns against them,” declaims narrator Andrew Lincoln, “they’re not just enduring … they are fighting back. These animals are,” he adds, Zeus-like in what one imagines are a particularly large pair of chinos, “… a FORCE OF NATURE!” Cue a dramatic montage of climate-battered creatures, each of which has presumably been captured in the moments before it rolled up its sleeves and invited the weather to step outside “for a word”.

There are elephants up to their trunks in churning storm water. There is a lizard clinging to a plant stalk as it’s blown sideways by a gale. There is, inevitably, a polar bear – long established as the poster-beast for the climate crisis – floating mournfully into the distance on a small disc of ice. These scenes are accompanied by disembodied snippets from global news reports – each a ghostly transmission from Doom FM. “West Africa’s worst heatwave in living memory,” rumbles one. “Arctic is warming at around three times faster than the rest of the globe,” booms another.

It’s all a bit late-90s Hollywood disaster movie, a bit Earth Song; the thunderous soundtrack and shots of crashing waves and sorrowing elephants adds up to a vision of catastrophe that offers little room for subtlety. Instead, we get a closeup of chimps holding hands and Lincoln doing this … and this … and sometimes … THIS to the final three words of every sentence, a maddening quirk that makes it doubly difficult to take lines such as “When water is hard to come by, peace … turns to violence” seriously.

Still, the photography is tremendous, so let’s do our best to focus on that.

Off we go, then, to Kenya, where cameras capture the dreadful majesty of the skies as they wreak record-breaking havoc on a pair of cheetah siblings in the flood-struck Maasai Mara national reserve. It’s quite something. There are clouds that look like fists and the sort of clouds that cock their leg over cricket grounds and run away laughing as spectators scramble for their building-society umbrellas.

Cheetahs, alas, don’t have umbrellas. Plus, they are terrible at cricket. And so they just stand there looking drenched and miserable, like sulky teens at a bus stop. But the flood waters continue to rise, and so the brothers are forced to cross a roiling river to reach lunch (antelopes). It’s a poignant sight, the swimming-averse cats bobbing and lurching through the water like chickens through wallpaper paste.

“The bigger the storm, the greater the heroes,” weeps Lincoln as the cheetahs eventually reach the other side. Heroes? “Fighting back”? Or just everyday victims of a human-made disaster, forced to struggle for survival as the world hems, haws and makes documentaries that, however well-meaning, turn it all into a pompom-shaking spectacle?

Back in South Dakota, the owls emerge from their storm-burrow, wobbly but alive. Phew. Whether they can endure another five episodes of Lincoln’s italics, however, remains … TO BE SEEN.

Force of Nature aired on ITV1 and is on ITVX now.

US pauses Iran attacks for second night after Trump advised to halt bombing

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 18:45:41 GMT

Top military officials say campaign has reached its limit of effectiveness and warn of dwindling stocks of munitions

The US has paused strikes on Iran for a second night as top military officials advised Donald Trump to halt his bombing campaign, and diplomatic negotiations have continued to avoid a return to all-out war.

Trump is said to be weighing up diplomatic and military options in the nearly five-month-old conflict, with Benjamin Netanyahu expected to visit the White House on Tuesday. The Israeli prime minister is a vocal critic of Washington’s negotiations with Iranian leaders and has pressed for the US to continue its strikes against Iran.

Netanyahu is under considerable political pressure to show that his military campaigns against Iran and Hezbollah in Lebanon have yielded results before elections scheduled for October.

Tehran said on Sunday it would pause what it called “retaliatory” attacks against US allies in the region. “These [US] attacks continued until two nights ago, but over the past two nights the Americans have stopped their attacks,” said the army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia. “Our strategy has essentially been retaliatory, we have also halted our retaliatory operations.”

Senior officials in the Trump administration are reported to have told the president about dwindling munitions stockpiles that could hamper a sustained military campaign in the region.

Axios reported on Sunday that Adm Bradley Cooper, the top US military commander in the region, had told Trump the US military campaign had reached the limits of its effectiveness.

The message was said to affect Trump’s decision to hold strikes on Iran for the first time in nearly two weeks. Cooper told Trump the US had nearly exhausted the list of targets that it had developed to attack in Iran, and without a return to major combat operations there was little point in continuing the bombing campaign, the news website reported.

Asked on Sunday on NBC’s Meet the Press whether Trump was ruling out additional strikes in Iran, the president’s UN ambassador Mike Waltz said: “I wouldn’t go that far at all. The president is keeping all options on the table.”

The lull in fighting, which began on Friday evening, follows nearly two weeks of strikes against Iran and the collapse of a ceasefire brokered by Trump. Washington blamed Iran for strikes on US forces and allies in the region and its closure of the strait of Hormuz, a conduit for an estimated 20% of the world’s oil and gas.

Senior diplomats from Iran and Oman were said to be holding negotiations on Sunday on reopening the vital waterway and an official in Tehran confirmed colleagues had been in touch with US negotiators to prevent a return to war. Iran has demanded payment and control over which ships pass through the strait.

“Mediators are working and trying to prevent tension from escalating,” the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, told a press conference on Sunday.

But an Iranian army spokesperson signalled defiance, saying the US had no clear strategy and was “experiencing strategic decision-making fatigue”.

The US vice-president, JD Vance, and Dan Caine, the chair of the joint chiefs of staff, warned Trump of the risks of a renewed military campaign against Iran at an Oval Office meeting on Friday, according to media outlets. The president then ordered the military to call off new strikes, which he had warned could “knock out everything they have”.

“We’re talking to [the Iranians] right now,” Trump told reporters on Friday. “I think they’re getting more and more serious as the days go by. We’re locked and loaded and ready to go, but we’re talking to them.”

At a White House Correspondents’ Association dinner that evening he said he did not think Iran was ready to make a deal but he was ready to listen.

Caine warned Trump about dwindling munitions stockpiles, which include Patriot missile interceptors and offensive weapons like Tomahawk cruise missiles. Vance campaigned on his opposition to US military interventions in the Middle East and has grown more vocal in his opposition to the war in Iran.

Netanyahu’s office announced on Sunday that he would convene a meeting of his security cabinet before leaving for Washington on Monday. He played a crucial role in lobbying Trump to launch joint strikes against Iran in February and has said that US negotiators must take a strong line on Iran’s nuclear and ballistic missile programme. US negotiators have instead prioritised opening the strait of Hormuz.

Netanyahu will travel to Washington amid some of the worst violence this year in the West Bank, where his military is launching an “extensive” operation after the deaths of four Palestinians and two Israelis when armed settlers entered a Palestinian village on Thursday.

The US and the UK under its new prime minister, Andy Burnham, are discussing plans for a high-level meeting in London this week to discuss the potential for a coalition to protect ships in the strait of Hormuz and de-mine the waterway. The discussions will be an early test for Burnham’s administration. The Labour government has so far refused to allow Washington to use a British airbase for offensive operations against Iran.

A man suspected of driving a van into a crowd near Berlin’s Pride festival then going on a knife rampage in an Islamist terror attack has been shot dead by police, German officials have said.

Police confirmed on Sunday evening that the chief suspect had been shot dead, reportedly during an operation at an allotment garden complex ⁠in the capital’s Spandau district.

One woman was killed on Saturday evening and 29 others were injured after a man drove a rented minivan into a crowd of pedestrians, then attacked people with what appeared to be a machete. The attack took place in the Tiergarten park near the Brandenburg Gate at about 10pm local time on Saturday, close to one of Europe’s biggest LGBTQ+ celebrations.

The attack forced organisers to cut short one of Europe’s largest Pride events and came as Germany remained on edge after a series of deadly vehicle and knife attacks.

The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, named the chief suspect as 21-year-old Abdul Ballout. “We are dealing ​here with ‌a suspected ‌perpetrator, who had previously drawn attention ‌to himself through a high volume of criminal offences, radicalisation and affiliation with the Islamist scene,” he told ‌a press conference near the site of the attack. He said Ballout had a criminal conviction and had been sentenced as a juvenile to a year and 10 months in prison, but that the sentence had been suspended.

German media reported that Ballout, a German national with Lebanese roots, was a supporter of Islamic State and last year travelled to the Middle East in a failed attempt to join the group. He was then convicted in Germany of “preparing a serious act of subversive violence”, the news outlets Bild and Der Spiegel reported.

Police and prosecutors had asked for help in finding Ballout, but warned the public to avoid “direct contact” with him, saying he may be armed and dangerous. Police searched an apartment in the Schöneberg district of Berlin near the scene of the attack in the early hours of Sunday, but said they had found no one there.

Before Ballout was shot, Der Spiegel spoke with his father, Tawfik, by telephone from Lebanon, where he was visiting relatives.

Describing Ballout as “generous, emotional, loving”, he said his son had lived with his mother, from whom Tawfik is divorced, and two of his three sisters. Ballout attended school until 10th grade, then bounced from job to job, in security or as a driver.

Tawfik described the family as Shia but “not extremely religious” and said it “does not support Islamic State”, an extremist Sunni group.

He and Ballout had fought about his hair and beard. “I did not allow him to wear a long beard,” he told Spiegel, calling it a symbol of extremism. Asked about a possible motive for the attack, he said: “He was brainwashed.”

Tawfik spoke with Ballout on Saturday, the day of the attack. “He called me and we spoke normally, like every day. He said he missed me and wished he was with us in Lebanon.”

The chancellor, Friedrich Merz, urged Germany to avoid division and intimidation in the aftermath of the attack. “We ​will think ​about ​consequences, we ​will ‌defend ​our freedom,” he said in a news conference.

Earlier, Merz vowed to punish those responsible, describing the “heinous act” as an “attack on our society” in a social media post. The flag at the German Bundestag was ordered to be lowered to half mast.

Police said the vehicle had struck multiple ⁠people after being driven into the Tiergarten. Shortly before 10pm the driver of the white minivan swerved into the park, close to where the route of the Pride march had been earlier in the day, hitting people on a path and crashing into a tree.

Bild cited a witness as saying that a man had emerged from the vehicle and fled on foot. A hunt involving helicopters and officers from several German states was under way across the capital on Sunday.

Julian Methig, who attended the event, described it as a nightmare come true. “It’s one of the worst days for the queer community and a day I personally hoped I’d never have to experience … I’m shocked,” he said.

Hundreds of thousands of people had gathered in Berlin in warm summer sunshine to celebrate the Pride parade. It is known in Germany as Christopher Street Day (CSD), named after the site of the Stonewall Inn in New York City where riots against police raids touched off the modern LGBTQ+ rights movement. CSD was first held in West Berlin in 1979.

Berlin’s mayor, Kai Wegner, called the deadly assault “an attack on our free and cosmopolitan society”.

“Following a peaceful and colourful CSD, the rally for a tolerant and peaceful Berlin was attacked in the most brutal manner,” he said on X. “Berlin is the city of freedom – and our freedom has today been attacked in the most appalling way. My thoughts are with the victims, their families and friends.”

For the first time in its history, CSD began on Friday night this year with a pro-democracy political rally. Berlin will hold a regional election in September along with two other states.

The parade on Saturday ran under the motto “taking a stand is hot”, which organisers said was “in response to increasing hostility” to LGBTQ+ people in Germany.

More than 80 floats and 50 groups on foot joined the procession through the city centre past Potsdamer Platz and the Victory Column monument in the Tiergarten, culminating in a rally at the Brandenburg Gate.

Earlier in the day one person was arrested for resisting police orders at a far-right counterprotest.

Before last year’s parade, Berlin LGBTQ+ organisations sounded the alarm that attacks had become more frequent while hard-won rights were under threat. Campaigners said a rise in hostility had accompanied the surge in support for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), now the most popular party in national opinion polls, as well as an increase in Islamist-inspired attacks.

European leaders offered solidarity, including heads of government in Belgium, the Netherlands and Sweden. “Italy firmly condemns and opposes all forms of hate and extremism,” the Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, wrote on X, adding: “We stand with Germany and the German people.” The French president, Emmanuel Macron, said: “Faced with hatred and violence, our response will always be unity, freedom, and resolve.”

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, a German centre-right politician allied with Merz, sent her deepest sympathy to the victims of the attack, describing the CSD parade as standing for “freedom, dignity and equality – the fundamental values of the EU”.

Britain’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said he was “horrified by the appalling attack in Berlin” and had spoken to his counterpart, Johann Wadephul, “to convey the UK’s solidarity: we stand with Germany”.

Far-right leaders were also quick to comment on the attacks. The co-leader of the AfD Tino Chrupalla wrote on X: “We will not allow religious extremists to divide our country with violence and intolerance!”

The president of France’s far-right National Rally, Jordan Bardella, wrote: “The Islamist threat remains a major issue in Europe and continues to target what they hate most about our civilisation – and what we cherish so much – freedom.”

Every new UK home should have air conditioning, say Liberal Democrats

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 17:34:32 GMT

Exclusive: Party says housing stock ‘woefully unprepared’ for extreme heat and new rules for builders must be set

All new UK homes should be built with air conditioning to cope with the effects of the climate crisis, according to the Liberal Democrats.

The party says British homes are dangerously unsuited to rising temperatures, meaning passive cooling measures such as planting more trees in residential areas are necessary.

The Lib Dems also want air conditioning to be mandatory in essential public buildings such as schools and health facilities.

The problem of overwarm homes has been highlighted by a UK Health Protection Agency yellow alert for high temperatures to run from Tuesday morning until Friday morning for the south-east, south-west and east of England, the Midlands, and Yorkshire and the Humber.

Temperatures in London are forecast to reach 32C (90F) on Wednesday, before cooling. Some other parts of the UK will be wet with notably lower temperatures.

As well as being hot, much of the summer has been exceptionally dry. In July so far, there has been just 5% of the average rainfall across England, falling to 1% in the south, bringing droughts and severe risk of wildfires.

The Lib Dems’ “climate ready” programme would make it a legal requirement for new homes to have either air conditioning or another cooling system. They say this is especially important for older people or those in poor health.

The number of UK homes with air conditioning has doubled in the past three years amid rising temperatures, according to industry estimates. However, this still comes to only about 4m of the estimated 30m-plus homes in the country.

According to polling commissioned by the Lib Dems, 28% of people said they had bought a fan or an air conditioning unit during the recent heatwaves, with 26% of respondents saying the conditions had left them feeling unwell or faint.

Tim Farron, the party’s environment spokesperson, said: “This latest set of relentless heatwaves has taught us that Britain is woefully unprepared for extreme heat, and families across Britain are paying for the cost of inaction.

“With another heatwave on the horizon, the government must step in with a new plan that takes the onus off already-struggling Brits and commits developers to build homes fit for the future – insulated properly and equipped with air conditioning.”

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 17:00:16 GMT

King’s Fund report finds men and women live, on average, for 80 years and nearly 84 years, but gains are in south

The north-south divide in life expectancy in England has grown over the past decade, with people in northern regions facing more illnesses such as heart disease and cancer, but also suicides and deaths related to alcohol and drug misuse.

Provisional figures show life expectancy reached an all-time high in 2025, with men and women in England living, on average, for 80 years and nearly 84 years respectively, but the gains were overwhelmingly in the south, the King’s Fund said.

Despite suffering the sharpest fall in lifespan during the Covid pandemic, life expectancy in London rose by nearly a year in the decade to 2023-25. The south-east, south-west and east of England also recorded gains.

But the half of England’s population who live in five northern regions, namely the north-west, the north-east, Yorkshire and the Humber, West Midlands and East Midlands, experienced little or no rise in life expectancy over the same period, reflecting greater levels of deprivation.

According to the health charity, people in London can now expect to live three years longer than those in the north-east. Even starker disparities emerged at the local level, with life expectancy in Blackpool, Lancashire, being 10 years shorter for men and eight years shorter for women than in Hart, Hampshire.

“In the most deprived 30% of areas, life expectancy either fell or didn’t improve over the past decade and that’s a disturbing story,” said Veena Raleigh, a senior fellow at the King’s Fund. “Meanwhile, it went up by half a year in the least deprived 30% of areas.”

“Over the past decade, the north has fallen further behind, and the plans for levelling up and the regeneration of the north haven’t materialised,” Raleigh added. “This isn’t just a question of fixing the health service. It requires a cross-government drive to also address the wider, underlying determinants of health, for example, ensuring people have secure jobs, fair pay, adequate housing, clean air, accessible transport and affordable access to healthy diets.”

The government’s 10-year plan for the NHS aims to increase healthy life expectancy – the number of years people spend in good health – for everyone in England, while halving the gap between the richest and poorest. But the King’s Fund called the goal “unrealistic”, requiring improvements in population health on a scale not seen in decades.

Healthy life expectancy fell in all regions of England in the decade to 2022-24, with people now spending on average about 2.5 years longer in poor health, the charity found. The regional divide has remained unchanged at about six to seven years, but can reach 20 years between the most and least deprived regions. The figures mean those in the most deprived parts of England have shorter lives and spend more years in poor health.

“Although the government’s 10-year health plan promises a shift from sickness to prevention, the focus is mainly on reducing waiting lists and waiting times,” Raleigh said. “Public health and prevention of ill health need to be much higher up the policy agenda, for example, to tackle the rising prevalence of obesity.

India’s Cockroach Janta party protest victory signals trouble ahead for Modi

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 16:42:31 GMT

Ally forced to resign, with opposition parties reinvigorated and strongman leader’s grip over media channels rocked

Even the night before Narendra Modi accepted the resignation of his education minister, India’s prime minister appeared confident that the largest mass uprising to take place in his 12 years in power would do little to rattle his government.

Addressing his “young friends” in a late-night Instagram selfie reel on Friday, he thanked the people – who were mobilised en masse across the country, shouting anti-government slogans – for their “thoughtful suggestions”.

Less than 24 hours later, Modi, who has fiercely cultivated his strongman image for years, had bowed to public pressure and accepted the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan. It was, say analysts, the remarkable humbling of a government that has ruled with almost untouchable impunity since 2014.

Over that past week, a gen Z movement that called itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) mobilised unprecedented protests in the name of justice for millions of young people, after the leaking of a crucial exam paper forced 2 million students to resit the test and was blamed for more than a dozen suicides.

The resignation of Pradhan, Modi’s loyal political ally, remained their first and foremost demand for accountability, even as the protests expanded into a wider fight for democracy. Yet Pradhan went unmentioned by Modi in his Instagram address.

On Saturday morning, more people than ever were pouring into Delhi’s historic Jantar Mantar site – the centre of the protests – and unrest was spreading fast to other cities, including states ruled by Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).

It was not only physical space that had been captured by the cockroach movement. Since coming to power, the BJP has proved enormously effective at capturing the online narrative, deploying its powerful, highly organised IT cell to mobilise and attack any perceived criticism of the government, whether it came from citizens, politicians or journalists.

But this proved no match for the millions of gen Z memes and reels that began to flood Instagram over this past week, fearlessly insulting Modi and pillorying the government, each more creative and incendiary than the next. Modi’s last-ditch attempts to speak directly to the youth on Instagram were simply met with more ridicule and spin-off memes.

Modi had also lost another medium critical to the BJP’s domination over the national narrative – the mainstream TV news channels widely acknowledged to have been co-opted by the BJP government over the past 12 years and turned into mouthpieces for its rightwing Hindu nationalist ideology.

Initially, the channels ignored the protests, and when they did cover them it was to suggest the protesters were being bankrolled by sinister foreign forces and Pakistani terror groups. In response, the protesters turned on the channels, using social media to expose their “lies”. When the protests escalated, Modi remained conspicuously absent from the airwaves.

Pradhan’s resignation came as it appeared that all other options for the government had gone. The option of a ruthless crackdown appeared untenable given the mass outcry to the police violence that had hit protesters on Monday.

“The online space was totally conquered by the protesters and regime-loving media was seriously delegitimised,” said Ashutosh Varshney, a professor of international studies at Brown University in Rhode Island. “The anger was so comprehensive there was no option left but for Pradhan to go.”

But this was more than the loss of a minister, Varshney said, it was also the first time in 12 years that the Modi government had lost control of the political narrative. “This is a repressive government,” he said. “It wants obedience, it wants no critical discussion and it generates fear. But now the climate of fear has collapsed.”

Analysts say the resignation of Pradhan could also have implications for Modi’s power over his own cabinet. Pradhan was one of Modi’s most loyal ministers and ideological footsoldiers, and had implemented policies exactly as senior party figures had wanted. He had also helped the BJP win Odisha state for the first time in the general election, bringing in crucial seats.

“Modi knows once you start firing your most loyal ministers, it sets up the incentives for defections in other ministers as well,” said the political columnist Pratap Bhanu Mehta. “If your own cabinet starts to hedge for a future where they may not be backed by your own government, that’s when you are in trouble.”

Prior to this week’s unrest, Modi had been riding high on a string of important state electoral victories, in particular the BJP’s first triumph in West Bengal, a politically important state that had long pushed back against its Hindu nationalist politics.

The BJP appeared to have fully bounced back from the blow in the 2024 elections, when the party failed to win an outright parliamentary majority and had to scramble together a large enough alliance to take power. At the same time, the much-beleaguered opposition had continued to lose countless state elections and their allegations of voting impropriety by the BJP fell mostly on deaf ears.

Yet the emergence of the cockroaches has reinvigorated not only India’s youth, but its political opposition parties as well. Jumping on the bandwagon, the opposition Congress party has had its best week in years as it mobilised protests and shut down parliament. The party’s leader, Rahul Gandhi, was dramatically dragged away by police outside Modi’s house in support of students.

Analysts say that dissent, which had been systematically crushed over the past 12 years, has now been re-galvanised as an effective tool to hold the government – and in particular the prime minister – to account.

“After a long time, there’s an assertion of political agency across different sections of society,” said Mehta. “And the minute you see that agency out in the street, it empowers lots of other agents.”

The next big test of the electoral implications of the CJP movement will come early next year, when India’s largest and most politically important state holds its state elections. Holding on to power in Uttar Pradesh, the BJP’s political heartland, is seen as crucial for the party and would have major implications for the next general election in 2029.

The grievances of India’s newly-politicised youth are extensive, including a chronic lack of graduate jobs and stagnant wages. Just how the CJP intends to politically mobilise after its striking victory on Saturday remains to be seen. Leaders and supporters insist this is just the “beginning”, particularly in their push for education reform. Their founder, Abhijeet Dipke, has some past experience as a political party organiser, but has not made his own ambitions known.

Yet analysts said that one of the most crucial impacts of the CJP had been to reopen a rapidly closing democratic space and make it seem possible that a new kind of political opposition could emerge, one reflective of the voices heard on the streets of India this week.

Saurav Das, a CJP spokesperson, said it was encouraging people involved in the movement to go into politics. “This is one of our goals,” he said. “We need to increase youth participation in politics, because right now it’s controlled by uncles and aunties who are only interested in looking after their own lifestyles and don’t understand the needs of our generation. The answer also has to be political.”

The Guardian view on a US-Saudi nuclear agreement: an offer that further erodes international safeguards

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 16:29:49 GMT

Even if no reactors are built, Donald Trump’s announcement of a double-standards deal with Riyadh has wrought further damage in a new era of proliferation

Even as he threatened to escalate an unlawful war sold in part as preventing Iran from gaining a nuclear weapon, Donald Trump opened the door to proliferation in the region on Wednesday. The US announced that it had signed a deal with Saudi Arabia which would potentially allow the kingdom to enrich uranium in future and to avoid the fullest inspection rights for the international watchdog.

Experts have long warned that a civilian nuclear programme could create a path towards a nuclear-armed Riyadh. Mohammed bin Salman, the Saudi crown prince and de facto leader, has said that if Tehran gets a nuclear weapon, “we will have to get one”. Concerns are magnified by the agreement’s terms. Washington previously argued that the “gold standard” was the United Arab Emirates’ agreement to permanently forgo enrichment and accept full monitoring by the UN’s International Atomic Energy Agency. Weakening it sets a precedent that Russia or China could also cite in nuclear deals in future.

The turmoil that Mr Trump has created in the Middle East is encouraging governments both to hedge their bets and to tool up. The US paused attacks on Iran at the weekend, after 13 successive days of strikes, amid reports that it is concerned about declining interceptor stockpiles, but no exit is in sight. As António Guterres, the UN secretary general, said on Thursday, the region “is teetering on the edge of [the] unimaginable … One crisis feeds another. One escalation triggers the next.”

Gulf states premised their security on American-guaranteed order. But Benjamin Netanyahu’s strike on Hamas leaders in Qatar last year showed that the US shield would not protect them from Israel (itself an undeclared nuclear power). The reckless war on Iran has made US military presence an invitation to damage. Washington may be looking to bind Riyadh closer with a reactor deal, though the billions of dollars involved is probably a bigger incentive for Mr Trump. The crumbling of the region’s internal architecture – most visibly with the UAE’s departure from Opec – adds to the dangers of proliferation. Players are acting less predictably.

The US president threw the Saudi deal into doubt within hours by declaring it contingent on Riyadh recognising Israel. That had long been a precondition for an agreement, but Israel’s war of annihilation in Gaza has shored up the Saudi position that recognition cannot happen without a Palestinian state. Yet even if no reactors are built, the announcement itself acts as legitimation of and encouragement for the pursuit of nuclear capabilities by others. Negotiations produced an Obama-era nuclear deal with which Tehran complied – until Mr Trump trashed the agreement. His war appears to have produced a more aggressive, risk-taking Iranian regime, as foretold; further military action is more likely to spur than end nuclear threat. The prospect of Riyadh acquiring a bomb is further encouragement.

Look further afield. The last US-Russia nuclear arms control treaty expired in February. China is rapidly expanding its arsenal. Asian and European states which counted on the US nuclear umbrella prior to Mr Trump are discussing acquiring or enhancing their own capabilities. Most of them at least understand that diplomacy, multilateralism and global standards are a better choice than a race for the bomb. Mr Trump does not believe in international institutions. But upholding existing nuclear safeguards would be in US interests too as we enter a new age of proliferation.

The Guardian view on a new director at Tate: an old institution must tackle fresh issues

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 16:27:49 GMT

A decline in visitor numbers, staff strikes and budget cuts – Jessica Morgan faces many challenges as she takes on the biggest role in the British arts scene

A lack of clear vision, low morale, dwindling popularity and financial shortfalls – this may sound like a description of the previous Labour government, but these are also criticisms levelled at the UK’s most powerful arts institution, Tate. Maria Balshaw’s tenure as the first female director of Tate – comprising Tate Modern, Tate Britain, Tate Liverpool and Tate St Ives – lasted nine years and saw as many culture secretaries. One of Sir Keir Starmer’s last acts as prime minister was to approve the appointment of her successor, Jessica Morgan, a former curator at Tate and head of the Dia Art Foundation in New York.

With record-breaking Frida Kahlo and Tracey Emin shows currently at Tate Modern, suggestions that Ms Morgan is inheriting an institution in a state of “existential crisis” seem exaggerated. Tate Britain, often overshadowed by its more fashionable younger sister, pulled in crowds for its Turner & Constable and Lee Miller exhibitions. These blockbusters in the past year also rebut accusations that Ms Balshaw focused on little-known artists instead of bankable stars. Her commitment to diversifying the collection will surely be taken up by Ms Morgan, who also has a strong track record in promoting marginalised artists. Ms Balshaw is leaving on a high.

But after the double blow of Brexit and Covid, Tate has had a turbulent few years. The number of London visitors last year was still more than 2 million below pre-pandemic levels, with the number of 16- to 24-year-olds from Europe nearly halved. Yet Tate Modern remains one of the top 10 most visited museums in the world. The reopening of Tate Liverpool, which closed for refurbishment in 2023, has been delayed until 2027 because of lack of funding. Last year’s redundancies and staff strikes across the galleries showed an institution under pressure.

It is a far cry from when Nicholas Serota spearheaded Tate Modern just over 25 years ago on the crest of Cool Britannia and the rise of the Young British Artists. Olafur Eliasson’s The Weather Project, which filled the Turbine Hall with a giant sun and entranced over 2 million visitors in 2003, seemed to herald a bright future. But recent Turbine Hall commissions have lost their shine. Even the Turner prize looks tired, with the Guardian’s Jonathan Jones lamenting its retreat “into wilful obscurity” and some critics calling for it to be scrapped.

Looming external challenges include the National Gallery’s recent announcement of plans to ditch its 1900 cut-off, thereby encroaching on Tate Modern’s territory, and the possibility of an end to free museum access in the UK. Both raise fundamental questions for the direction of Tate. Then there is the increasingly problematic issue of funding. Ms Balshaw was right to take a stand against arts donations from fossil fuel companies.

According to a profile in The Gentlewoman, Ms Morgan is not just “one of the great collection-builders of our time”, but is also (though British) “armed with an American unflappability about asking rich people for money”. Gavin Turk, one of the YBAs, compared the role to “the England football manager job now”; the director must be able to support artists and “convince the public with the shows they put on”. Like the new prime minister, Ms Morgan has been hailed as “an agent of change”. How to make lasting change, without alienating core supporters, while inspiring confidence at home and abroad – all when budgets are tight – is the momentous task facing both.

Aziz Abdul faces England’s Damar Thomas in Glasgow

Damar Thomas, the English super-heavyweight, must overcome the grandson of Idi Amin, the former Ugandan dictator and self-proclaimed “King of Scotland”, if he is to progress into the medal rounds of Commonwealth Games boxing competition in Glasgow on Wednesday.

Aziz Abdul, known as “Ringo”, is not shy of his family connection to Amin, a brutal military dictator who seized power in 1971, killing up to 500,000 people and expelling Uganda’s entire Asian population before he was deposed and sent into exile eight years later.

Amin was an accomplished boxer who held the Ugandan light-heavyweight title for nine consecutive years from 1951 to 1960. Having lost a bout to Peter Sseruwagi in 1958, he orchestrated a rematch after becoming president, delivering a staged knockout of his opponent while still wearing his suit jacket and tie.

“My grandfather’s achievements inspired me,” the 25-year-old Abdul said. “He was a heavyweight boxer like myself, and I am so proud of him. Lions give back to lions. A lion cannot give back to a dog or a camel. A lion must resemble a lion. It is what it is. I am a real warrior. I am the son of the son.”

Amin declared himself the “King of Scotland” in 1976, having developed a fascination with the country during his time serving in the King’s African Rifles regiment in his 20s. His remark inspired an Oscar-winning film, The Last King Of Scotland, starring the Glasgow-born actor James McAvoy.

Abdul hails from the same remote West Nile region as his grandfather, who died in 2003, and displays the same bullish confidence despite a daunting draw. Thomas, a 21-year-old European youth champion, is aiming to become the fourth consecutive English winner of the +90kg title.

Abdul said he will rely on his mysterious “Ringo punch” to get the job done before the judges get the chance to intervene, making good on the advice of Amin, who once advised that “the only way to defeat an enemy who is against the country is to win by knockout”.

“I am very happy to be fighting the English fighter,” Abdul added. “I have waited for this moment for three years. But now we are not in Africa, we are in Europe. As my grandpa used to say, you need to win by knockout, so that’s what we have trained for and that’s what I hope to do.

The City trader turned wealth tax campaigner Gary Stevenson has announced he is quitting the YouTube channel that made his name, citing health concerns.

His announcement, in a 48-minute address to camera, came after a mixed reaction to a televised documentary that brought him to a wider audience but drew some scepticism from left-leaning tax experts as well as more rightwing critics.

Stevenson, whose weekly YouTube channel Gary’s Economics took off during the Covid pandemic and grew to 1.64 million subscribers, posted an abridged 18-minute signoff on social media on Sunday morning entitled “It’s time to say goodbye”.

He said it would be the last weekly video, saying they had become “harder and harder as he had got more tired”.

The former City trader, born in 1986 in east London, came to wider prominence through the channel and his published memoir, Trading Game, in which he described how he made millions as a Citibank employee in the years after the financial crisis.

Retiring with burnout and disillusioned by the City, the self-styled anti-inequality campaigner argued for a 2% tax on individual wealth over £10m, which he said would raise £24bn a year for the Treasury.

Stevenson has been an influential online voice in raising awareness of inequality and linking it to falling living standards, predicting the rises in the cost of living and warning about the danger to society of constant accumulation by the growing billionaire class.

However, a Channel 4 documentary released last month, How to Get Filthy Rich with Gary Stevenson, in which he took his arguments to those who would incur the tax, was poorly received.

The Guardian’s Lucy Mangan wrote that the presenter was “outdone and undone by almost all of his interviewees … left floundering, without convincing comebacks”, concluding that it was “a faintly embarrassing waste of time”.

The expert tax lawyer and investigator Dan Neidle told Stevenson “to separate your emotional reaction to inequality from a rational assessment of the best tools for it” and described his plans as “populist claptrap”.

A slightly more sympathetic review in the Telegraph said Stevenson had “all the traits of the self-aggrandising online influencer class … so used to addressing his followers straight down the camera that engaging in debate with people of differing views leaves him floundering”.

Despite the reception to the documentary, Stevenson’s proposal for a wealth tax is gaining traction. The new prime minister, Andy Burnham, is fielding growing calls to increase taxes on the ultra-rich.

He started one Premier League game last season despite the problems Liverpool had in attack because of injuries to Alexander Isak and Hugo Ekitiké, and his last start came in the FA Cup fourth-round win against Brighton on 14 February. A change of head coach, Chiesa hopes, will herald a change in fortune as a Liverpool player.

“It is always a fresh start at the beginning of the year,” said the 28-year-old, who produced a fine finish in Liverpool’s 4-2 friendly defeat of Sunderland in Nashville on Saturday. “Maybe there have been too many fresh starts [for him]. But I don’t care, I am trying to do my best for this new manager.

“Last season under Arne Slot, I was trying to do my best. Last year I felt ready for a bigger role, then it depended on the coach whether he wanted me to play or not. Of course I wanted to play more but it is what it is. The gaffer had his gameplans, he took his decisions, I have nothing to say about that. It is football. This year, let us say it is a new chapter. There is a new manager and I have to focus on that.”

Chiesa admits he has not discussed his future with Iraola since the Basque coach succeeded Slot in June. “The only conversations I had were about pressing and tactics,” he said. “He put me striker against Sunderland and he wants me there.”

But the Italy international, who has two years remaining on his Liverpool contract, claimed his priority is to prove himself to the head coach rather than seek a return to Serie A. Como and former club Juventus have been linked with a move for the forward.

“Right now, at the moment, I am happy here at Liverpool,” said Chiesa. “I love the club, I love the fans, I love everything. I am doing the best I can to have a chance here. And then we will see. At the minute, the only thing I am thinking about is Liverpool.”

Liverpool secured Champions League qualification on the final day of a troubled season in May in what proved to be Slot’s final game in charge. Chiesa insists that was no cause for celebration at a club of Liverpool’s stature and there must be improvement next term.

Ed Miliband indicates development and climate will be at heart of UK foreign policy

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 16:00:15 GMT

Exclusive: Foreign secretary to take up World Bank seat and play active role in shaping changes to global lender

Britain’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is to indicate he will put the climate crisis and overseas development at the heart of UK international relations by taking up the country’s seat on the board at the World Bank.

The position, which is usually delegated to a junior minister, means Miliband will play an active role in shaping the changes to the World Bank that developing countries have called for, and ensuring the climate remains a core focus for overseas aid.

Miliband, who was energy and net zero secretary under Keir Starmer, will say: “International development is not an add-on to British foreign policy – it is central to it. By taking on the role of UK governor to the World Bank, I want to send an unambiguous signal that this government is serious about its global leadership on development and climate.”

His announcement comes as fires continue to devastate swathes of France and Spain, and after Scotland called for military aid to tackle a blaze that engulfed the Cairngorms. Conditions approaching drought across England and parts of Wales have prompted hosepipe bans, and the heatwave that swept across Europe in June is estimated to have cost the continent’s grain farmers €2bn (£1.7bn) in lost revenue.

By taking up the World Bank seat personally, Miliband is sending a clear signal that while other politicians even now argue against net zero policies, the Foreign Office will continue to drive climate action.

The move comes at a crucial time for the international lender, which has come under heavy pressure from the Trump administration to reverse a previous focus on climate finance. Last month, the publicly funded bank scrapped its goal for 45% of its finance to be directed to climate-related ends.

Experts welcomed Miliband’s decision as a boost to climate action. Lord Stern, a professor of economics at the London School of Economics, said the foreign secretary’s take-up of the UK governor’s seat would “send a powerful and important signal” to the world.

“As a former chief economist and senior vice-president of the World Bank, I know that the UK can punch above its weight,” he said. “But only if the leadership is there from the top. In recent years, that has slipped. Ed Miliband will be restoring development and climate to the priority in our international relationships that they must have, in a world facing climate and biodiversity crises, and with real and growing threats to the wellbeing of the world’s poorest.”

Other countries have been wary of challenging the US on its anti-climate stance, for fear of reprisals and after widespread cuts to developed countries’ overseas aid. The UK is one of six countries with its own seat at the World Bank board.

Mohamed Adow, a director of Power Shift Africa, a thinktank, said Miliband could champion changes at the lender that would help the poor.

“The real test is whether the UK uses its influence to push the World Bank to deliver far more finance for climate action and adaptation, to get money to countries faster, and ensure the poorest nations are not forced deeper into debt to respond to a crisis they did least to cause,” Adow said. “If this appointment marks the start of renewed British leadership on global climate and development, it will be warmly welcomed across Africa.”

Miliband will face a shrinking aid budget and tough decisions over allocation. Starmer slashed overseas aid to 0.3% of gross national income, a sharp reduction from 0.5% under the Conservatives and the 0.7% reached under the last Labour government. Climate finance was also cut by 14%, from £11.6bn for the period 2021 to 2026 to £2bn a year.

Earlier on Sunday, passengers posted online that they were unable to get hot drinks, wash their hands or fill water bottles at the airport in Sussex.

The problem also had an impact in the wider Sussex and Kent area, water suppliers said.

SES Water said there had been interruptions to water supplies in parts of the TN11, RH1, RH6 and RH10 postcode areas.

At 2pm the company had said its Bough Beech water treatment works were running again but the water needed to be treated before services could return to normal.

On Facebook, one user posted: “Gasping for a drink & crossing my legs right now. This is ridiculous! Gatwick airport has shut all restaurants and most toilets due to a water outage. Not a great start to the holiday.”

Ofwat has no effective powers of enforcement, it seems.

The new prime minister should consider imposing a very large tax burden on water company shareholders to fund the replacement of old pipes and the building of new reservoirs. Our water bills are the highest they’ve ever been, our need for water is greater than ever, but leaky pipes are causing a water shortage.

Arts and humanities have a role in understanding space exploration

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 15:58:12 GMT

Prof Abbie Garrington reflects on an interview with the physicist Laura Grego about the battle for our skies

Where are the arts and humanities in current debates about space research? The physicist Laura Grego tells us we “have to be aware of what is happening in space”, that we should probe Elon Musk’s potential “appropriation” of space via satellite, and that our spacefaring era raises questions about our stewardship of the Earth for future generations, and the significance of human culture (‘Most people don’t know we’ve set up a doomsday system’: physicist Laura Grego on satellites, nuclear weapons and the battle for our skies, 20 July).

Meanwhile, your interviewer Aida Edemariam notes both the Artemis mission’s potential to inspire, and the relegation of most of us to an audience agog, with no say in civilisational decisions about major space missions.

The sciences cannot tackle these matters alone. Successive UK governments have prioritised Stem subjects, while our forthcoming national space strategy will focus on economic growth and national security, so major leaps in technologies of exploration and surveillance come to the fore in what is effectively a second space race. Yet listening to Grego, it’s clear we also need new collaborative structures, theories of jurisdiction and laws; new philosophies of the human, the unique status of human culture, and interplanetary environmental responsibility; and a sharp eye on the history of human hubris.

Durham University’s Space Research Centre, and the new Leverhulme Centre for Humanity and Space at the University of Leicester, might show us the way. Addressing arts and humanities layoffs at our universities (at Exeter and Edinburgh most recently), we rightly worry about what the British Academy calls “cold spots” around the UK where students will miss out on enriching subjects.

We should also be talking about these cuts as a national diminishment of subjects which, among many other functions, are essential to the UK’s flourishing in a new phase of space exploration. Prof Abbie GarringtonUniversity of Durham

Or should I say his “confession”, as the social power of the shampoo message is strong enough to make most of us “no pooers” keep a low profile.

I’ve not used shampoo for at least five years. I rub my hair through in the shower every morning, and either towel or air-dry it. Every day is a now a good-hair day – mine is thick, glossy and easy to style, with a very slight waxy feel that comes with the natural oils that hair products are designed to strip away and then replace (badly). I would only shampoo my hair now if I swam through something nasty in the sea or if a bird crapped on me. Paddy EasonLondon

I went through a “no poo” phase in 2012. It was a turbo-hippy phase where I learned about the method from a man who had the most beautiful, luscious long hair, and he’d been doing this for 10 years. He washed his hair with water. So, convinced, I tried it. I lasted nine months, waiting for my hair to get the same texture. It just remained greasy. But I discovered sulphate-free and paraben-free shampoo, and it changed my life. Kerri ThorntonGlasgow

Lando Norris wins F1 Hungarian GP for first victory of season as Piastri retires

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 15:14:42 GMT

World champion wins from pole; Piastri’s gearbox fails

Verstappen second, championship leader Antonelli third

Lando Norris finally had reason to celebrate after a testing opening to the season, as McLaren’s defending Formula One world champion took his first win of the year at the Hungarian Grand Prix.

However, while the victory was thoroughly deserved in an incident-packed race, there was an all too familiar feel to the bigger picture as Kimi Antonelli emerged from a weekend that might have been considered damage limitation for the Mercedes driver having once more extended his advantage at the top of the drivers’ championship.

Norris was implacable with an assured drive from pole at the Hungaroring, achieving McLaren’s record 14th win at the circuit. He maintained his cool having lost the lead to his teammate, Oscar Piastri, in the second corner and then showed relentless pace in going on to retake it through the pit stops. The Australian was unlucky and was left fuming that he had been blocked and struck while trying to lap the backmarker Carlos Sainz in a Williams at a crucial point.

Ultimately Piastri had to retire with a gearbox problem but by then Norris had the race by the scruff of the neck and, in clean air out front, had powered into a commanding lead. By the flag he led Max Verstappen by 15 seconds, as the upgrades McLaren brought to Hungary proved to be working to great effect, especially in the British driver’s hands.

Behind him, Antonelli again put the squeeze on his title rivals by returning big points from an unlikely position. The Italian started from seventh, after a three-place grid penalty, but put in a very strong comeback drive to take third place. Moreover, Antonelli’s Mercedes teammate George Russell was left once more to curse a run of ill-fortune that haunts him as a blight he seems unable to shrug off.

Russell’s car went into anti-stall on the grid, dropping him to 20th, a mechanical problem that led Toto Wolff, the team principal, to say Mercedes had to stop making mistakes. As Russell had applied a little throttle on the grid the power had surged, so he backed off it and the anti-stall was activated. He drove hard to come back to seventh but has dropped even more points to the Italian as the sport goes into its summer break, with Antonelli now leading Lewis Hamilton by 50 points and Russell by 59.

Like Russell, Piastri can consider himself to be on the very unlucky side of the ledger. He had been leading but was impeded and struck by Sainz as he tried to lap the Spaniard. Piastri was very nearly knocked off the track but just held control to race on.

An act of kindness, or mitzvah, teaches us to be part of something bigger than ourselves

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 15:00:16 GMT

More than anything, I want my kids to grow into people who notice others and who care about the world around them

Making sense of it is a column about spirituality and how it can be used to navigate everyday life

Several times a week, I write small notes on pretty stationery for my three-year-old daughter to take to kinder the next day.

Sometimes the note is about how she shared a toy with a sibling, other times it is about how she helped someone without being asked and often it is praising her for saying thank you or please.

In our family, we call them mitzvah notes.

The Hebrew word mitzvah is often translated as a good deed, but perhaps the best way to describe a mitzvah is an intentional act of goodness and kindness.

My daughter proudly takes her mitzvah notes to kinder, where her teacher reads them out loud to the whole class. The notes are then pinned to a wall filled with other children’s mitzvah notes, celebrating the good deeds of her three-year-old peers.

So, while other children covet stickers or prizes, my daughter is thrilled when she gets a mitzvah note and loves it when she has one to take to school.

As a parent, I spend a lot of time thinking about what values I want to pass on to my kids. Of course, I want my children to be capable and confident, and I want them to work hard, and develop resilience. But more than anything, I want them to grow into people who notice others, and who care about the world around them. I want them to understand that even the smallest acts of goodness and kindness can have a ripple effect far beyond what we can ever see.

There is a verse in the Bible, in the Book of Proverbs, that says: “Train a child according to their path, and even when they are old, they will not depart from it.”

I have always loved this quote, because to me it represents the idea that children grow into the identities we help them see in themselves.

When I want my children to help clean up their rooms and they are feeling particularly reluctant, instead of focusing on what they are not doing, I usually try to say something like, “I love when you help mummy clean up your room.”

By framing the request like this, I am reminding them of who I think they are. That as their mum, I see them as someone who helps, someone who cares and someone who tries to do the right thing.

This is what makes mitzvah notes so powerful. They are not just about praising a single action, but rather, they are about building a mindset where children want to be noticed for the good deeds that they do. They encourage children to look outward rather than inward, and they teach every human that they are part of something bigger than themselves.

After the Bondi terror attack, many people were left asking what they could do in the face of such darkness.

One response was a renewed focus on acts of kindness, and with consultation from the Jewish community, a national day to perform mitzvot was announced for people of all faiths to try to bring more light into the world. Across Australia, people volunteered at soup kitchens, cleaned beaches, visited elderly people in nursing homes, and found small ways to be kind to others.

None of those acts could undo the tragedy that occurred, but they reflected a belief that darkness spreads when people withdraw from one another, while goodness grows when people choose to do small acts of goodness and kindness for each other.

And perhaps that is why I love mitzvah notes so much.

They are small notes, jotted down in a minute or less, yet they carry a much bigger message. They tell a child, “I saw what you did, and I love that you are doing small acts of kindness,” and they encourage them to continue doing small acts of goodness and kindness.

And if enough children grow up believing that being kind and thoughtful is part of who they are, then perhaps those small notes are doing far more than recognising a good deed. Perhaps they are helping raise the sort of people our world needs right now.

Nomi Kaltmann is an Australian lawyer and journalist. She is a proud member of Melbourne’s Jewish community

From TikTok appearances to ‘sugar rush’ policies, new prime minister is taking different approach to predecessor

Six weeks ago Andy Burnham was not even an MP; now the former mayor of Greater Manchester is the most important political figure in Britain. After orchestrating a bloodless coup against Keir Starmer, in which he was crowned as Labour leader unopposed, the new prime minister has started his tenure in Downing Street with some eye-catching policies and a radically different approach to communication. A week into the job, how do their leadership styles compare?

Ever since his first big speech at the People’s History Museum in Manchester, at which he took no questions but made all the headlines anyway, Burnham has resisted media scrutiny. He did just three interviews as an MP before becoming prime minister – and since entering No 10 has had a brief huddle with political editors and several broadcast pool clips. Instead, his early focus seems to be on social media, answering softball questions on Reddit, appearing alongside viral TikTok stars Bus Aunty and Max Klymenko, and replying to X posts by members of the public.

While Keir Starmer has upped his social media game in recent weeks, his Downing Street operation recognised that “traditional” media still had power to drive the narrative and – while he didn’t much like it – he regularly subjected himself to scrutiny. Burnham’s team say he will take more questions, but it hasn’t happened yet.

Before he became prime minister, Burnham promised to do politics differently, and he didn’t just mean wearing T-shirts and jeans. “I want to answer questions honestly in this job … I’m determined to keep working in that way.” One of his big selling points with Labour MPs was that he could connect more naturally with the public than Starmer, who was often criticised for sticking to the script and coming across as wooden.

But, as Burnham has already found, his words now carry greater weight. He has already been accused of performing U-turns over issues including raising the income tax threshold – when he was really just speaking openly about his ideas before they were fully formed. “It’s funny, these days you can’t answer a question honestly without then people reading everything else into it,” he said. His critics may call him naive, but his more relaxed style may go down well with the public.

Grabbing public attention has been one of the big ambitions for Burnham’s first week in office – partly so voters know he’s there, but also to show that he’s different from Starmer, and will shout about what his government is doing. As a result, there have been a series of “sugar rush” cost of living announcements designed to give the public some much-needed breathing space – a VAT cut on electricity bills, a £2 bus fare cap and a 20% business rate cut for pubs.

In contrast, Starmer wanted to focus on long-term solutions over what he called “short-term sticking plasters”. Burnham’s energy bills announcement – the equivalent of reducing electricity bills by £45 a year on average – crystallised their different approaches. It is to be paid for by scrapping the digital ID system, which advocates argue could have saved the government tens of billions in the long term by making public services more efficient. The question remains: what happens when the sugar hit wears off?

Burnham’s first big announcement on returning to Westminster was that he was going to set up No 10 North as the “nerve centre of a rewired Britain” to oversee a devolution of power and resources across the UK. While opposition parties have dismissed this as a gimmick, the new PM says he is determined to oversee a genuine shift of power from Whitehall to local communities via his Manchester operation.

after newsletter promotion

Yet he has also created a powerful new PM’s department taking in both No 10s, parts of the Cabinet Office, Treasury and housing ministry – all overseen by his close ally Louise Haigh, to become the “dominant driver of the UK’s economy”. Antonia Romeo, the United Kingdom’s most senior civil servant, has reportedly been given a seat in the coveted space of No 10’s outer office just outside the prime minister’s study.

Starmer also promised to kickstart a new era of devolution, passing a bill allowing mayors to ask for new powers at the end of April – just before the local election trouncing that precipitated his downfall. He also pledged to reverse what he called “the tepid bath of managed decline” in Whitehall, putting his chief secretary, Darren Jones, in charge of its “rewiring” in January this year. Jones said civil servants who did not meet expectations would be “shown the door” – in the end, he followed his boss through it six months later.

Burnham, who first became an MP in 2001 before resigning to become mayor of Greater Manchester in 2017, is steeped in the party’s lores and traditions. Back in 2009 he told the Guardian that the three most important things in his life, aside from family, were “Everton FC, the Labour party and the Catholic church – in that order”. After becoming a candidate to lead the party at his third time of asking, he insisted in a letter to the parliamentary Labour party that he would never use party discipline to “stifle debate” and wanted to create a “different culture where everyone has a part to play”.

MPs, apart from angry Starmer loyalists, lapped it up. Not least because of the contrast to the hard line against dissent that Starmer and his team showed in the early days of his tenure, when many were suspended for defying the party line. But there are already those questioning Burnham’s pledge to end factional infighting after he removed or demoted more than half of the outgoing prime minister’s cabinet in his first reshuffle.

Exfoliate, use ice and conceal eyebags wisely – makeup artists on how to look fabulous, at every age

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 15:00:15 GMT

Are you stuck in a makeup rut? Or maybe just beginning to wear cosmetics? Here, experts reveal how to to find the right products for you

Makeup trends change over time – and so does our skin. How can you enhance what you have and refresh your look? Here, makeup artists share the fundamentals of applying cosmetics, at every age.

Whatever your age, “first and foremost is skincare,” says Kate Hughes, who works as a freelance makeup artist in London and Ibiza. “No good skincare, no good makeup. Full stop. I’m a big advocate of this.”

Hughes, who specialises in midlife beauty, explains that as we age, the turnover of our cells slows down. “The dead skin cells stay on top of the skin, giving you that dull look, and we want to look fresh – dewy is the buzzword.” People often say her skin is glowing and ask how she manages this at 56. “It is because I exfoliate three to four times a week, sometimes every day.” If you are starting from scratch, Hughes suggests exfoliating once a week at first, then slowly building up. “You could start off with exfoliating pads, anything from Boots’ own to First Aid Beauty, and then go on to a liquid exfoliant, like Paula’s Choice 2% BHA Liquid Exfoliant.”

Children are getting into cosmetics younger than ever before. “I don’t think there is a ‘right’ age to start wearing makeup,” says makeup artist Bobbi Brown, founder of Jones Road Beauty and Bobbi Brown cosmetics, who lives in New Jersey. “It depends on the child, their maturity and, honestly, their interest.”

Brown advises keeping it simple: “A little lip gloss, a tinted moisturiser, maybe a touch of blush or mascara when they’re older. The goal isn’t to look like someone else. It is to look like yourself, just a little more polished. Too much makeup is when it starts to feel like you’re covering yourself up instead of enhancing what is already there. Confidence will always be the best thing you can wear.”

From adolescence on, hiding spots is often the focus. “The biggest mistake I see is people trying to cover every blemish with a thick layer of makeup,” says Brown. “It usually ends up drawing more attention to it. Use a lightweight complexion product if you want to even out your skin, but don’t feel you need full coverage everywhere. Spot conceal only where you need it, using a concealer that matches your skin tone, then blend the edges so it disappears into your skin. Less is almost always more.”

“Pinpoint concealing is one of my most-asked-about techniques,” says Lisa Eldridge, a New Zealand-born, London-based makeup artist who received an MBE for her work in 2025. “My philosophy involves resisting the urge to apply a thick layer of blanket coverage to the skin, and precisely concealing only the areas you feel are absolutely necessary to disguise, moving focus to the skin in between your problem areas.”

Hughes is spending the summer working in Ibiza, where it is 80% humidity and 30C at 9am. How can you prevent makeup from melting off? “Use a grippy primer – Maybelline do a fabulous one – then spray your face with a setting spray, put your makeup on and spray again. If you layer makeup, you get more longevity in the heat. The sandwich method, we call it.” But this is more for special occasions than every day, Hughes adds.

Hughes also stresses the importance of wearing a high SPF and staying out of the sun: “If I sit outside, I’m in the shade. I wear a baseball cap and glasses all the time. I wear SPF on my body and my face religiously. The face factor 50s are brilliant now: Nivea has brought out a couple that are like primers. You don’t feel like you’ve got suntan lotion underneath your makeup, which can feel claustrophobic. A dermatologist said to me you can either have good skin or a suntan. You can’t have both.”

Eye bags are a common issue from middle age onwards, thanks to ageing skin and exhaustion levels. It can be tempting to want to hide them. “As we get older, the skin under our eyes becomes thinner and drier, so heavy concealer tends to settle into fine lines and emphasise texture,” says Brown. “Instead, focus on hydration first. A good eye cream and moisturiser will make any makeup you apply look better.”

“If you have bags, it’s all about finding the right eye cream for you,” agrees Antonio Cruz, a Venezuelan makeup artist in Manchester. “Eye creams with caffeine are fantastic. You have to be consistent, because a lot of people buy a cream, use it once, they are not sure [if it works], put it away” – and it definitely won’t work then. “You need to wear it for at least for 28 days,” says Cruz. “It doesn’t need to be expensive. What matters is how consistent you are in applying that eye cream, moisturiser, retinol. The more skincare you do, the less makeup you will need.”

“You’ve got to regulate sleep,” says Hughes, which can be easier said than done. “Eye bags come from within, not from outside. If I’ve had a bad night’s sleep, I’ve got some ice rollers in my freezer – they take down the puffiness and really tighten the skin.”

“One of my favourite remedies for refreshing tired eyes are homemade green tea ice cubes,” says Eldridge. “They are great for boosting circulation and for draining the fluid under the eyes. Make a cup of strong green tea, allow it to cool, then pour into an ice-cube tray. Once frozen, wrap a single cube in a piece of muslin or gauze and use the cube to gently massage and press under and around the eyes for a few minutes.”

“Then you need to be quite creative with your concealer,” says Hughes. “Find a really hydrating concealer with good pigment. Again, layer it. Apply a little bit, blend, then apply more. I probably put four to five coats of concealer on my face. If you didn’t blend that correctly in between, it would look awful. I can use Rimmel or Chanel – I’m still going to get the same finish. Application is king.”

“A lot of people are happy to apply foundation by hand,” says Cruz, “but the bristles of a brush would be better at blending the foundation into the skin,” to give a smoother effect. A sponge like a Beauty Blender can work well, says Hughes, but on the whole she has more of a “whatever works for you” approach – although she does stress that if you use your hands, quite a lot of makeup will get lost on them. “Some days I’ll put my concealer on with my fingers because I’m in a rush. I use brushes if I want to get a really good finish.”

“Your goal shouldn’t be to erase every line or wrinkle,” says Brown. “As skin changes, I find that less makeup usually looks better. Focus on skincare, hydration and lightweight formulas that let your skin show through. Heavy foundation and too much powder can make skin look older.”

If you are worried about signs of ageing, focus on your favourite features, says Hughes. “So many people say to me: ‘I really don’t like this about myself.’ Well, then put a bright lip on, or do a really soft, smoky eye, and that will take away the focus on the thing that you don’t like.”

Cruz used to work for YSL at the Trafford Centre in Manchester and saw customers who “probably learned how to do their makeup in the 70s and 80s and just carried on with those techniques”. To update your look, he advises chatting to beauty counter makeup artists and possibly having a makeup lesson (top tip: bring along what you already have rather than buying all new stuff), or look online for inspiration.

Hughes recommends recreating the actor Zendaya’s recent eye makeup that went viral – “eyeshadow in the corner of the eyes that gives you a fresh and glowy look”. For more mature skin, rather than a shimmery shadow go for “a lighter concealer, blended right in, which can really open up the eyes”.

Linasha Kotalawala, a makeup artist and beauty content creator in west London, loves the trend for brightly coloured liner and mascara: “I am obsessed with an NYX liner in a metallic, bluish mermaid colour – it is so beautiful on the skin – and then I apply Marc Jacobs’ blue mascara on top.” She says after the post-Covid clean girl aesthetic, renewed attention on colour is “making makeup fun again”.

Those who came of age in the early 00s may be fixated on cat-eye flicks, which can look dated. How can you wean yourself off them? “Small adjustments can make a big difference,” says Eldridge. “The black eyeliner you may have loved for decades can start to close the eye slightly, whereas softening the tone or lifting the placement can create a fresher, more wide awake look. Or you could apply a powder shadow over liquid liner to soften it while keeping impact – a trick I use for the red carpet because it photographs beautifully.”

“You will be surprised how many men love it, or secretly love it,” says Cruz, who personally likes to go “full glam”, to show off his credentials. “I normally joke to men: ‘Don’t worry, you won’t look like me.’”

Cruz did prime minister Andy Burnham’s makeup for a BBC interview three years ago: “He had been on that TV show a few times, so he knew the deal. You would be surprised by the amount of men who, after we do a little bit of powder or something, they notice a difference, and it gives them a boost of confidence.”

Eldridge says: “One of the most popular products for men is concealer. We all need help sometimes to conceal a late night or a temporary blemish. As with everyone, the main thing to avoid is anything that’s too light-reflective. Men’s skin tends to be thicker than women’s, so anything thick or drying will be too visible. If it’s undetectable coverage you’re going for, look for sheer textures.”

When you get new makeup, make sure you practise putting it on at home, and don’t just apply it for the first time when you are about to go out, advises Cruz. Often, “people only do their makeup when their friends are waiting for them or they have to take a train, and it’s very rushed, like it’s an afterthought.”

Matching a foundation correctly is one of the hardest things to do, says Kotalawala, who recommends Fenty, Mac and Estée Lauder for their range of shades.

Cruz says: “You don’t have to apply the product to your skin – hold the packaging close to your face to see which one speaks to you. He also recommends putting on the outfit you will be wearing to see the final effect of a certain shade.

To find your perfect lip colour, says Brown, “the easiest trick is to bite your lips and look at the colour they naturally turn,” says Brown. “That’s usually the most flattering lip shade for you. From there, look for a lipstick or balm that’s close to that natural flush. It will enhance your features without overpowering them.”

“Blusher,” says Cruz. “If you’re feeling ill, just put on a little extra blusher. If you’re having a sad day, put on a little blusher. I do that myself. Blusher makes you look a bit more awake.”

“Find a cream multi-use product that you can put on your cheeks and lips,” says Hughes. “MUA does a blush balm in lots of different colours. You can put that on your cheeks to give you an instant pop, and can press it into your lips for a colour freshness.”

“A ‘blonzer’ – in between a blusher and a bronzer,” says Kotalawala, and in particular one that gives a burnt-red warmth, which “looks incredible on deeper skin tones”.

The kindness of strangers: When Mum was hospitalised on a family holiday, our hotel’s owners were heaven-sent

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 15:00:15 GMT

I was just 10 at the time but my siblings and I will never forget the sense of safety, comfort and warmth they offered

Read more in the kindness of strangers series

We were doing the groceries when a blood vessel burst in my mother’s brain. I was 10 years old and on a family holiday to France that very suddenly changed its tenor. In the following weeks Mum went through brain surgery, suffered a stroke and was placed in intensive care.

We had been staying in a gîte but moved to a small hotel closer to the hospital. It was a terrifying and stressful time, even as a young kid who knew things were serious – but didn’t understand quite how serious.

So it was an unexpected blessing that the owners of our new hotel, Jean-Claude and Therese, were heaven-sent. Jean-Claude, a fabulous chef, would cook us kids whatever we wanted for dinner (most often spaghetti bolognese, much to our father’s embarrassment). When Therese caught me hand washing our clothes in the sink, she intervened and began doing our laundry for us. Both dished out hugs as required. And they introduced our father to English-speaking locals who were able to help him navigate the French medical system.

One weekend the entire hotel had been pre-booked for a wedding, meaning there was no room for us. Rather than allowing us to find another hotel for a couple of nights, Jean-Claude arranged for his mother to take us in. She was a lovely, non-English speaking octogenarian with a pet canary, kind enough to open her doors to a family she’d never met and could not communicate with.

Many decades have passed and we’ve since lost both Mum and Dad but my siblings and I will never forget Jean-Claude and Therese. At a time when we needed it most, they not only helped my dad with the practical matters that accompany a critically ill wife overseas but offered my siblings and me a priceless sense of safety, comfort and warmth.

I hope I can show half as much kindness for a stranger in need, should I ever have the opportunity.

From making your day to changing your life, we want to hear about chance encounters that have stuck with you.
