Joshua emerges from Prenga fight with urgent questions while Fury is uninspiring

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 13:54:00 GMT

Joshua’s lack of punch resistance is clear, which could place him in danger in the highly anticipated £150m fight with Tyson Fury

The bedlam and madness lasted for just five minutes and 43 seconds and, after Anthony Joshua was back in the sanctuary of his dressing room, he claimed to have learned “a valuable lesson”. Joshua had been knocked down twice by Kristian Prenga before he rescued himself in the second round with a brutal stoppage of the previously obscure Albanian.

Joshua also looked ahead to the hugely anticipated fight with Tyson Fury after the two faded former world champions came through wildly contrasting bouts which were meant to be routine exhibitions this weekend. “I’m gonna come back stronger now,” Joshua claimed as he tried to clear the concussive fog from his brain after the worst round of his tumultuous career.

But the sad truth had already risen up with piercing clarity after just 20 seconds of that first round. A sweeping right hand, which was the first meaningful punch of the fight, rocked Joshua and set him up for Prenga’s jolting uppercut. They were decent blows but it was disturbing to see how little punch resistance Joshua retains. He still cuts a sculpted figure of hard muscle but he looked lost and scrambled as he tumbled to the canvas. Joshua managed to roll over and, pressing his white gloves down on the blue canvas, he pushed himself up.

His legs were rickety as a grimace of a smile crossed his confused face. After he took a count of eight, Joshua was soon in trouble again. A sharp right cross sent him reeling into the ropes and the referee could have given him another count. Every time Prenga landed the right hand, even without undue force, Joshua was vulnerable.

Another uppercut sent him down again, even if this time his gloves only brushed the canvas before he was up again. Joshua’s courage was obvious but, in those desolate moments, the idea that he would survive another onslaught and face Fury in November seemed beyond fanciful.

But then, inexplicably, everything changed. During the break between rounds it was almost as if a loaded message had been given to Prenga that he should pack away his artillery and stop ruining the $200m (£150m) showdown between Fury and Joshua. In reality it seemed more a case that Prenga had shocked himself by dragging Joshua to the brink of a shattering defeat.

Rather than coming out to close the show, Prenga backed away. He allowed his dazed victim to seize control and start unloading punches. The Albanian was pinned in a corner and, throwing nothing of consequence in return, he was suddenly under immense pressure. Successive combinations made him sag before a ferocious right hand poleaxed Prenga.

Joshua deserves praise for his fortitude and finishing power. But even that clinical knockout could not wipe away the images of him weaving like a battered old tree about to crash to the ground whenever he was tagged by blows he would have once shrugged aside.

Having been injured seven months ago in the car accident which killed Sina Ghami and Latif “Latz” Ayodele, his close friends and key members of his camp, Joshua paid tribute to them: “It’s more than punch power. That was spirit. That was Latz, that was Sina, that was their families. It hurts to even talk about it. It has been tough. It’s my brothers.”

Joshua was close to tears. His distress was understandable but it was more worrying when he suggested that personal tragedy had given him higher powers of recovery. “You know what I learned? I can’t be stopped, man – I can’t be denied.”

His family, friends and promoters should all pause and, in the coming days, take great care of him. It would be best if they advised Joshua he is no longer equipped to absorb heavy punishment from even a merely competent heavyweight. Younger fighters such as Moses Itauma and Daniel Dubois, who administered a crushing knockout of Joshua in 2024, would have hurt him badly had they, rather than Prenga, been in the ring.

It’s true Fury was uninspiring when beating Mariusz Wach, a mediocre 46-year-old Polish heavyweight, after seven one-sided rounds in Thailand on Friday night.

Wach still managed to tag Fury a couple of times as the old Gypsy King is no longer an elusive ring technician. But Fury remains a fighter to his core and he could cause serious damage against such a reduced version of Joshua.

“We’ve signed the contract,” Joshua’s promoter, Eddie Hearn, said after his fighter’s lucky escape. “Everything is done. But tonight wasn’t about Tyson Fury. It was about the strength Anthony Joshua has shown to be here. No one knows what he’s been through the last seven months. When he went down in the first round, I thought he’d come back too soon.”

Yet, as Hearn conceded later, the signed contracts stipulate that Fury and Joshua will fight in the UK in November. It is now widely expected that the contest will take place in the US instead and so a new set of contracts could delay the circus yet again.

Reflecting on his near nightmare against Prenga, Joshua added: “It was a tough moment but I learned a valuable lesson. Start faster. Come out, fuck this boxing, and be ready. You can do it in 20 seconds. If Prenga had a bit more luck on his side, he could have had me out of there.”

He also suggested that “today was a real good eye-opener.” It was, in the sense that his lack of punch resistance was stripped bare for all to see. In a business more sensible and compassionate than boxing, those close to Joshua would try to persuade him that the time has come for him to walk away with his riches and senses still intact.

Instead, he will be enticed back into the ring to fight Fury – in a contest between two old heavyweights which now seems freighted as much with danger and potential calamity as colossal amounts of money.

Australia dispatch England with ease in Commonwealth Games netball clash

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 13:38:38 GMT

Australia 66-47 England

Sophie Garbin pours in 41 goals from 42 attempts

Eight years after England’s dramatic last-gasp triumph over Australia on the Gold Coast, netball’s greatest Commonwealth rivalry was renewed in Glasgow. But this time there was no fairytale finish for the Roses as the defending champions dismantled England 66-47 at the Hydro, the Diamonds extending their record against this opposition at the Games to seven wins from eight meetings.

Ever since Helen Housby’s last-second winner stunned the Diamonds in the 2018 final, every meeting between these two heavyweights has carried extra edge. Australia gained a measure of revenge by beating England on the way to gold in Birmingham four years ago and Sunday’s Commonwealth Games pool clash was another marker of where the sport’s fiercest rivalry stands.

Australia were quicker, sharper and more clinical from the opening whistle, with their star-studded attack of Sophie Garbin and Kiera Austin immediately exposing England’s defence.

“It was very physical out there, but that’s what we expected and that’s what we prepared for,” said Garbin. “Obviously it’s nice to get the win, but England put up a really good fight.

“It’s really exciting, especially playing over here in Glasgow. We knew we had a lot of Scots barracking for us. I think everyone told us to go and smash the English girls, so we knew we’d have a lot of support here, but they would as well. It’s awesome. That’s what you want – to play these games in front of these crowds in this amazing arena. It was really exciting.”

The Diamonds raced into an early 10-4 lead as Austin began dictating proceedings, while England struggled to live with Australia’s relentless pressure through the court. Sasha Glasgow was withdrawn before the end of the opening quarter as the interim head coach, Anna Stembridge, searched for answers, and Lois Pearson’s move into goal attack briefly stemmed the tide.

England clawed back to 13-9, but every glimpse of momentum was extinguished by Australia’s ruthless efficiency. Garbin repeatedly found space on the baseline, finishing with 41 goals from 42 attempts, while Austin contributed 15 goals alongside 19 assists and 17 feeds.

By the end of the opening quarter Australia led 18-11. England attempted to shake things up early in the second period, introducing Jayda Pechová into defence while shifting the captain Fran Williams into goal defence. The changes initially worked, with Pechová disrupting Australia’s rhythm as England opened the quarter with a 4-1 burst.

Jamie-Lee Price and Austin restored Australia’s composure, while England’s frustration began to show. Liv Tchine remained the Roses’ brightest attacking outlet, using her height and movement to keep England competitive, but Courtney Bruce and Jo Weston continually forced difficult feeds and turnovers.

Bruce and Tchine exchanged plenty of contact in the circle, while the contest became increasingly feisty as England tried to unsettle Australia’s defensive unit. Tchine’s shove into Bruce’s back late in the second quarter summed up the growing frustration as the Diamonds stretched their advantage to 35-24 at half-time.

If England harboured hopes of another famous fightback, Australia extinguished them in the third quarter. With a 21-goal cushion entering the final quarter, the contest was effectively over.

“That’s definitely not the result that we came for but it’s also not the performance,” said Williams. “We were just far off our best and we never really got some momentum to get our teeth into the game, which is a shame. It’s really tough when a game blows out like that in the second half. You’ve got to make sure that you’re still going after those small wins and little fights.”

England fan favourite Eleanor Cardwell entered to a huge reception from the Glasgow crowd and immediately injected fresh energy into the attack. Her battle with Sarah Klau added another flashpoint to an already bruising encounter, with Klau receiving an official warning after sending Cardwell tumbling to the floor. England marginally won the final quarter, but by then the damage had long been done.

Restricted eating hours may reduce cognitive decline in older age, researchers find

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 13:30:12 GMT

Preliminary study shows older people who avoided food four hours before bed did better in problem solving tests

Confining mealtimes and snacks to a nine-hour window and avoiding food for four hours before bed may help stave off cognitive decline in older age, researchers say.

A pilot study of older women living with overweight or obesity found hints of improvement in mental skills among those who ate within the restricted period compared with those who spread their meals over a longer time.

The finding is preliminary given the numbers in the trial, but if confirmed in larger studies, the work suggests people could help to protect their cognitive abilities by eating within a relatively narrow window and not eating late into the night.

Losing weight alone can help slow cognitive decline in older age, said Prof Sue Shapses, a nutritional scientist at Rutgers University in New Jersey, US, but there may be “additional benefits” for people who do not eat outside an eight to nine-hour window, and stop eating four hours before going to sleep.

Dementia is the leading cause of death in the UK and the seventh worldwide, leading to nearly 2 million deaths globally each year. Some risk factors are unavoidable, such as age and genetics, but experts believe nearly half of cases could be prevented or delayed through changes to lifestyle. Obesity in middle age can raise the risk of dementia in later life by 30%.

Shapses ran a small clinical trial in which 47 women aged 50 to 79, who were living with overweight or obesity, were encouraged to cut 500 calories from their daily diet for six months. Within the group, 26 were advised to eat only within a nine-hour window. Typically, this meant eating between 10am and 6pm, while the rest of the volunteers spread their meals over about 12 hours.

At the end of the trial, both groups had similar weight loss averaging about 7kg (15lbs). But cognitive tests revealed that those who confined their eating to the narrow window performed better than the others on spatial planning and problem solving tests. There were also hints that they made fewer errors on memory and learning tests, though on some multitasking and reaction time tests both groups performed the same.

Shapses called the effects “modest” but said they suggested time-restricted eating may improve people’s ability to remember information for everyday tasks and reduce mistakes linked to memory, attention and problem solving. Details were presented at Nutrition 2026, the annual meeting of the American Society for Nutrition in Maryland.

The researchers now plan to investigate why it may be important to consider when we eat as well as what we eat. The benefits could be driven by a complex interplay of circadian rhythms, metabolism and inflammation.

In many countries, the UK and US included, it is common to eat over a 14-hour period, leaving only 10 hours overnight without food. But research points to clear health benefits from extending overnight fasting. A review published in January found that finishing eating before 7pm was associated with significant improvements in body weight, BMI, waist circumference, blood pressure and markers of metabolic health.

Prof Wendy Hall, the head of nutritional sciences at King’s College London, who was not involved in the study, said confining mealtimes to a narrow window may have benefits for the brain.

“Time-restricted eating is a plausible approach to supporting cognitive health in midlife and older adults with overweight, not only because it may help with weight management but also because avoiding large meals late in the evening may improve blood sugar control, vascular function and inflammation,” she said.

Hall cautioned that the findings were preliminary and that it was important to see the full peer-reviewed study to determine whether any improvements were clinically meaningful.

‘It was like something was crawling over me’ – the worrying rise of shingles among millennial women

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 13:00:14 GMT

Stress, the cost of living, long working hours and even excessive exercise have all been touted as reasons the illness is rising among women in their 30s and 40s. What can be done to help them?

The “lightning strike” pain was like nothing Francine Jones had experienced before. “That is the only way I can describe it,” she says, of the stabbing in her torso that would occur every 10 minutes or so. “It was a really sharp, intense pain, as if someone was giving me an electric shock … it took my breath away.”

It had started in May with a strange pricking sensation under her bra. Then 10 large blisters, plus a host of smaller ones, formed in a band from her stomach to her back. They burned, “like someone was putting an iron on me. I don’t think I wore underwear for five or six weeks.” Showering, or even a cold flannel, would make her skin burn. Then came “the itch”, which lasted for five weeks and was so intense that she was lucky if she slept for four hours a night. “It was like something was crawling all over me all the time.” I can hear her wincing.

Jones is describing the stages of shingles she experienced. “Stages” is her terminology; there is no set pattern. It is her way of describing how the illness progressed. One night, she even feared she was having a heart attack. “I felt like I had a constant stitch and it intensified to where I was unable to walk,” she recalls. “I tried to take a deep breath and then the pain got worse. I was crying my eyes out.”

The healthcare assistant from Hereford is 39, not an age at which you might expect someone to get shingles. Yet she is not as much of a rarity as you might expect. Her story reflects a concerning trend: a 2019 US research paper reported that the sharpest rise in shingles cases was among those aged 30 to 49. Between 1998 and 2017, cases of shingles in this cohort more than doubled, overtaking the trajectory of older groups, although the latter experienced more cases overall. (Cases across all groups have been rising steadily in the US for decades, a trend for which experts do not appear to have a clear explanation, although they speculate that increased stress and depression, contributing to weakened immunity – a key cause of shingles – may play a role.)

After being diagnosed by a pharmacist, Jones was prescribed antiviral medication for seven days, then the nerve pain medication Gabapentin, which she is still taking. She has been off work for two months and still experiences sporadic aching in her side, as if she has twisted badly.

“I always thought it was old people who got shingles,” she says. In fact, a US study published in the journal Clinical Infectious Diseases this year found that those aged 30 to 39 with certain conditions, including asthma, diabetes, depression and stress, had a higher risk of shingles than those aged 50 to 59 who were immunocompetent. Experts say the uptake of the shingles vaccine in the over-50s in the US is still too low to offer an explanation for this.

Shingles, also known as herpes zoster, is a reactivation of the varicella zoster (chickenpox) virus, which lies dormant in the sensory dorsal root ganglia – a cluster of neuron cell bodies just outside the spinal cord – after the contraction, often in childhood, of chickenpox. Reactivation can be triggered when immunity is impaired and T-cells in our blood can no longer keep it in check. The first symptom is usually pain or tingling in one area of the skin, sometimes accompanied by headaches and generally feeling unwell. This is typically followed by blisters. Pain is caused by inflamed nerves – one complication can be postherpetic neuralgia (persistent pain for more than 90 days), which occurs in around 20% of patients.

According to the NHS, around a quarter of us will experience shingles in our lifetime and the incidence increases with age, which is why the shingles vaccination is offered to those over 65 in the UK and those over 50 in the US. Cases in the UK are above the five year average, according to the Royal College of GPs Research and Surveillance Centre. It believes this may, in part, reflect additional diagnoses through the Pharmacy First scheme, which allows pharmacists as well as GPs to diagnose shingles and prescribe treatment.

“I’ve had shingles eight times in the last two years. I’m 38 years old,” wrote one woman, in a Facebook support group for those with shingles. “I had shingles in April for the first time at 36,” said another. Others have similar stories: “I got it last year at 32”; “I had it at 41 this time last year but I’ve only just finished recovering”; “I’m 44, got shingles last year and it was horrific, the pain!” The majority of voices are female. Across most age groups, women have a 56% higher chance of developing shingles, thought to be because their immune systems work differently from men’s (women are more prone to autoimmune conditions, for example).

In the US, one hypothesis for the rise in shingles is that the introduction in 1995 of the chickenpox vaccine for children, which eventually lowered rates of infection in young age groups, means adults who have not been vaccinated are missing out on exposure to chickenpox, and therefore the boosts to their own resilience to shingles.

Indeed, the 2019 study expected to find this, especially when it came to explaining the rise in shingles in the millennial cohort, who are too old to have had the chickenpox vaccine and too young for the shingles vaccine.

The less chickenpox, the less shingles resilience hypothesis sounds plausible, but Jennifer Moffat, associate professor of microbiology and immunology at the State University of New York Upstate Medical University, explains that this theory was disproved in the 2019 study because chickenpox and shingles rates did not tally as expected. “As chickenpox decreased, the rate of zoster was on the same trajectory in 30-year-olds as it always was,” she says. She adds that it is now believed that resilience is naturally built, with or without exposure to chickenpox. “Scientists and physicians now believe the virus occasionally reactivates without symptoms, which provides an internal immune boost. Only when that person has impaired immunity does it cause a rash and the symptoms of shingles.”

Moffat adds: “It only takes a small gap in your immune function to let this virus pop out. Having a respiratory disease like Covid or flu … getting a bad sunburn, having type 2 diabetes or even treatment with steroids (which suppress immune system responses) can lead to an eruption of shingles.” She also believes, “something else is happening on a very large scale that is putting people at higher risk for reactivation – the declining health of humans in general. Less activity, poor diet, more stress, even maybe a warming climate.” Her list goes on: “Lack of social supports, eating ultra-processed foods, not cooking at home, not sleeping enough, higher income inequality, lack of access to healthcare – this last [one] is a major problem for young people in the US,” she points out.

But why are millennial women especially struggling? Coupled with their immune systems being more prone to shingles than men’s, Moffat speculates that their health and mental health may be more compromised as they face a wide range of lifestyle pressures in midlife. “Well, if you looked at their general health, I imagine you’d find higher rates of high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes,” Moffat says. She finds the Clinical Infectious Diseases study compelling. “Having depression at ages 30 to 39 puts you at as high a risk for shingles as a person in their 50s,” she says. “How many women do you know who feel great? They’re trying to earn, to care for their families, maintain homes. They have [older] parents, small children. There’s so much pressure on women, and I think health is not as easy to obtain any more. I think women are very squeezed in that age group.”

Jones faced an acute period of personal stress before her shingles, but says life is generally quite stressful anyway. “The cost of living goes up, people are working more hours.” She says she would force herself to get to the gym at 8.30am on Sundays and sometimes do two classes a day. Studies have observed that exercising seven days a week can potentially increase the risk of developing shingles.

It is stress that Daisy, now 51, believes may have been behind her three shingles flare-ups. She was 43 when she first had it in 2018. She noticed half her body felt sore and that there was a rash “the size of a penny under my arm”. Her GP initially gave her cream for heat rash. “I had post-shingles pain for a couple of years … dots and bolts of pain,” she says. She had recently started a new job and suffered a bereavement.

In 2022, her shingles returned. “I was managing quite a demanding day job, studying, going to the gym, living life as a single woman,” she says. In 2023, it emerged a third time after a period of illnesses including laryngitis and Covid. She was also taking exams and had started perimenopause.

Consultant dermatologist Dr Adil Sheraz explains that early diagnosis, pre-rash (some shingles cases never display one), can be missed and younger people can also be overlooked. This is problematic because antivirals are most effective if taken within 72 hours of the first symptoms. “I have seen it missed many times,” he says. “If the patient comes in quite late, we still treat them, but often you miss the treatment phase.”

Antivirals are taken for around 7-10 days, “after which the active infection goes away”, Sheraz explains. “You are then left with redness for quite some time. And then a certain percentage of patients will be left with nerve pain that may go on for many years.”

His younger patients do tend to be immunocompromised – although the shingles vaccine is now available for people aged 18 and over who have a severely weakened immune system or take immunosuppressant medication. It is growing use of the latter, he speculates, due to significant advances in drug technology and the treatment of autoimmune conditions, that may be another reason for the rise in cases of shingles. “Up to 10 years ago, we would never use these types of immune suppressants for eczema, for example, or for blistering conditions,” he says.

While shingles usually presents on the torso, it can appear anywhere, including the face. Proximity to the eye can risk blindness. Hayley, 42, from north Wales, suffered corneal scarring after her shingles was repeatedly missed. Aged 38, she began feeling an ache near her ear, jaw stiffness and then her eyebrow swelled. “Then my whole eye swelled,” she says. “It looked like I’d been punched.”

Her GP diagnosed an infected salivary gland. A week later, a rash appeared under her eyebrow and her eye also felt sore, akin to a “chopping onions” sensation. The rash and swelling subsided (the blisters have left a scar), but then her GP diagnosed allergic conjunctivitis. “I had trouble looking up,” she recalls. “I was sitting in a dark room. I couldn’t really watch TV, read a book. Doing computer work, I had to keep walking away.”

It was an optician who referred her to the hospital, where shingles was diagnosed almost two months later, and antivirals and steroids were prescribed. Thankfully, the corneal scarring was outside her field of vision.

Moffat would welcome shingles vaccination at a younger age. “Shingles is terrible, it’s painful, it’s disfiguring,” she explains. For now, looking after your wellbeing is the best prevention for younger people, she believes.

When we speak, Jones admits she is taking a rest day due to the re-emergence of her twisting pain. “I try to listen to my body now,” she explains. She won’t be at the gym on a Sunday morning any time soon.

*Some names have been changed

The Pitt is powerful – but it’s the rawness of The Bear that truly portrays hospital work

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 13:00:14 GMT

Both restaurant work and medicine involve abusive training and relentless devotion to minutiae – and the joy of offering comfort

I pass a mother heaving in grief while her son’s heart monitors flatline. It is the last time she will ever hold his hand. For me, this is another day on call in the intensive care unit as a pediatric physician. For her, this is the day her life shatters.

Later that night, a striking, charismatic surgeon from work treats me to an exquisite meal. Served outside a trailer, humidity barreling through our scrubs, the food is neither extravagant nor decadent. It is, however, the most succulent Texas barbecue brisket I will ever taste. This is the night I rest my head on his shoulder and he doesn’t flinch. This is the night an “us” was born.

A shared humanity links doctors and chefs. We both craft life’s most tender moments. Some will ricochet off your brain for years, dull with ache. Others will leave you heady, craving more. The television series The Pitt has garnered well-deserved praise for its excellent depiction of an emergency room staff battling insurance companies, mass shootings and mental health crises. In fact, I was one of many healthcare providers who shared my insight for The Pitt, and consulted to help craft narratives true to reality, so I deeply respect its advocacy for destigmatizing mental healthcare for physicians.

And yet, I have never been more convinced that The Bear is actually the reigning television show for accuracy in its depiction of hospital medicine. From the delayed gratification of abusive, humiliating training to the chaotic intensity of its work-hard-play-hard ethos, training for chefs is, in many ways, comparable to physician pedagogy. Both professions spend infinite hours mastering minutiae no one will ever discern. Both lose themselves in the relentless pursuit of precision, and in their dedication to service, an art form few will appreciate.

We inhabit two of the last true apprenticeships, marred by years of exploitation, insults and chronic sleep deprivation. It is the perfect recipe for both professions to suffer from disproportionately higher rates of depression, anxiety, addiction, and even suicide. On The Bear, Jeremy Allen White’s Carmy once described his former boss at an elite restaurant as: “Very, probably, mentally ill. Dead inside. Cold. Never turns it off. Accomplishes more by 10am than most people do in a lifetime. I don’t think he sleeps. I don’t think he eats. I don’t think he loves.” Ask any doctor about their most feared mentor in residency, and they’d sputter these words out with the same cadence.

In one scene, this boss berates his employees for their slowness and orders them to repeat: “Chef, I’m so tough,” while he taunts: “You are not tough ... You are talentless … You should be dead.”

It brought to mind the first day of gross anatomy class in medical school. One of our professors joked that if we were to attempt suicide, as many doctors do, that we should at least not shame the profession by surviving. They would gladly show us on a cadaver how to “do it right” so at least we weren’t total failures.

We – doctors and chefs - dissolve into our professions chasing illusions of perfection. For me, it is the chance to save your life or to assuage your pain. For a chef, it is the hope that the couple who got engaged at his restaurant retells their proposal story breathlessly for years to come, that he enshrined that memory with the tenderness it deserves.

While The Pitt is what you might desire from your ideal physician, it’s the frenetic back-of-the-house pulsing turbulence in The Bear that I recognize. The audience gets glimpses of the staff’s camaraderie, which, similar to hospitals, is airtight. These are the only people who truly comprehend the grueling mess it takes to make this look this easy.

I remember one night in the ER, a child had been brutally beaten and was dead on arrival. I meticulously washed matted blood from her hair, cloaked her in a hospital blanket and tried to restore some of her dignity. I gave her body, cradled, to her mother, where she lay one last time. And then I hurried along. My next patient was already angry about the wait. This is the raw reality that public-facing professions grapple with. Whether we are wearing scrubs or chef’s uniforms, we serve as punching bags; society has license to exorcise its demons onto us.

But The Bear is not only an exacting look in the mirror – not just the mental health woes, not just life’s most dramatic days. It is also a celebration of the joy of the ordinary, luxuriating in the perfect bite. The Bear gets even the most cynical of us to revel in the purest of humanity: offering comfort to another human, hoping that our presence will make their pain more bearable in some way. We show up for life’s most gutting times, but also at its most promising: the moment a baby’s first cry reverberates, or just as the candlelight across the table flickers ever so gently. Food, when done right, offers healing too.

The Bear also captures the intimacy of a shared language and bodily familiarity unspoken amongst both doctors and chefs. After working decades alongside one another at godforsaken hours of the night, we know each other’s eyebrow arch. We recognize a vocal tremor infinitesimally longer than it should be. We pick each other up when we fail. We have no choice. It’s a bond borne of collective fatigue, and one of sharing abject frustration and sacred silences in the same day.

As for my handsome surgeon, he would later ask me to meet him at a Michelin starred restaurant. I would get my hair done and wear lace. An hour and two glasses into the evening, I would take off my heels as the waiter asked me if I wanted to call it a night. I don’t remember much about that relationship, unceremoniously pronounced dead when he stood me up that night. But I will never bid goodbye to the exquisite flavor of that Texas brisket, which remains a glimmer of magnificence in an otherwise harrowing day. My memories return far more to the taste of that barbecue than to the taste of his kiss, so all things considered? Worth it.

Seema Jilani is a pediatric hospitalist who has treated critically ill children on medical evacuation flights. Her humanitarian work has taken her to Afghanistan, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Ukraine, Bosnia, Gaza and the West Bank, and on refugee rescue boats off the coast of Libya. Her radio documentary, Israel and Palestine: The Human Cost of the Occupation, was nominated for the Peabody Award

In the UK, the charity Mind is available on 0300 123 3393 and Childline on 0800 1111. In Australia, support is available at Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636, Lifeline on 13 11 14, and at MensLine on 1300 789 978

Why does everything feel so joyless? Welcome to the age of decadence without pleasure

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 13:00:14 GMT

Decadence in our era comes in technologically mediated forms, emptied of desire and obsessed with self-optimisation

Do you want to have a good time? You know, really enjoy yourself? Click here, and tell us your desires. Maybe it’s a new outfit, or some exotic cuisine delivered anonymously and steaming hot to your door. Maybe it’s porn or gambling. Perhaps you prefer the infinite scroll, the endlessly unfurling ribbon of glossy images and videos starring people you’ll never meet doing things you’ll never do. Or maybe you favor talking to a chatbot who will assure you that you are the most special of all its users.

For anyone with an Internet connection and a little discretionary income, the contemporary moment offers a superabundance of seductive distractions. Why then the pervasive mood of emptiness? Why are so many at once overstimulated and bored?

Welcome to the era of decadence without pleasure.

The concept of decadence as a marker of cultural decline coinciding with a high level of wealth has been around since the twilight of the ancient Greeks and Romans. After the Roman emperor Elagabalus took the throne at 14, he served flamingo brains, seasoned his food with pearls, and, according to one account, smothered guests to death with an avalanche of rose petals. But his vices were outdone by Nero, who had his enemies sewn into wild animal skins and devoured by dogs in an elaborate garden spectacle.

So decadence has an inescapably pejorative ring, suggesting decay, excess and a falling away from norms and ideals. Critics of decadence have usually hailed from the political right, and the same is true today: consider conservative New York Times columnist Ross Douthat’s critique of cultural and economic stagnation in his 2020 book The Decadent Society, or billionaire investor Peter Thiel’s complaints about faltering innovation and the supposed decline of the west. JD Vance likes to invoke the fall of Rome, warning, in his 2026 memoir Communion, that the US is “a great civilization” tumbling into “disrepair”. But plenty of thinkers on the left also worry that modern wealthy societies have entered a period of paralysis, under the shadow of what the Italian theorist Franco “Bifo” Berardi calls “the slow cancellation of the future”.

That all sounds bad. Yet a passionate minority has sometimes found, in decadence, reasons for hope. Cultures later judged decadent produced extraordinary upwellings of art, like the flare of a dying star. Think of the undulating arabesques of Rococo painting before the French Revolution, or the lush shimmering silks of the late Ottomans, or the experimental cinema and nightlife of Weimar Berlin.

Nowhere was the cultural potential of decadence more visible than in the late-19th century. In France, Britain and (with less gusto) in the United States, artists such as Oscar Wilde, Aubrey Beardsley, Joris-Karl Huysmans and Rachilde developed new literary and visual styles championing extravagance, sensuousness and the superiority of artifice. It is to these avant-garde experiments that we owe green carnations (the fakest of flowers), frivolous dandies obsessed with perfumes, a bejeweled tortoise crushed to death by the weight of its splendor, and erotic nightmares including a woman with monstrous flowers growing between her thighs and a male anatomical model whose legs spread at the click of a spring so that he can be penetrated by his female lover. Such taboo-busting grotesquery protested against the inertia of modern civilization by applying moral and aesthetic shock treatment.

The decadents, however, were not just provocateurs. Their revolt against Victorian society’s deadening enslavement to usefulness, materialism and conventionality put forward a positive philosophy of life, a certain way of thinking about pleasure. Against their era’s obsession with use-value and profit, the decadents insisted that pleasure was, or ought to be, “useless”, enjoyed for its own sake in life’s passing moments. “Not the fruit of experience, but experience itself, is the end,” intoned the essayist Walter Pater, one of the guiding lights of English decadence, in his masterpiece The Renaissance. A reclusive Oxford don, Pater was said to have once stopped High Street traffic to stroke a cat. Why? For the sensation of fur beneath his fingers. The virtue of decadent pleasure is that it is useless, an end in itself.

The fixations of fin-de-siècle decadence that inspired Oscar Wilde and company are still with us, but in shrivelled, technologically mediated forms. GLP-1s turn the delights of eating into a problem to be managed. Anti-ageing remedies and “looksmaxxing” turn decadence’s preoccupation with self-styling into a (literally painful) form of self-optimisation. AI restages decadence’s love of artifice by outsourcing human thinking to a chatty, eager-to-please machine butler.

The problem with contemporary culture isn’t that we’re too decadent. We have inherited the surfaces of decadence – luxury, excess, artifice, bodily display – but have surrendered the fin de siècle’s commitment to pleasure. The result is a culture in which pleasure is subordinated to programs of optimisation and replaced at scale by numbing algorithmic stimulation and promises of instant gratification. Whether you’re after goods, food, art or ideas, you can get more, faster, now.

But quantity and speed can’t make up for the paradox at the heart of today’s decadence: the fact that it’s often “meh” and oddly joyless. It’s a sign of the times that this spring, Amazon’s Chinese rival launched in the UK and Europe under a name that promises to deliver emotional fulfilment: Joybuy.

Bryan Johnson, the frequently shirtless tech tycoon who has funnelled his fortune into what he calls the “Don’t Die” movement, has turned his quest for immortality into a prolonged exhibition of ascetic self-management. His lifestyle is harrowingly spartan: he doesn’t drink alcohol, avoids the sun, never goes out in the evening, and subsists primarily on lentils, boiled broccoli and macadamia nuts. Yet his regimen is, in its peculiar way, one of prurient excess. He swallows up to 111 pills a day, tracks his night-time erections, and once tapped his teenage son for blood plasma. His fight against death costs a reported $2m a year.

Johnson presents himself as a man of the future, but he has a 19th-century double. While pallid, faintly androgynous men with money and strange habits are not rare in decadent literature, the most famous is Duke Jean des Esseintes, the hero of Joris-Karl Huysmans’s 1884 novel Against the Grain, a work considered the Bible of decadence. The last scion of an aristocratic French family, des Esseintes creates for himself a cloistered world of voluptuous artifice: padded walls, rare books, exotic flowers, fragrant bonbons, subtle liqueurs, perfumes so sweet they verge on rancid.

Like Johnson, des Esseintes is medically fragile, obsessed with death, and preoccupied with the minutiae of his private sensations. Like Johnson, he sees his retreat from ordinary society into a tightly controlled artificial environment as an experiment that tests the limits of human possibility. But whereas des Esseintes’s withdrawal is an immersion into the subtleties of sensation, Johnson’s “Don’t Die” movement treats the delights of the senses as suspect, even fatal. Des Esseintes hosts a funeral banquet for his “dead virility” in a dining room draped in black, opening on to charcoaled gardens, with guests dining on black-bordered plates filled with black food (rye bread, caviar, black pudding, cuts of meat dripping with liquorice-coloured sauce). Johnson, by contrast, treats impotence as a technical problem, repeatedly shocking his penis to increase his erections.

Johnson’s programme is extreme, but he is not an anomaly. His lifestyle makes visible, in exaggerated form, new attitudes toward pleasure and embodiment being pushed by today’s tech billionaires. While some superwealthy people in or around Palo Alto are biohacking for longevity with the help of concierge medics, others are treating even sexual pleasure as a domain to be perfected through medical interventions. For example, at Dr Sally Greenwald’s exclusive OB-GYN practice, nicknamed the “Billionaire’s Vagina Club” – Greenwald describes her clientele as “the top 0.001%” – middle-aged women can improve their “sexspan” through bespoke advice, hormonal cocktails and tracking devices. “Sex equals sleep, stress reduction, cardiovascular engagement, relational fulfilment, and pelvic-floor health, and each of those equals health,” Greenwald says.

These attitudes reflect the fantasies of a narrow elite obsessed with human enhancement and – above all else – the prolongation of their own survival. The class politics of pleasureless decadence can be roughly summarized as: biohacking and quantified asceticism for the rich, algorithmic stimulation for the rest.

In contexts of extreme inequality, rich people tend to set the terms by which pleasure is understood and experienced. The very fact of inequality injures pleasure, because in a stratified society, food, art, travel and other delights can devolve into occasions to demonstrate rank or taste. Our present social order, however, is not just radically unequal; it’s dominated by a ruling class that distrusts pleasure and sensation. What passes for “fun” among today’s top 0.001% amounts to anything but: think of the 80-hour workweeks championed by tech titans like Elon Musk, or Equinox gym’s “Optimize” longevity membership costing $40,000 a year, or courtside seats at Knicks games inside the miniature surveillance state that is Madison Square Garden. And because of their outsized political and cultural influence, their sway over public and private investment, and their habit of not paying their share of tax, the pleasurelessness of the ultra-monied classes trickles down to the rest of us.

“I think trying to optimise things … is actually the divine spark within us,” recently professed the German biotech billionaire Christian Angermayer, a champion of “humanmaxxing”, the use of drugs and supplements to enhance the body. Divinity aside, it seems pertinent to mention that the person content with every day sensations makes for a poor consumer. But get people outside the plutocratic class to reconceive their minds and bodies as sites of perpetual self-improvement, and you have, in Angermayer’s words, “a total addressable market of ideally 100%”.

The most culturally revealing such market is for GLP-1s such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro. One in eight American adults report taking GLP-1 injectables for weight loss, according to a 2025 Gallup poll, and far more express interest in taking them. The global market for this class of drugs is expected to reach $190bn by 2035. For many, these medications confer real benefits. Yet it seems fair to ask: what does the widespread embrace of appetite-governing pharmaceuticals suggest about our culture’s handling of pleasure and desire?

GLP-1s reshape the felt relation between desire and satisfaction, as research has already begun to show. While more studies are needed, some users report a diminution of pleasure across several areas of their lives: they complain of lethargy, decreased libido, emotional flatness and a weakened connection to the social dimensions of eating.

The decadence of the fin de siècle celebrated cornucopian abundance. Take for example Aubrey Beardsley’s 1896 drawing The Fruit Bearers, depicting two figures bearing colossal bowls of fruit, lush grapes overhanging, a peacock in the background observing the opulent procession. In contrast, today’s anhedonic decadence celebrates the inhibition, even the transcendence, of appetite. While in haute cuisine the trappings of indulgence are preserved – some upmarket eateries now offer “small appetite” menus featuring caviar and foie gras – the tendency is toward delicate minimalism. Because eating is a quintessentially communal activity, an intervention in how people eat is also an intervention in how we socialize.

It seems reasonable to expect, meanwhile, that the widespread uptake of such drugs may contribute to a tightening not just of belts but of beauty norms. Looksmaxxing, an online subculture aimed primarily at young men, presents a darker strain of physical perfectionism, treating the body as a site of correction. Of course, women have long been ground down by painful and impossible beauty standards. What’s striking about looksmaxxing is the migration of this kind of disciplinary logic into a male subculture that speaks of beauty in terms of brutal domination: anyone can be “mogged” (outshone by a more handsome man), and one of the purposes of maxxing is to increase one’s “sexual market value”. Key to this subculture is the rejection of subjective taste in favor of mathematical norms (looksmaxxers prize certain ratios of facial proportion, measuring, for instance, the height of the forehead or the distance between the pupils).

“[T]o make oneself beautiful is a universal instinct,” a young Max Beerbohm wrote in his 1894 essay A Defence of Cosmetics, a send-up of decadence’s cult of artifice. Whereas the fin-de-siècle decadents with their love of makeup treated the face as a mask to play with or an enigma to contemplate, looksmaxxers recast the face as a set of homogenizing metrics requiring arduous correction. “The men are weeping in the gym,” writes Andrew McMillan in his prescient 2015 poem about punitive male beauty standards:

they have got too close to the glass

and now they are laying

in the broken pools of their own faces.

The fin de siècle had its own cult of masculine self-display in the form of the dandy, with his carefully tailored coat, polished shoes and pigskin gloves. The dandy’s concern for appearance was just part of the era’s wide-ranging love of stylization. “The first duty in life is to be as artificial as possible,” Oscar Wilde proclaimed. “What the second duty is no one has yet discovered.” Wilde and other decadents prized the made over the natural. Artifice was a way of intensifying the given world, overlaying the hard facts of life with a glittering sheen or a more pleasant smell. After all, what is the dandy’s perfume but a victory for pleasure over necessity?

AI marks a triumph of artifice more sweeping than the old decadents could have imagined. Yet far from bolstering our capacity for perceptual intensity, AI presents new threats to both. Its productions – LinkedIn posts about the virtues of entrepreneurship, cartoon soap operas about the infidelities of anthropomorphized fruits – are eerily hollow, with no felt experience, embodiment or sensation behind them. AI is the pleasureless decadence machine.

Already our algorithmically driven culture is saturated with a deluge of slop that promises numbing, empty stimulation. The old decadents were fascinated by the prospect of mental oblivion, the loss of self-control in the face of overwhelming beauty. Today, AI researchers warn of “human enfeeblement” as tech companies seek to draw users into relations of dependency and infantilization, with machines to do their “thinking” for them.

While the fin-de-siècle left imprints on visual art, fashion, music and other art forms, it was primarily as a literary movement that its decadence made cultural interventions. Crucial to decadent writing was a taste for language – lilting rhythms, overheated exclamations – that would affect the reader viscerally, leaving her trembling, her moral assumptions upended. In contrast, LLMs leach language of pleasure by blandifying it: the algorithm steers language away from the idiosyncratic and toward the predictable.

Pleasure isn’t just about hedonism or indulgence in “useless” objects. It is one of the principal ways we, as embodied beings, perceive value. Pain teaches us not to touch the hot stove twice; pleasure guides us toward the sweetness of clean water and fresh air. Pleasure is not infallible: some things that feel good are cruel, addictive, or destructive. But the embodied experience of pleasure is crucial to how we learn and how we make judgments about what is good, beautiful and worth pursuing. These are not judgments we can wisely cede to disembodied machines.

“There is no pleasure or pain for an AI, no skin in the game,” the philosopher Carissa Véliz writes in her recent book Prophecy. As a result, an AI “cannot care, and therefore cannot value”. Without some felt relation to pleasure and pain, judgments of value and taste become abstract and bloodless.

Because of its commitment to embodied pleasure, fin-de-siècle decadence offers powerful lessons for the increasingly disembodied, tech-optimised world championed by elites. This is not to suggest, however, that the old decadents were living uncomplicated lives of satisfaction and joy. WB Yeats called the poets of 1890s London “the tragic generation”. The decadents could be moody and morbid, susceptible to ennui, spleen and other Baudelairean ailments. In other words, they were all too human. Some died young, succumbing to alcoholism or tuberculosis; others abandoned the religion of art to join the Catholic church. Fin-de-siècle decadence had, moreover, an aristocratic and misogynistic bent. Many of its most influential English champions were highly educated men who regarded ordinary life with aloofness, even contempt.

From the start, however, decadence was both an elite and a minoritarian movement, spearheaded largely by men (and some women) of privilege – but responsible for injecting a new awareness of queerness into public consciousness.

Oscar Wilde’s 1890 novel The Picture of Dorian Gray is a story of a thrill-seeker’s descent into decadent squalor – hedonism, moral bankruptcy, irresponsible self-indulgence and the exploitation of others – in the name of never ageing. But when Victorian society raged at Dorian’s monstrosity, Wilde countered that “vice and virtue are to the artist materials for an art” that can reveal humanity to itself. Sure, Dorian was a perverted Peter Pan, a bad boy who didn’t want to grow up and face consequences. But his scandalous romp reflected society’s concealed desires back to itself.

In fin-de-siècle decadence, we can also see a growing appreciation of female desire. The 1892 poetry collection Sight and Song by Michael Field – the pen name of two lesbian lovers who wrote as one – turns an explicitly female gaze on the art-historical canon. A poem in response to Leonardo da Vinci’s drawing of Leda, the princess seduced by Zeus in the form of a swan, grants Leda all the power: “She draws the fondled creature to her will.” Their Saint Sebastian is, by contrast, a passive icon of masculine beauty, “with body fresh for use, for pleasure fit, / With its energies and needs together knit”.

So too have Black and postcolonial artists drawn from late-19th-century decadence in asserting their own claims to pleasure. Bruce Nugent’s homoerotic story Smoke, Lilies and Jade (1926), one of the more audacious works of the Harlem Renaissance, opens with the Black hero, Alex, lying on his bed, exhaling blue smoke from a cigarette. Alex idly ponders Wilde’s remark that “a cigarette is the most perfect pleasure because it leaves one unsatisfied” before passing into the streets in search of more gratifying pleasures. He meets a white man he calls Beauty, and the two embrace: Alex “could feel Beauty’s body … close against his … hot … tense … white … and soft”. That sentence’s panting prose gives away the game – Alex knows that enjoying the pleasure forbidden to him is the ultimate decadent act.

And now? A renewed, democratic decadence could stage a revolt against optimisation, encouraging ordinary people to brace themselves against the siren simulations of the digital world. Because contemporary culture looks decadent but feels punishing and devoid of meaning, a New Decadence could respond powerfully to this essential contradiction. Every day acts of aesthetic perception – such as Walter Pater stopping traffic to stroke a cat – matter. But if a New Decadence is to emerge, we need artists to invent it and individuals to pause and appreciate its disruptive energies.

So far, neodecadent energies in art have been submerged in satirical entertainments about rich people behaving badly – films like Saltburn or TV shows like The White Lotus that reproduce the structure of pleasureless decadence by equating pleasure with status, power and consumption.

There are signs, however, of something more original and less reactive emerging, an art that foregrounds the senses for an era that distrusts the body. The sensuous cinema of Peter Strickland; the frightening but gorgeous blood-coloured sculptures of Anish Kapoor; the reinvigoration of Black decadence in Shola von Reinhold’s novel Lote; the Dionysian reimagining of the fin de siècle in John Corigliano’s opera The Lord of Cries – none of this amounts to a coherent movement. Yet all these works offer, to their respective artforms, materials from which a New Decadence could arise – a movement that could give pleasure back to people, make the social body’s pulses race again, and force fresh blood through today’s complacent, anemic culture.

Walter Pater prefaced his study of the Renaissance with a sort of epicurean pleasure script, a series of diagnostic questions you can ask yourself to get a better handle on what you experience:

What is this song or picture, this engaging personality presented in life or in a book, to me? What effect does it really produce on me? Does it give me pleasure? and if so, what sort or degree of pleasure? How is my nature modified by its presence, and under its influence?

Your answers to these questions, he argues, have the virtue of satisfying your soul. Giving your attention to what you are feeling, analyzing your impressions, being moved and attentive to life’s everyday experiences – this is where real pleasure lies, so long as your pleasure harms no one else’s.

Why strive for pleasure? Why long for it? Because – contra the Bryan Johnsons of the world – we will die. “A counted number of pulses only,” Pater writes, “is given to us of a variegated, dramatic life.” Like Johnson, like the humanmaxxers, Pater counts his pulses. “Our one chance lies,” he writes, “in expanding that interval, in getting as many pulsations as possible into the given time.”

How different Pater’s pulse-counting is from that of the biometric ascetics. Against the pressure to optimise life, decadence issues a different command: feel it.

.

I was a terrible teen. Now my son is turning into one, karma is coming for me

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 13:00:13 GMT

My mum loves to remind me how sullen, furious and monosyllabic I was. Now she can’t wait to see how I’ll handle parenting an adolescent

The “Baader-Meinhof phenomenon” is a more satisfying name for frequency illusion – noticing a concept, word or product more often just after becoming aware of it. And after reading a fascinating article by a professor who insists that when a teenager makes “the stupid choice”, their brain is actually “working exactly as designed”, I’m suddenly seeing teens everywhere. Not just literally, because it’s the school holidays – hanging about in groups, being scarily tall and all dressed identically – but also in news stories, adverts for adolescent skincare, old clips of Harry Enfield’s Kevin and Perry sketches. Not unrelated: my son’s 12th birthday is fast approaching. This is the very last year my little boy will be nice and preteen, and I’m being reminded from all angles, by all algorithms. Soak up every second while there’s still time! Tick tock, tick tock! Thanks, Baader-Meinhof.

Teenage minds function “in a way that has been shaped by evolution for a unique and uniquely challenging time of life,” according to Dr Evelyn Svingen, assistant professor of criminology at the University of Birmingham. This is reassuring and concerning in equal measures – in the future my son’s going to make dumb decisions, but it’s OK, because that’s what he’s meant to do. Sheesh.

However, the most awful part of preparing to parent a teen is that I’m certain karma is coming for me. My mum physically rubs her hands together with glee whenever the subject arises, already snuggling into her front row seat, ready to enjoy the show. I was the most terrible teenager who has ever stomped across the earth, then slammed the door while screaming “I hate you!” And I’m worried that what goes around will come around. The way my mum tells it – and boy does she still tell it now, decades later – I went up to bed on the eve of my 13th birthday a delightful angel, sunshine personified, cartoon birds landing on my finger. The next morning, I had transformed into the princess of darkness. The sky went black, there was an ominous clap of thunder, and sullen, furious and monosyllabic, I appeared at the breakfast table.

Over the next few years I made every stupid choice going (although, look Mum, it turns out my brain was working exactly as designed). But to be honest, what haunts me most now isn’t the risks I took, the dangerous situations I blundered into, or the mistakes I made, it’s how embarrassed I was by my parents, simply because they existed.

I remember walking into the town where I grew up with my dad once, purposely dawdling to ensure I was five paces behind him, so no one would see us together. Some of this was because he was wearing a deeply unfashionable anorak, but mostly it was because being out in public with either parent was horrific. I didn’t consider for a millisecond what that experience was like for him. The irony that now, 14 years after his death, I would give almost anything to walk down a road with him is not lost on me.

But it’s astonishing how quickly that switch flicked; one day I was happily holding my dad’s hand, chatting away, thrilled to spend as much time with him as possible, the next lagging behind him and eye-rolling like Trinny and Susannah. I can recall that feeling so vividly, and while of course I want my son to be safe through his teen years, it’s humbling to acknowledge that I also really want him to still like his parents, even if only behind closed doors, when nobody’s looking.

His descent into teenagerdom has already started. Driving with him last week I realised I needed to pop into a supermarket, and he was mortified by the idea, in case any of his schoolfriends were around. I suggested he stay in the car, but waiting in the car for your mum is apparently a fate worse than being seen in Sainsbury’s with her, if you can imagine such a thing.

This is an essential stage of growing up. I know we have to try to understand. I know we have to not take it too personally. I know we have to let him go … but not too far, hopefully. Tick tock, tick tock.

Polly Hudson is a freelance writer

Lena Headey looks back: ‘I told Harvey Weinstein where to go. A decade of possibilities disappeared’

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 13:00:12 GMT

The Game of Thrones actor on her feral youth, not playing the fame game, and being protective of her daughter

Born in Hamilton, Bermuda, in 1973 and raised in West Yorkshire and Somerset, Lena Headey is an actor, writer and director. She made her film debut in Waterland in 1992. Her career spans 300, Terminator: The Sarah Connor Chronicles and Game of Thrones, in which she played Cersei Lannister from 2011 to 2019, earning five Emmy nominations. Intimacy, which she writes, directs and stars in, is an eight-part comedy audio drama for BBC Sounds and Radio 4.

I was an OG onesie wearer. This was taken on Christmas Day in our house in Bermuda. My parents were in the police force, and for some reason one day the Yorkshire branch decided: “We’re all going to go to Bermuda for some training.” I don’t remember much from that time, but I know that it was hot, everyone had scooters, and that it was fun.

My mum says I was an independent kid. If my parents ever tried to help me, I’d shout at them: “Leave it, leave it, leave it!” I was playful and adventurous and liked to wander far from home. We left Bermuda when I was six and moved to Somerset, where my brother was born. Having police as parents didn’t make them rule-abiding or strict. Instead – being a kid of the 70s and 80s – they would go to work while us kids were allowed to do whatever we wanted. I had a feral decade, one full of dangerous things done outside, and I feel very grateful for it.

I had no ambitions to become an actor as a child, but I was obsessed with films and loved drama classes, mainly because they were the easy part of school. I found the academic side of learning difficult, but socially I survived. I had friends, and was always down for a good time.

From 11 to my late teens, I had a particularly difficult time mentally, to the extent that when I was 14 I ran away from home. I got on a bus to Birmingham to meet some older guys that I’d met on holiday. I had their addresses as we had sent letters to each other. What happened next? I smoked a bunch of weed, ran out of money and went back home. After that, my parents took me to the doctor. When he asked what was wrong, why I ran away, I said: “I don’t know. Everything just feels shit.” The doctor’s response was: “You seem depressed.” That was that, no further help.

When I started acting properly in my late teens, the whole world opened up and I felt much happier. I was 17 when our school entered a play into a competition, and we went to the National Theatre to perform it. They put our photographs up in the lobby, and some casting directors saw them and asked a bunch of us to audition for a film called Waterland. I didn’t have an agent, but I drove to London for the audition at the Groucho Club. I got the part and remember thinking: “Great! Now I get to leave school.”

Even though I was green and clueless, my memories of making that film are of joy and collaboration. The director, Stephen Gyllenhaal, was brilliant and the cast were all young and we got on with each other. On set, there was no hierarchy, no distinction between cast and crew – we were all in it together. On the other hand, I felt deeply vulnerable and uncomfortable being naked and pretending to have sex with another actor. Nothing’s changed – I’m still never the most enthusiastic with that side of the job. I don’t think any actor wakes up and goes: “Oh my God, today’s the day I get to wear a thong and shag someone.”

After Waterland I embarked on a decade of auditioning. Sometimes it was heartbreaking, and sometimes I’d nail a job and feel fantastic. But in general, my 20s and 30s were tough. I hadn’t found my own value as a woman and was trading on external, social value rather than who I really was.

Throughout my career, I’ve had great experiences in the industry, and some really bad ones too. I was lucky with Harvey Weinstein. He didn’t get his hands on me because his keycard didn’t work for the hotel room he had taken me to. I was young, cocky and drunk in our first encounter – and so when I realised what was happening I essentially told him to fuck himself. While I was fortunate nothing worse happened, I didn’t ever get another Miramax film after that. A decade and a half of possibilities disappeared. I felt I was blacklisted because I refused to do what he wanted.

I was 35 when I auditioned for Cersei in Game of Thrones. It was in a tiny room at HBO in LA. I put everything I had into it. Then I heard a phone go off – it was one of the exec’s. She got up and answered the call and left the room. I watched her walk out, and said: “Are you joking?” At that moment I thought: “I’m never getting this. I am obviously very uncharismatic and unengaging.” Turns out that is quite normal, and I was wrong.

Sign up to Inside Saturday

after newsletter promotion

Game of Thrones threw me into visibility on a scale I hadn’t experienced before and it was a strange dynamic to contend with. The show ran for a decade of my life, one in which I went through a divorce and became a mother, twice. Even though I was in a big show and making money, and had financial security for the first time as an actor – and for the last time, it turns out – I was still wrangling with major life changes while being in the public eye. There were lots of weird moments, such as going on holiday with the kids, being half-naked in the sand and someone coming up to me and saying: “Can we do a quick video?” I’d have to say: “Nah, not really.”

Fame is not for me. I could employ a stylist and go to the opening of this and that. But I’m really lazy. I look at people who seem to get lots of work and opportunities and ask: “Why didn’t I get that job?” My agent will reply: “Well, if you did a bit more press or agreed to having a publicist, things might be different.” After that, I often think: “Nah, forget it.” The trade-off for having lots of work is that you have to get out there, always pushing to be seen. Which is tough when you have Jomo: the joy of missing out.

It’s often said that women become invisible when they reach midlife. While it is true, I’ve never liked being available; that feeling of shrinking under the weight of feeling scared and alone when you’re by yourself on a train or in a cab. I’ve had way more horrible experiences than what happened with Harvey, but that is life. My main takeaway is that I never, ever, want those things to happen to my children. The biggest stress of being a parent is wanting your children not to feel the same pain or disappointment or violence or sadness. When I’m out with my daughter, who is gorgeous and only 11, I see the power of her beauty in the eyes of men that really shouldn’t be looking at her. I hate it. So I don’t miss being leered at, at all. There’s a liberation to getting older.

When I see that photo, I wish that I could protect my younger self from some of the things she would go through. But I can’t. Instead, I’m appreciative that I can protect my girl instead.

Pedro Sánchez says Spain is suffering effects of climate crisis as firefighters battle wildfires in France

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 12:56:30 GMT

Blazes near Madrid coming under control but efforts to contain huge fire near Bordeaux hampered by windy conditions

Authorities in France are battling to contain a huge wildfire near Bordeaux in the south-west as Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, warned Spain and the Iberian peninsula were suffering the effects of the climate emergency.

Efforts to extinguish the blaze in the Gironde region of France – which has consumed an area four times the size of Paris and caused nearly 220,000 people to be evacuated – were hampered by windy conditions on Saturday night.

In Spain, fires west of Madrid were being brought under control, but Sánchez spoke of “difficult hours”.

Wildfires have forced approximately 375,000 people to flee their homes in France and Spain. In France nearly 260,000 have been forced to flee, while in neighbouring Spain 116,000 have been evacuated this week.

Bordeaux’s mayor, Thomas Cazenave, described the Gironde blaze as being “at the gates of the metropolitan area”, between 15 and 20 miles (25-30km) from the city itself, which has a population of 268,000. An evacuation of the city was not on the cards, he said.

Nearly 260,000 people have been evacuated across France as a whole, including 36,000 ordered to leave another wildfire zone in the Landes region farther south earlier this week.

Sophie Brocas, the prefect of the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region, which includes the Gironde, said that the highly unpredictable nature of this wildfire was a phenomenon never seen before in France. “I urge tourists not to come to Gironde as long as the fire has not been contained,” she said. “I invite tourists who are already here to think about going to another destination. We don’t know where the fire is going to go.”

France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said on Sunday the previous night had been difficult and “the situation remains very unfavourable”. He said the Gironde fire had become “extremely virulent and unpredictable again” on Saturday night, generating its own wind and spreading erratically towards the Bordeaux metropolitan area. It had become calmer by the end of the night, he said.

Since Wednesday, the fire in Gironde has injured 75 firefighters, 10 of whom have been evacuated, according to the latest situation report published on Sunday by the prefecture.

Sebastien Bouvier, federal secretary of France’s CFDT union, said firefighters did not have adequate equipment to protect themselves from the fires’ toxic fumes.

About 2,500 firefighters (including a Swiss team), 1,500 military personnel and about 1,200 police had been deployed to Gironde, Nuñez said, as he praised the contribution of 450 volunteers from civil security organisations.

He said another five Gironde municipalities had been evacuated overnight.

One firefighter told Agence France-Presse that the fire had formed a pyrocumulonimbus, a fire-generated thunderstorm that “creates its own wind, with whirlwinds, becoming erratic and uncontrollable”.

A spokesperson for the National Firefighters Federation of France said that while known in wildfire-prone Australia and Canada, one had never been seen before in France. The federation’s Lt Col Éric Brocardi told AFP there was a need to understand a “natural force beyond our control”. He said: “It’s a David v Goliath scenario: the idea is that, at some point, we’ll find a weak spot and strike there.”

Police in Gironde made three arrests over the weekend, including one man smoking in the forest and two having barbecues in a forest area.

Authorities in Spain said major areas of fire near Madrid had been contained and cooled down, according to a senior officer with Spain’s military emergencies unit.

“We’re facing some difficult hours, although it’s true that the latest update has shown that last night was very positive in terms of the fire’s evolution and efforts to control it,” Sánchez said.

Speaking at an advance firefighters’ command post west of Madrid, the prime minister warned that Spain and Portugal were experiencing the varied consequences of the climate emergency, from fires and storms to heavy snowfalls. “The entire Iberian peninsula is suffering the effects of the climate emergency in a very specific way,” he said.

While the fire near Madrid was being brought under control, emergency workers battled to extinguish a new fire near the Mediterranean port city of València, where at least 15,000 people were evacuated. “The fire is beyond our capacity to extinguish, it has a perimeter of about 21km,” the València region’s president, Juanfran Pérez Llorca, said late on Saturday.

after newsletter promotion

Spain’s interior ministry said on Saturday evening that a man had died in a fire in the Valèncian town of Manises. He had been found in a car in a ravine, officials said.

Authorities also ordered the evacuation of eight more municipalities near Toledo, south of Madrid, on Saturday, bringing the number of people forced to flee their homes by wildfires in Spain in recent days to 116,000, the Associated Press reported.

Spain’s environment minister, Sara Aagesen, said the wildfire that has burned through 50,000 hectares of land in the central province of Ávila was “the largest forest fire in our country’s recent history”.

The blazes are the latest episode in a summer of wildfires that threaten to burn an unprecedented expanse of land. Europe has endured a series of heatwaves since the spring, fuelled by the climate crisis, including the hottest-ever June, leaving vegetation tinder dry.

The EU commissioner for crisis management, Hadja Lahbib, told the BBC it was likely that damage from wildfires would exceed previous records. “Last year, one million hectares burned during the summer and so we are expecting to face another historic, sad record because the season has started earlier in the year,” she said.

Spain’s environment ministry said 32 major fires affecting 152,678 hectares (377,276 acres) had been recorded so far in 2026, compared with seven affecting 24,133 hectares in the same period in 2025.

The Gironde fire in France has so far burned 42,000 hectares, an area four times the size of Paris and one of the biggest devastations of land since the second world war.

At least 240 homes had been destroyed and many more damaged, a gendarme told BFMTV.

Firefighters are battling to slow the fire’s progression toward Bordeaux from the ground and air, with planes dropping water and retardants. Jérôme Steffe, the mayor of Cestas commune, 10 miles from Bordeaux city centre, told French media: “We are working together to put in place a firewall to block the advance of the flames.”

An exhibition centre in Bordeaux has been turned into an emergency shelter, providing camp beds and food for thousands of people, including hundreds of older people evacuated from care homes.

Cazenave said he had asked the central government for an economic crisis plan for the area because many businesses and workers had been evacuated from areas west of Bordeaux and the tourism industry had been heavily affected. He said it was impossible to say when people evacuated as a precaution could return to their homes.

“We don’t know how long this crisis will last, whether several days or several weeks,” he said.

The Landes fire has consumed 3,600 hectares and a rekindling of flames on Saturday had to be tackled from the air, Nuñez said. French authorities are also dealing with wildfires in the south-eastern Var region, where 3,000 people have been evacuated, as well as the Hautes-Alpes and Corsica.
