Loyal to the look: why Zohran Mamdani wears a suit in all seasons

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 12:00:11 GMT

Around town, on the pitch and even in the pool, the New York mayor keeps his suit on – what do his sartorial choices tell us?

Playing football. Playing in the sand. Dancing on a stage with Alicia Keys and the entire New York Knicks roster. Swimming in a swimming pool. Swimming in the ocean.

Traditionally, a suit and tie would be considered inappropriate attire for each of these activities. Yet over the past year Zohran Mamdani has seemingly been on a one-man crusade to prove otherwise: to convince people that a formal suit is, actually, suitable for all activities.

That’s because the New York mayor hardly ever wears anything but a suit: frequently purchased from Suit Supply, almost always in a dark colour and worn with a formal tie, mostly paired with smart black boots. He’s hardly the first male politician to embrace the suit – it’s the de facto uniform, after all, of those seeking to project seriousness and solemnity – but few, if any, have been quite as wedded to the formal blazer and matching trousers.

Cheering on the Knicks at Madison Square Garden in May, Mamdani stood out for his decision to wear a dark suit and tie. After the Knicks won, he took the unusual decision to wear the team’s jersey over his shirt and tie, but under his suit jacket. In June, he wore a navy suit, white shirt, and blue striped tie for a press opportunity with children at the beach.

Those aren’t even the most unusual examples.

On New Year’s Day 2025, while running for mayor, he wore a suit to take part in the Polar Bear Club plunge, a New York tradition whereby people go swimming in the frigid Atlantic. “I’m freezing … your rent as the next mayor of New York City,” Mamdani said in an accompanying TikTok video, a message that was rather on the nose, but won him lots of press coverage.

Water proved again to be no obstacle when Mamdani leaped, fully suited, into a swimming pool in Harlem last month, to announce the opening of the city’s pools for summer. (Mamdani “broke the rules in the process”, the rightwing New York Post reported, “which requires all swimmers to wear bathing suits in the water”.)

The mayor is trapped, it seems, in a wool or possibly wool-blend prison of his own making. But why?

Mamdani’s most recent predecessors weren’t as tied to the suit. Bill De Blasio was keen on shorts – although, in a furore that won’t have gone unnoticed by Mamdani, the former mayor was mercilessly ridiculed for wearing the cargo variety – while Eric Adams was partial to a polo shirt, and sometimes a woolly cardigan.

“I think Mamdani wants to double down on appearing as a working mayor, as someone who is always on the job and on the clock,” said Ella Devi, a fashion commentator and, like Mamdani, Democratic Socialists of America member whose (typically negative) assessments of Republicans’ style have made her a target for conservatives.

“I think that he kind of wants to convey that he is committed to the job, through his sartorial choices. I think that is reflected in his attachment to the suiting.”

Devi added: “It’s also that he’s a young, Muslim, socialist.”

It seems likely that Mamdani, the repeated focus of rightwing media, is held to a higher bar than white centrist politicians. It’s an issue Hasan Piker, the Turkish American leftwing streamer, brought up recently, when he said conservatives are “more receptive to what I have to say” when he dresses smartly.

“I used to wear T-shirts all the time,” he told Dazed. “But then I figured I should start wearing a suit and a tie because there are a lot of adults watching on Fox News [the rightwing channel frequently airs clips of Piker speaking] – if they see me saying something in the clips, they’ll be more receptive to what I have to say if I’m in a more appealing format.”

The mayor’s office declined to comment on Mamdani’s wardrobe, but he addressed his penchant for suit-wearing in a recent interview with CNN.

Asked about his decision to jump into a swimming pool wearing a suit, the mayor said: “I think I misunderstood the term swimsuit. I do also have to say thank you, though, to Goodwill [a charity known for its shops that sell used clothing], because I got that suit for 30 bucks, because you can’t go ruining the other suits that you have. But I’m clearly learning that there might be a different way to dress when it’s 100-degree weather.”

Leftists have not always been known for formal dresswear. That remains true in some cases – the disgraced Maine senatorial candidate Graham Platner wore sweaters and T-shirts during his campaign; John Fetterman, the Democratic senator from Pennsylvania, has a passionate commitment to wearing basketball shorts – but that might be changing.

“If there’s a visual language that connotes credibility and authority, why not take advantage of it?” Nathan Robinson, the editor of the leftwing Current Affairs magazine wrote this month.

“You might see someone in a suit as serious, professional, ready to do business. You might think they belong in the Senate or a boardroom. That’s certainly what Mamdani is trying to convey with his suits. He understands that socialists face a challenge: we’re considered fringe. People think we don’t belong among those making important decisions. The suits are a subtle way of asserting the legitimacy and authority of socialist ideas.”

Mamdani has taken the concept further than most. A keen football player, he wore a black suit with a grey tie while doing keep-ups with a football in July, and when he played in a game that same month, Mamdani simply threw a football shirt over his suit – although he did ditch the jacket.

It was not always thus. A source who played for the same team as Mamdani before his election said that he did not play in a suit and tie, although they added: “He always showed up in a suit, or at least suit pants, and his famous boots, and would change on the pitch because he was also always running late.”

The source, who asked not to be named, but who now plays for a football team with the author of this article, continued, “But he never missed a tackle” – a remark which was possibly aimed at this writer.

The source said Mamdani used to play in “black shorts”. Asked if a suit would be appropriate attire for a football match, they said it would not. They explained: “Limited stretch in the materials, restricted range of motion, you get sweaty and probably don’t want to have to dry-clean a suit as often for cost and longevity purposes, likelihood of it getting grass stains or torn up during play, excessive wear from friction which would also compromise longevity of a likely costly piece of clothing less easily replaced, too hot to play in (comfortably).”

Having become so intertwined with the suit, the question might be: can Mamdani ever wear anything else? Can the mayor ditch the formalwear?

“I think that now he’s kind of trapped in the suit, and he knows that he’s trapped in the suit, because he’s made it his thing to always wear the suit,” Devi said.

“He has to stick with the bit, the suit bit. If he wears jeans, then the New York Post is just going to write about that for the next three weeks.”

With temperatures in New York recently hitting 38C (100F), Mamdani might be wishing he could wear something else – although Devi had a suggestion should the heat become too unbearable.

“He would never go for this, because it would not be seen as very socialist, but Thom Browne does some very good suit shorts for the future heatwaves. So that’s my advice to Mayor Mamdani,” she said.

It’s a fine idea, except according to Thom Browne’s website, those shorts retail at about $1,300, which might raise questions over Mamdani’s socialist credentials. It seems that, at least for now, Mamdani is stuck in the suit.

‘Burnham bounce’ risks deflating unless focus remains on struggling households

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 11:34:30 GMT

UK’s inequalities expose splits in consumer economy, with spending suffering and a decline in savings among the poorest

A “Burnham bounce”, sunshine and a strong World Cup run for the England men’s football team. Could this be a turnaround moment for Britain’s struggling consumer economy or yet another false start for the UK’s spluttering growth engine?

Last week the data company GfK credited Andy Burnham’s return to Westminster politics for lifting UK consumer confidence at its fastest monthly pace for almost three years in June.

The lion’s share of the improvement was driven by how consumers viewed the prospects for the British economy, with a 10-point advance in how they felt about the past year, and an eight-point gain for the next 12 months.

“The sense of a fresh start following the appointment of a new prime minister surely accounts for some of this bounce,” GfK said.

For the economy at large, keeping the tills ringing is important: household consumption accounts for about 60% of the total economy, providing the lifeblood for high streets, service providers, builders and makers nationwide.

Burnham’s decision to introduce a temporary VAT cut for electricity bills in Great Britain from October, cap bus fares at £2 across England, and a 20% cut in business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues, is designed to help. In a further boost, the headline rate of inflation fell by more than expected, to 2.6%.

However, when it comes to the British consumer there is more going on than immediately meets the eye.

Drill down into the GfK data, and some revealing trends emerge: older Britons, aged 65 and over, are among the gloomiest. By contrast, 16- to 29-year-olds are more optimistic – despite the challenges facing the younger generation from an AI-disrupted jobs market and sky-high rents and house prices.

Youth unemployment is at the highest level in a decade. But over-65s are more likely than the under-30s to predict a rise in joblessness. They also worry more about the economic outlook, their own financial situation and the property market.

Some of this will be down to data quality. Consumers can be unreliable readers of economic conditions. Their mood on survey day can play a role, as can the news agenda.

There are real splits in the consumer perception of the economy, too – exposed by the UK’s deep inequalities. Time and again the poorest, unsurprisingly, have the gloomiest outlook. And it is not hard to see why.

Official figures show UK households spend £676.60 a week on average, with housing, fuel and power accounting for about a fifth of the total. Transport is the next most consumed category, followed by other spending including package holidays, leisure, communications and food and drink. Health and education make up just 3% of weekly spending on average.

There are worrying signs the wealthiest are pulling ahead. The latest official figures for the year to March 2025 show weekly spending by the richest fifth of households increased at twice the rate of the poorest fifth’s, rising by £98.10 (10%) to £1,083.60 compared with £18.10 (5%) to £407.30.

Since the onset of the cost of living crisis in late 2021, the average consumer price level has risen by more than a quarter. But in some categories – including for food and energy – it has risen by significantly more.

On top of this, the Bank of England has driven interest rates to elevated levels to combat the inflationary splurge – heaping pressure on borrowers. But a large group of older Britons are mortgage-free, and so have been more insulated.

after newsletter promotion

With these headwinds it is hardly surprising consumer spending has suffered: official figures show consumer-facing services output remains about 6% below its pre-pandemic level. Travel agents, food and drink, and hoteliers are among the hardest hit.

Threadneedle Street predicts real incomes will have fallen by about 0.5% in the year to the end of June. And with the volatile Middle East conflict expected to stoke inflation over the coming months, the belt-tightening for the British consumer is only likely to continue.

The counterpoint to the spending weakness has been a high household saving ratio, which measures the proportion of disposable income left unspent. At 8.9%, it is currently among the highest levels in a decade.

Households pushed the ratio to 27.5% during the pandemic lockdowns, when they were unable to spend much of their income. Billions of pounds were banked – helping to power the consumption boom, and inflationary burst, after the easing of restrictions.

However, not everyone was in a position to squirrel away money. Bank research shows the highest 40% of earners and retirees saved the most, while the poorest fifth of households suffered a decline in savings.

Reflecting regional divisions, savings were concentrated among affluent people in richer southern English neighbourhoods, where the Centre for Cities thinktank found households banked £12 for every £1 saved in poorer areas – mostly in northern English cities and towns.

For the “Burnham bounce” to be sustainable, it will require a continued turnaround in consumer confidence. That will need a laser-like focus on the households struggling the most.

From the strait of Hormuz to the North Sea, a global maritime war rages around us – and more than the price of oil is at stake

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 11:09:27 GMT

The collapse of the rules-based order is not confined to the land: we’re imperilled as centuries of maritime cooperation sink beneath the waves

The US military campaign to protect merchant shipping from Iranian attacks by asserting direct maritime control in the strait of Hormuz is not an idea unique to Donald Trump’s administration. Almost exactly 200 years ago, in the period 1825-27, a powerful US naval squadron led by Commodore John Rodgers was sent to the Mediterranean to defend American ships from the depredations of Greek corsairs and pirates.

For all the new-minted republic’s brave talk of liberty, the US squadron did not assist Greece’s ongoing “regime change” struggle for independence from the Ottoman empire. Its sole, self-serving purpose was to defend US trade, markets and business interests. After abandoning his call for a people’s revolution in Tehran, this, too, is what Trump’s reckless war with Iran has now boiled down to.

Although the US has not ratified the 1982 UN convention on the law of the sea, which establishes a legal right of freedom of passage without interference by littoral states, it has historically upheld the principle of freedom of navigation or mare liberum (the free sea) developed by Hugo Grotius, a 17th-century Dutch jurist. Rejecting Iran’s claims, Marco Rubio, US secretary of state, declared in June that “no country is allowed to charge tolls or fees on an international waterway”.

Yet Trump has since suggested the US itself may yet do exactly that and impose tolls. Although he later rowed back, last month’s “memorandum of understanding” with Iran accepts that it has a right, with Oman, to monetise transit through the strait of Hormuz. Despite the resumption of US attacks and Trump’s increasingly hysterical threats, the MOU currently remains the only basis for a future peace deal.

Two-faced Trump’s equivocal stance reflects a wider breakdown in the “free sea” consensus underpinning maritime law – and hastens the overall degradation of the international rules-based order. Trump believes nation states (or at least the US) have an absolute right to act unilaterally in their own interests, unconstrained by laws, treaties or regard for the “global commons” of the high seas.

The destabilising ramifications of this approach, emulated by other countries, grow clearer by the day. This new 21st-century war of the sea does not involve titanic clashes between Bismarck-class battleships or huge naval showdowns such as Jutland and Midway. But its frontlines are the same as ever: defence, security, borders, free trade, money, power.

Today’s war of the sea has many aspects. One is the spreading impact of precedents set by the Hormuz standoff. In Yemen, Iran-aligned Houthi militias have begun a copycat blockade of the Bab al-Mandab strait, at the mouth of the Red Sea, in reprisal, they claim, for attacks by Saudi Arabia. Two oil tankers were struck this week, further spooking energy markets and presaging wider escalation.

Also potentially fatal for international norms is the post-Hormuz debate in Indonesia about imposing tolls in the strait of Malacca, through which 22% of global maritime shipping passes. Might Turkey adopt the US-Iran approach and charge for passage through the Bosphorus? Or Spain in the strait of Gibraltar? The dire implications for global trade and supply chains are obvious. About 80% of goods traded worldwide by volume go by sea.

Friction over seaborne trade aside, overt maritime clashes between regional rivals are increasing, particularly in the South China Sea and the waters around Taiwan. Expansionist China’s creation of artificial, militarised islands on obscure reefs and sporadic confrontations with neighbours such as the Philippines are the root cause. Like the US, Beijing rejects international law when it doesn’t suit it – notably the 2016 ruling by the permanent court of arbitration, which found its claim to sovereignty over most of the South China Sea lacked a legal basis.

China crossed another red line last week when one of its missile destroyers undertook a live-fire drill inside Japan’s exclusive economic zone, about 180km (110 miles) from Okinotori, Japan’s southernmost island. Tokyo and Beijing have longstanding maritime disputes. But tensions rose sharply after Japan’s new prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, suggested a Chinese bid to seize Taiwan could trigger a Japanese military response. Few weeks go by without reports of Chinese air and sea exercises in preparation for a not-so-hypothetical amphibious assault on Taiwan.

The fact a Russian frigate accompanied the offending Chinese warship off Japan points to another major actor in the global war of the sea. Vladimir Putin’s once-vaunted Black Sea fleet has suffered severe losses, caused by Ukraine’s missiles and drones, since 2022. Its ships no longer control the Black Sea, mostly cowering in port. As if to compensate, hybrid “grey zone” Russian military maritime operations against Ukraine’s European allies are expanding. Baltic undersea pipelines and communications cables have proven vulnerable targets.

Russia has also stepped up surface fleet and submarine activities in the North Atlantic approaches, the North Sea and the Channel, where it is suspected of mapping underwater infrastructure with a view to future sabotage. Last Monday, one of its warships went a step further, marking Andy Burnham’s first day as UK prime minister with a rare live-fire drill 70kn (45 miles) south of Plymouth, home of the Royal Navy.

It was the latest in a string of hostile actions designed to provoke, intimidate and test British and European defences. Last month, a Russian frigate fired warning shots near a private yacht off the Isle of Wight. The incident seems trivial until it is set in the wider context of a rapidly building Nato-Russia at-sea confrontation. Then it begins to look scary.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

The sense of increasing inter-state maritime lawlessness is fed by numerous other recent incidents, such as the unlawful US sinking of an Iranian warship off Sri Lanka in March, last week’s bitter clash between Chinese and Philippine ships, Trump’s revived threats to forcibly annex the Danish-owned island of Greenland and his bombing of civilian boats off Venezuela. A Chinese nuclear submarine test-fired a long-range ballistic missile in the South Pacific this month to the outrage of Australia, which is itself acquiring nuclear-powered subs.

All this instability is fuelling an accelerating global arms race. Little wonder Burnham’s revamped government faces pressure to greatly increase defence spending, especially on the badly depleted Royal Navy. Current UK plans include upgrades to the Trident at-sea nuclear deterrent.

This many-fronted war of the sea tells a bigger story still: of how centuries-old, hard-won maritime cooperation and collaboration protocols are breaking down, of how international legal norms and rules – whether the issue is free trade, offshore defence, sovereignty, borders, fisheries, deep-sea mining or environmental pollution – are sinking beneath the waves.

It’s a story about a world where one country can impose its will on others less powerful and less wealthy, rather than seeking their agreement; where the fundamental concept of global commons or shared space is shot to hell. It’s about Lord Palmerston-style gunboat diplomacy writ large. It’s about a world all at sea.

Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

How do we defeat authoritarianism? By building a sense of belonging

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 11:00:12 GMT

Eighty-five million Americans are disaffected and less likely to vote, our survey found. Our democratic revival depends on a sense of community

Our country is at a crossroads between democracy and authoritarianism. And the only antidote is an organized, engaged citizenry. But at this critical moment when we need people to lean into the fight for our future, we find that far too many people have given up.

In a comprehensive, multiracial study, Sojourn Strategies, Ariel Research Partners and Richard Shafranek found that 35% of the US electorate – 85 million people – are disaffected, characterized by high levels of disillusionment and low levels of trust in government and politics. Our democratic revival depends on solutions that transform people from disaffected bystanders into powerful civic agents.

The desire for community is where we find hope. Almost six in 10 of the disaffected (58%) would like to feel more connected to other people. These feelings provide organizers with an opening to invite new people into community where they can build a sense of belonging and develop collective agency. The research also shows that the disaffected electorate is reachable: they are more likely to act when they feel like they belong and can see the tangible impact of their actions.

The disaffected electorate is the same as the overall population as far as race, ethnicity and gender – although disaffected people tend to be younger, have fewer resources and are less likely to be college educated. What surprised us in the research was the finding that the disaffected are as civically engaged as the general population, with the exception of voting. Disaffected people have almost the same likelihood to talk to a friend or a family member about a political issue (61% of the overall population and 60% of the disaffected electorate) or to search online for information about politics (both at 42%). Yet while 65% of the overall population would vote if the midterm elections were held today, only 56% of disaffected voters say the same.

Most institutions, including the traditional political industry, write these folks off as apathetic. But the research shows something very different. They care a great deal about their families, neighbors and communities. They want to see progress on issues they care about. They just don’t see the connection between voting and making their lives better.

So, what is going on? A common thread within this group of disaffected people is that they are extremely isolated with no or few friends or organizational affiliations. Almost half (49%) do not belong to an online community, church, mosque or synagogue or other religious groups, a community or political group, a labor union, or other community spaces. But collective spaces that we call “civic homes” are where people develop a sense of belonging and agency that is critical to their belief in the power of voting to drive change. Thus, investment in the organizing groups that operate as civic homes is a critical solution to our current democratic crisis.

Civic homes are developed by organizers as places where people can meet each other, feel seen and heard, work together on issues that matter to them, experience concrete benefits and make life better for themselves and the people they care about. Our research shows that even small increases in feelings of belonging within a civic home are associated with significant increases in voting and taking other civic and political actions.

Take Angeles in Nevada, for example. She was working long hours as a car wash supervisor, earning wages that never seemed to stretch far enough. Every month, she wondered whether her family would be able to cover rent. A few years ago, an organizer with Make the Road Nevada invited Angeles to a monthly membership meeting. During the discussion, Angeles heard her neighbors sharing similar struggles such as difficulties in making rent, stagnant wages, lack of affordable childcare and a feeling that those in power were not listening. This experience made Angeles feel seen and she began to develop a sense of belonging. She got connected to Make the Road Nevada’s Know Your Rights workshops, which helped her learn about the voting process and made her feel included. This year, Angeles will cast her first ballot as a US citizen. Not because a candidate’s campaign finally reached her. But because her people did.

Shared culture creates a feeling of belonging. Familiar food, language, music and even games are what make people feel at home. For example, a non-profit called Power Interfaith is running an innovative Soul Food Dinners program in Pennsylvania. These are nonjudgmental spaces where young, disaffected Black people, especially young men, can have honest conversations about their lives and visions of the future over a meal. Part of the focus is on young Black men who are skeptical about civic engagement and voting, but guided by their faith – a group that is undiscovered and under-researched.

The Soul Food Dinner project is similar to Georgia Alliance’s We the People initiative, which hosted intergenerational conversations among younger and older Black people as a strategy for rebuilding a sense of agency and belonging across differences. Older participants often arrived believing young people were disengaged or apathetic, while younger participants frequently viewed older generations as dismissive, out of touch or unwilling to share power. The series created opportunities for participants to ask deeper questions, listen to one another’s lived experiences and recognize shared values beneath different forms of expression. As participants moved beyond stereotypes, the emotional ground softened for collaboration, curiosity and mutual respect. Pre- and post-event feelings of power increased on both sides of the conversations, a measure that correlates to voter turnout in the Black community.

In the state next door, game facilitators with North Carolina Asian Americans Together are hosting Mahjong nights with communal hotpot meals for people in their late teens and 20s. The young people who come feel disconnected from traditional politics, but care very much about the cost of living, immigration, healthcare and making life better for their communities. The blend of familiar foods, games and conversations create connections and make people feel comfortable before they are invited into civic engagement, such as registering to vote or attending an organizing meeting.

Building trust and belonging that allows people to be transformed into civic agents is deep relational work. And it takes time. But the payoff is powerful. Transactional civic engagement aimed at a discrete outcome is a quick hit, like a sugar rush: it might feel great in the moment, but the long-term effect is weak and empty. Working to support people to become powerful civic actors through belonging and collective agency results in strong, durable architects of a hopeful future.

The stories of everyday people across the US standing up, getting organized and driving change to make life better for themselves, their families, and their communities is a tremendous source of hope. Take Elnora Gavin in Benton Harbor, Michigan. Working with a local civic organization, We the People Michigan, she organized a base of supporters and won $114m in school debt relief for majority-Black school districts in her state.

And she is not alone. More and more people in communities are using organizing strategies to build powerful civic homes that can be containers for people-driven collective action. In these turbulent times, people are choosing to lean into people-centered organizations and movements where they can find belonging, develop collective agency and make a better future possible.

Julie Fernandes is managing director of the Democracy & Power Innovation Fund, a community of organizers, researchers and funders who are working together to strengthen state-based community organizing, and associate director of the Rockefeller Family Fund

Katrina Gamble, PhD, is founder and CEO of Sojourn Strategies, a Black woman-owned social impact consulting firm that brings a people-centered approach to advocacy campaigns, research and philanthropic advising

‘We want to win the league’: Arsenal’s new recruits ink in WSL success

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 11:00:12 GMT

Despite a busy transfer window with Beth Mead moving on and seven new signings, academy graduates such as Lotte Wubben-Moy remain key to trophies

Georgia Stanway looks at her arms and then down at her legs on day one of Arsenal’s pre-season. “As you can see, I’m covered in tattoos,” she says. “I only see the bare skin, the space, so I need to keep collecting more.”

Tattooing and being tattooed is her creative outlet, her way of expressing herself off the pitch. But seeing space is key to the 27‑year‑old England midfielder being exceptional on the pitch.

Stanway’s unveiling video, after her move from Bayern Munich, showed a delicate, cursive script reading “whatever the weather” tattooed on her arm. It was a bold statement to get the lyric from North London Forever, Arsenal’s anthem, etched into her skin before she has stepped on to the Emirates Stadium pitch in red and white. “It shows I’m going to give absolutely everything for this club. I want to hit the ground running, play my game, connect with my teammates, connect with the fans and look forward to an exciting future at the club.”

Stanway is emblematic of Arsenal’s summer of change, one of seven signings so far. Meanwhile, Lotte Wubben-Moy, a lifelong fan who joined Arsenal’s academy at 13, represents the core and culture that is a point of focus at the club. It is a culture players want to be a part of, so much so it leads to getting a tattoo on day one of being there. “She has set a very high bar,” says Wubben-Moy, with a grin. “That’s Georgia. She goes all in and I like that.”

Wubben-Moy is ready to stake a claim in Arsenal’s starting XI after struggling to nail down a position in defence despite having performed exceptionally well when covering for injured players. “I’ve always felt ready,” says the 27-year-old. “When I get my moment, I deliver. Historically, as a club, we’re built on defensive solidity. If we have a solid defence, it allows us to create and score. That should be the stepping stone towards victories. So I will continue to contribute to the defensive solidity in whatever way, shape or form that is. But I want my spot.”

There was widespread recognition that Arsenal’s squad needed a revamp, that the age needed to be lowered and changes made if they were going to take the next step. That meant big names leaving, most notably Beth Mead and Katie McCabe. “They’re both absolute legends of the game and we have so much respect for them,” says Jodie Taylor, the former Arsenal striker who became the club’s technical director in January. “But we always knew this window was going to come with some changes.”

“Change is inevitable in women’s football,” says Wubben-Moy. “If you speak to a player and they don’t say they’re nimble, you’ve got someone that’s not built for the game. We’ve become a nimble team, a team that can move with the ebb and flow of women’s football.

“That’s not just within the playing group, it’s something replicated within the staff, the boardroom, the commercial team, the comms team. Everyone is so willing to move and to dictate what we want.

“If you’d asked me about change four or five years ago, I’d have been a bit intimidated, but now I know what to do and I’m part of the driver of it. The opportunity we have and that I see for us as a team, as a collective, is something that really excites me.”

Arsenal’s approach to Stanway’s recruitment was a contributing factor to her wanting to join the club. “Arsenal came in early doors,” she says. “I really enjoyed they were super loyal from the beginning and wanted me even when I wasn’t available. It’s a nice feeling being wanted.

“The last four years in Munich were unbelievable, but I knew I wanted to take the next step and I felt at Arsenal there was an opportunity for me to be able to progress, to make my game better and to play with world-class players.”

Arsenal have done most of their business early, with Stanway joined by experienced internationals Selina Cerci, Géraldine Reuteler, Ona Batlle and Misa Rodríguez, as well as young talents Lisa Baum and Isabella Damm. No major international tournament and seven signings in for day one of pre-season is a big boost for Renée Slegers and her coaching staff, particularly after two seasons of slow starts to domestic campaigns.

“The market is not easy, though, it’s constantly changing and the pool of elite talent is small and several clubs are fishing from it,” says Taylor. “You try and plan as much as you can, but you also have to be reactive in the market. We’re always trying to keep an eye on the future, but we have to be quite agile.

“We can talk about positional needs, qualities, ages and succession planning, but if a player’s not available or they just don’t exist, it can be like trying to fit square pegs and round holes. As well as looking at current needs and positional profiles, we talk a lot about our core style of play, but we also want to play with variety, be unpredictable and have different qualities in players too.”

The players who have come in have brought energy, says Wubben-Moy, who was on an emotional rollercoaster during Arsenal men’s Premier League and women’s Champions Cup-winning parade, with the bus looping past Highbury Corner, where she filmed her contract renewal video, and past Islington town hall, where she got married to cyclist Tao Geoghegan Hart a few weeks later.

“I like to focus on what they’re entering,” says Wubben-Moy, “which is a culture that has been created by history, by players and staff that are the core of this team and who have all lived through the changes to different degrees: Kelly [Smith], Renée, myself, Leah [Williamson], Kim [Little], Jodie too. We’ve been privy to lots of different things but all of us are holding on to and releasing, in a healthy way, the things we know we need to. It’s efficient, we’re focused, we know what we do next.

“It’s like you’re cooking the most beautiful recipe and then you add the final small ingredients that make the marginal difference, that elevate, and you create something that’s beautiful and that you can relish and enjoy. That’s what we’re in the process of now with a beautiful long pre-season. I’m desperate to get it out of the way so we can then serve what we’re cooking to the fans and be like: ‘Let’s eat and we’ll all eat together for the whole year.’”

The average attendance of more than 34,000 fans for WSL games at the Emirates last season and the club’s pioneering history in women’s football, as well as the Champions League win in 2025, are huge selling points, and all concerned at Arsenal want more, including a first Women’s Super League title since 2019.

“We’re in a great place,” says Taylor. “But we would have liked to have won more trophies last season and that is our huge ambition coming into this year. I’ll flat out say it: we want to win the league. We are an ambitious club and with the signings we’ve made we feel like we’re in a great place to do that.”

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 10:00:08 GMT

Will’s lack of self-worth is creating a barrier between him and Fi, but talking more could help them adjust to their mismatched libidos

How do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymously

double quotation markI worry that Will sees me more as a mother figure than a sexual being

The other morning, I woke up horny and suggested a quickie, but Will said he was too tired – it was too early. When I found him masturbating in bed the next day, I felt so rejected. I drove to work in floods of tears. I knew my feelings weren’t rational – there’s nothing wrong with masturbating – but they were real. All I could think was: couldn’t we have had those two minutes of intimacy yesterday?

I love sex and the connection it brings. I could have sex every day, but Will says no about 80% of the time. For me, sex creates closeness. For Will, the opposite is true: he has to feel close before having sex – and his depression, performance anxiety and low confidence mean his libido is lower than mine.

Until a couple of weeks ago, we hadn’t had sex in more than six months. My previous relationship was sexless for five years, and I don’t want to end up living with a friend again. But I’ve realised I played a part in that too. I find being vulnerable difficult, so instead of talking honestly about sex and how important it is to me, I put up a wall.

It’s hard to know how to drive sex when you have mismatched libidos. I usually initiate with a joke like, “Do you want to put your stick in my hole?” When he says no, I assume it’s my failure, that I asked in the wrong way. I worry that I desire him more than he desires me.

I also worry that Will sees me more as a mother figure than a sexual being. When we moved in together last autumn, our differences became more obvious. I was the fixer, the one who gets things done; Will was out of work and in bed for four months with a broken back. He felt worthless.

Finding Will masturbating led to the healthiest conversation I’ve had in a relationship. He understood that hearing how attracted he is to me isn’t enough – I need to feel desired through his actions. We’re back to having sex about once a week, which is enough for me to get the validation and reassurance I need. He’s teaching me how to slow down and open up more.

Things changed after we moved in together. Life became more about house admin than sex, and I injured my back, which completely killed intimacy. When Fi found me masturbating after I’d turned down sex, it wasn’t about choosing masturbation over her. I was doing it to try to get back to sleep. Sex with Fi is completely different – I need to be emotionally present because I care so much about whether she’s enjoying it too.

Even though we seem to be out of the rut now, Fi says she doesn’t want to initiate any more so she doesn’t get rejected. She worries it’s about her, but it isn’t at all – I think she’s amazing. But that’s part of the problem – because I don’t think I’m worth anything, being with someone amazing is overwhelming. I try to reassure her how incredibly sexy I find her, that I love her. And when we do have sex, it’s dynamite.

Am I a chicken-shop lefty? Here’s what a French fast food row taught me about politics

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 07:00:04 GMT

Feathers are flying over the halal chicken chain Master Poulet opening a branch in gentrified Saint-Ouen-sur-Seine – it’s an issue of wealth and class we know only too well

How do you like your progressive politics? Are you net-zero left or anti-identity politics left? A “legalising drugs” kind of radical or someone whose public sector solidarity includes police? Nato or Nat-no? The reputation for infighting in lefty spaces – where policy disagreements harden into personal tests of morality – needs neither introduction nor encouragement.

But reading about the left-on-left battle at Master Poulet, a French chicken chain that just opened its first UK branch, I found myself mulling a question that felt more than a little personal: am I chicken shop left?

OK, OK, this might just be a me problem. I’ve always had an interest in chicken shops. Maybe it’s personal: chicken shops, offering cheap halal takes on mainstream fare, have long been a pursuit of south Asian immigrants who hoped, like my own family, for a better life in this brave new world (talk about a wing and a prayer). But they are also bound up in Black British youth culture: neighbourhood incubators for music, affordable places to hang, landmarks of “the ends”. Chicken shops tell the story of a mixed, working-class Britain, with all its whimsy.

There’s Morris Cassanova AKA “Mr Chicken”, the late graphic designer who claimed to have designed 90% of the chicken shop signs in London. Or just the sheer nerve of the Americana. I still chuckle whenever I pass a Dixy Chicken, imagining what the Confederate south might think of a halal business from Solihull bearing its name. Add the peri boom, Amelia Dimoldenberg’s hit YouTube channel Chicken Shop Date and Rishi Sunak discussing his Nando’s order (“It’s good broccoli,” he said), and the chicken shop’s modern cultural legacy is something to crow about.

Anyway, back to the boeuf – sorry, I mean poulet – in France. Back in April, Karim Bouamrane, the Socialist party (PS) mayor of Saint-Ouen-sur-Seine, near Paris, tried to block a Master Poulet branch that had opened outside the town hall. Literally, with concrete blocks at the doors. A court ordered them removed, so he swapped them for giant colourful plant pots. The shop responded with quippy signs (“we are open … no offence to Karim”, read one), delighting French social media with this meta game of chicken. Bouamrane insisted it was all about quality of life, as late deliveries and cooking smells disturbed residents. Not everyone was convinced.

Saint-Ouen has transformed in recent years, not least due to regeneration pegged to the Paris Olympics. Critics accuse the mayor of overseeing a gentrification drive that has seen property prices surge, arguing that’s his real issue: he wants to chase out cheap food (and the sorts of people who eat it). Master Poulet serves a drumstick of rotisserie chicken and potatoes for €4 (£3.40) – cheaper than a McDonald’s and probably no less healthy, yet McDonald’s is not a target. And given the tradition of rotisserie chicken in France, you do have to ask what exactly it is about the halal version that prompts complaints about bad odours.

Which may explain why politicians from the further-left La France Insoumise (LFI), have waded in, questioning whether Islamophobia and classism are at play, and accusing the mayor of abusing his power. One MP visited the shop in solidarity. His name? Éric Coquerel. I’ll just leave that there.

To be clear, I am far from an expert on French politics. The last time I thought much about the LFI and PS was in 2024, when they joined forces in the Nouveau Front Populaire (NFP) to hold back Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally. It worked, prompting many of us in the UK to ask, with Nigel Farage tipped for No 10, shouldn’t we – red, green, yellow or bin – be doing the same?

Bouamrane announced last month he would be running for president. But as I pecked at pommes frites on a warm London evening, it was hard to see how that successful arrangement of NFP could happen again. Bouamrane has since called LFI a colonialist party, for undermining French republicanism with its talk of race; while allegations of racism from LFI continue. Meanwhile, opinion polls put Le Pen on track for presidential glory. What leaves me crestfallen (at this point the puns are involuntary) isn’t the disagreement but what it heralds.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

So am I part of the chicken shop left? I don’t know, maybe. But perhaps that’s the wrong question. After the almighty flap over Master Poulet, I’m left feeling that politics should be less “ruling the roost” and more “birds of a feather”. Especially with a far-right fox prowling outside the henhouse.

Coco Khan is a freelance writer and co-host of the politics podcast Pod Save the UK

How Trump could undermine the midterms

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 05:00:04 GMT

The president really has no power over elections – but that hasn’t stopped Trump from laying the groundwork to challenge results in November

When Donald Trump commandeered primetime US television last Friday, he delivered a familiar, but still extraordinary, message. The president argued once again that the results of the 2020 election, which he lost to Joe Biden, were illegitimate.

US elections are “vulnerable to being rigged and stolen”, Trump alleged, claiming that “the trust of the American people was lost” when he was defeated.

Historically, incumbent parties underperform in midterm elections and with the president’s popularity sagging – he has an approval rating of just 37% – Republicans appear on course to lose seats in the US Senate and House of Representatives, as well as in state and local elections, in November.

Trump’s latest intervention, in which he accused China of interfering with the 2020 election, is viewed by US voting rights activists as just the latest escalation of a bid by the White House to influence, and potentially alter, the results of the 2026 midterm elections.

“The number one threat facing American elections is the continued lies coming out of the White House,” said the Arizona secretary of state, Adrian Fontes, the official responsible for overseeing the state’s elections.

The president is fighting to persuade Congress to approve legislation, the Save Act, that would allow the US federal government greater control over elections. Trump has also called for the federal government to take direct control of elections in some states, falsely claiming that his defeats there in 2020 were illegitimate.

There’s just one snag. “We have an election system that is not run by the federal government,” said Ben Berwick, who leads Protect Democracy’s election law and litigation team. “It’s run by states and local jurisdictions.”

The president, he added, “really has no power over elections”. So what can Trump actually do?

Republicans in a handful of states have already scrambled, at Trump’s urging, to redraw their congressional maps in the wake of a landmark decision by the US supreme court – controlled by a conservative supermajority – that effectively gutted a major section of the Voting Rights Act.

Louisiana led the way, tearing up its old map of four Republican and two Democratic districts in favor of a new one, which will probably give Republicans five of the state’s six congressional seats. Such efforts are designed to shift the outcome of future elections.

And with threats to mail-in voting, sowing fears about voting machines, as well as a steady stream of unfounded allegations of election fraud, many fear Trump appears to be laying the groundwork to challenge results that don’t go his way in November.

The memory of the deadly 6 January attack on the US Capitol in 2021, fueled by Trump’s denial of his election defeat, looms large.

“It’s reckless that the president will continue to do what he’s doing, and that the folks around him will continue to let him do what he’s doing, and potentially trigger that sort of behavior that could cost lives,” added Fontes. “This is a powder keg out there, and there’s a lot of folks who just just want to get on with their lives, who just want to get on to solving their own problems.”

Trump has repeatedly tried to restrict voting by mail, and likened it to cheating, despite doing so himself. It is a key focus of his administration’s efforts. In November, the administration could use the US Postal Service (USPS) to “control the flow of mail-in ballots, and potentially not send ballots to certain voters”, Berwick said.

Democratic voters are deemed more likely to cast their ballots by mail than Republicans: about one in four registered Democrats did so in 2024, according to the States United Democracy Center, alongside 1 in 5 registered Republicans.

Eight states and the District of Columbia rely almost exclusively on postal ballots. The USPS, at Trump’s direction, proposed a rule that would require states to turn over their voter roll information to the federal government, which would then tell states which voters were ineligible.

That proposal, enforced by an executive order in March, faces a wall of legal challenges and was ruled unconstitutional by a judge. Cases pursued by the civil rights group NAACP in Washington DC and the League of Women’s Voters in Massachusetts have challenged the plan in court.

Celina Stewart, CEO of the League of Women Voters, said the organization intervened to ensure the bid to restrict mail-in voting was “shut down” in time for state primary elections, taking place in the months ahead of November’s general election. “And so I think that was really important for us,” she said, “just to make sure that voters knew how that was going to work, and make sure that they understood what their rights were, and how they could execute their ballot effectively”.

At polling stations, Trump is also pointing to electronic voting machines, which he suggested in his 16 July TV address could be compromised by foreign actors. “China carried out what is believed to be the largest compromise of election data in history, resulting in China’s illicit acquisition of 220 million US voter files,” he said.

Declassified files from US investigators show that China downloaded publicly-available election data in 2022. Those same investigators concluded that China did not interfere in the election.

Voting rights advocates believe Trump may have been telegraphing his intent to try to block the use of some voting machines in a late-day election gambit, invoking national security as a rationale.

“The thing that maybe worries me the most is what we saw in Fulton county and elsewhere,” Berwick said, referring to an FBI raid in January that resulted in the seizure of 2020 ballots and election material in Georgia. The administration “may try to do something similar in the immediate post-election period under the sort of pretext of investigating ineligible voting, or votes cast by ineligible voters”, he suggested, “in a way that, if done in the immediate post-election period, would be designed to disrupt the ability of states to count votes and certify elections”.

In the meantime, the White House has actively undermined safeguards to the election system. The Election Assistance Commission, a US federal agency designed to help states overcome technical challenges in election administration, which currently has no commissioners. Trump fired the Democrat members, and allowed the Republicans to resign. More than a third of the staff of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency was meanwhile cut by Trump’s so-called “Department of Government Efficiency”, the cost-cutting drive fleetingly led by Elon Musk, including the entire team looking at cybersecurity threats in elections.

“One cannot help but notice the irony of the administration’s purported interest in securing our election systems, and yet gutting the very agency responsible for that,” said Hannah Fried, co-founder and CEO of All Voting is Local.

The Save Act, which is stalled in Congress, would require voters to present their passport or birth certificate to register to vote, and then to provide photo ID from a narrow list of valid identifications to vote in person. Campaigners argue such restrictions would disproportionately impact Black, Native, elderly and student voters.

The legislation would also sharply constrain voting by mail, too. And it would require states to turn over their voter rolls to the federal government.

Absent that legislation – which is constitutionally questionable – federal agencies under Trump may still try to pressure states to purge voter rolls using unreliable or unverified federal data sets. Courts have consistently blocked attempts by the federal government to force unvetted voter purges.

Some states – led by Republican officials – have already turned over voter rolls, when requested by the federal government.

Berwick highlighted the prospect of federal agencies like the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security seeking voter lists from states, “presumably to then send to states lists of voters they believe are ineligible, which are very likely to be inaccurate”.

While far-right figures like Steve Bannon, an ally and former adviser of Trump, have called for the deployment of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents or federal law enforcement at voting sites, and the president himself has explicitly raised the prospect, it is considered remote because federal law plainly outlaws the presence of troops or federal agents at polling places.

Voter intimidation has already manifested at early voting sites and drop boxes, said Stewart, of the League of Women Voters, who cited an incident in Arizona where armed contractors confronted voters. “The president in particular is pushing for increased ICE funding,” she said. “So you have to ask: for what?”

Stewart highlighted how her organization successfully sued to stop armed drop-box intimidation in 2022, securing a court order within 24 hours. The incident was a demonstration of “how quickly things like that can happen” she said, “but equally as quickly … how we can shut that down”.

Trump’s increasingly inflammatory rhetoric is itself a threat to the integrity of the 2026 election, said Georgia state senator Saira Draper, a leading voting administration expert, who warned that narrative attacks are designed to undermine outcomes, regardless of who wins.

“By sowing distrust in elections, no matter what the outcome is, he continues on the division, whether his party wins or not into the next term,” said Draper, who suggested that such constant rhetoric turns followers into “foot soldiers for the cause”.

Some of those foot soldiers sit on county boards of elections, which are required to certify elections. And some are running for office, successfully winning the Republican nomination, like Alex Kolodin, who helped lead failed legal efforts to overturn Arizona’s 2020 and 2022 election results, who is now the Republican candidate for Arizonan secretary of state: its top elections official.

After the 2020 election, some Republican elections board members refused to certify fair elections, threatening to disrupt the process. A mass refusal could cast doubt on the results in conservative states that have taken a Democratic turn in a swing year.

“This federal interference led by the president isn’t helping anybody,” said Fontes. “It’s not good for, in my view, any circumstance across the country, and it’s got everybody on pins and needles for no really good reason.

“I mean, what’s the really good reason why folks are afraid, that there’s something wrong with our elections? The only explanation is that Donald Trump can’t get over getting his butt kicked in 2020.”

Always remember how Macquarie built its millionaires on outrageous tolls and charges

The Guardian Sun, 26 Jul 2026 00:00:56 GMT

As Shemara Wikramanayake retires with shares worth hundreds of millions, the public is left counting the cost of high prices for utilities, roads and airports

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The recent retirement of the Macquarie Group CEO, Shemara Wikramanayake, marks the culmination of a highly successful career. She is leaving the company with shares worth hundreds of millions of dollars after nearly 40 years at the Sydney-based institution. Under her leadership, the “millionaires’ factory” has increased its annual revenue by about 80% and nearly doubled its profit.

Wikramanayake has also overseen and consolidated the group’s transition from a firm specialising in privatised infrastructure to a global merchant bank earning profits from commodity trading, specialist asset finance and wealth management.

Macquarie shareholders, who have tripled their money over the past eight years (with dividends and capital gains), have plenty of reason to be grateful.

The public, in Australia and elsewhere, may take a slightly more jaundiced view. The foundations of the millionaires’ factory were laid through a string of private infrastructure deals that greatly enriched Macquarie while delivering expensive or substandard services.

The biggest disaster of all has been Thames Water, privatised by the Thatcher government in the UK and acquired by a Macquarie-led consortium in 2006. After extracting billions in dividends for itself and other investors, and loading the company with debt, Macquarie sold out in 2017. By that time, the utility’s performance was so dire as to be unsalvageable. Nearly a decade later, the UK government is still grappling with the choice between an unpalatable renationalisation and a hybrid model that is likely to prove unworkable.

In June, Andy Burnham called for public ownership at Thames Water. As parts of Wales are in drought and the rest of the country is experiencing prolonged dry conditions, about 23 million people across the UK are under a hosepipe ban.

Another example worth mentioning is the privatisation of Sydney airport to a Macquarie-led consortium, which promptly raised a wide range of fees and charges. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has repeatedly concluded that the airport is a monopoly and that price monitoring is ineffectual. The issue was predictable – and predicted.

Macquarie was also a pioneer of the private toll road industry, which has left Australian cities saddled with costly transport systems, characterised in the words of a review of the Sydney toll-road system as a “poorly-functioning patchwork”. International deals such as Ontario’s Highway 407 were even worse for the public, though highly successful for Macquarie’s millionaires.

Macquarie Group is not the only corporate giant built on lucrative deals with the public. CSL, one of Australia’s most valuable companies, was created by the privatisation of the Commonwealth Serum Laboratories, which had produced a wide range of innovations. The privatised CSL was awarded a long-term contract to supply products derived from blood plasma at a far higher cost.

The resulting cashflow was ploughed into a global acquisition program that made CSL the giant it is today. Meanwhile, research on commercially less attractive products such as antivenoms and vaccines for tropical diseases was scaled down, abandoned or left to universities and public research institutes.

Other privatisations have followed a similar pattern of rhetoric about private sector efficiency combined with continued public largesse. Qantas has enjoyed the favoured treatment of a national flag carrier while disclaiming their obligations to either the travelling public or its own employees, beyond those dictated by profit maximisation. Telstra forced us to buy back, at massive expense, the telephone network built under public ownership and sold only a few years previously.

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

If there is any consolation here, it is that (long after the public) policymakers have finally woken up to the damage done by these deals. Not so long ago, Infrastructure Australia was proclaiming the benefits of innovative finance and universities were offering courses in “financial engineering”. Today these terms are rightly viewed with suspicion. As the UK commentator Anthony Hilton wrote after the crash of Carillion (a major participant in private finance initiatives):

double quotation markIts demise is also the consequence of the relentless application of a neo-liberal political philosophy that for years has elevated financial engineering above real engineering; off-balance-sheet finance above paying for things openly; and lauded the private sector above the public sector.

Ordinary people can express respect for the achievements of Shemara Wikramanayake at Macquarie Group. But every time you pay a toll or an outrageous airport parking charge, remember that the millionaires’ factory was built from the proceeds of charges like these.

John Quiggin is a professor at the University of Queensland’s School of Economics

From A Useful Ghost to Self Esteem: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead

The Guardian Sat, 25 Jul 2026 05:00:34 GMT

A woman is reincarnated as a vacuum cleaner in this Cannes prize-winning black comedy, and the uncompromising pop star hits the festival trail

A Useful GhostOut now Winner of best film at Cannes Critics’ Week, this tale of a woman reincarnated as a vacuum cleaner takes you to plenty of unexpected places, even when you discount the sort of unexpectedness suggested by the premise. Part Marxist thriller, part supernatural romance, and taking in foul-mouthed monks and drama with the in-laws along the way, Ratchapoom Boonbunchachoke’s directorial debut is an oddball treat.

On the SeaOut now Made mostly outside the traditional funding mechanisms for UK film, this independent second feature from Helen Walsh is a lovely, graceful depiction of repression and queer desire in a Welsh mussel-harvesting community. Barry Ward gives a fine performance as the married man who finds himself drawn to a younger itinerant worker (Lorne MacFadyen).

Aardman RetrospectiveCinemas nationwide In the run-up to the release of Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom, look out for summer holiday rereleases of a plethora of Aardman classics in cinemas, including A Matter of Loaf and Death, The Curse of the Were-Rabbit and the film that first introduced woolly hero Shaun, A Close Shave.

Pinocchio UnstrungOut now Director Rhys Frake-Waterfield was also behind Winnie-the-Pooh: Blood and Honey and its sequel. This new instalment in what the film-makers call The Twisted Childhood Universe features Robert Englund (Freddy Krueger) as the voice of Jiminy Cricket. Catherine Bray

Camp BestivalLulworth Castle, nr Wareham, 30 July to 2 August Rob da Bank’s enduring family-friendly festival returns with its mix of kids’ activities – bee-keeping has been added this year, alongside skateboard ramp lessons and trampolining – and music from Bastille, Fatboy Slim, Self Esteem and more. Michael Cragg

Elgar’s FirstRoyal Albert Hall, London, 29 JulyThe English composer’s magnificent Symphony No 1 gets top billing, but this concert also features the first major world premiere of the BBC Proms season. The World’s Wife by Brett Dean sets Carol Ann Duffy’s poetry and is performed by soprano Claire Booth and BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra conducted by Ryan Wigglesworth. Flora Willson

Luke CombsEdinburgh, 25 July; London, 31 July to 2 August The US country music superstar, who scored a UK hit with his cover of Fast Car in 2023, steps up to stadiums. With six albums under his belt, including this year’s deeply personal The Way I Am, expect a setlist brimming with crowd-pleasing self-reflection. MC

Edinburgh Jazz & Blues festivalVarious venues, 25 & 26 July This event consistently embraces international and Scottish artists. Its closing weekend includes folk-inflected sax-led quartet Harben Kay (25 July), Joni Mitchell-inspired singer Michelle Willis (25 July) and multi award-winning jazz/hip-hop sax star Soweto Kinch (26 July). John Fordham

Richard DaddRoyal Academy of Arts, London, 25 July to 25 October Step into a world of fairies and folklore in Beyond Bedlam, a look at the work of the Victorian artist. He remained forgotten by history until the 1960s, when his life in Victorian asylums became a source of inspiration for countless artists.

Michael PinskyMidlands Arts Centre, Birmingham, 25 July to 4 October For The Final Bid, Pinksy has filled this gallery with secondhand chairs, all hung from the ceiling, which visitors are invited to bid on. Each bid drives the chair higher up towards the ceiling, in a strange capitalistic ballet about value and detritus.

Clare WoodsPitzthanger Manor, London, 29 July to 8 November The exhibition, called Garden Without Seasons, sees meditative paintings and collages of the natural world in this Sir John Soane-designed country house, each work pushing the boundary between abstraction and figuration and asking viewers to slow down and contemplate.

Susan HughesMAC, Belfast, 30 July to 18 October This Belfast-based artist and fiddle player travelled around Ireland collecting stories about the mysteries, myths and collective power of traditional music. The result is this show filled with objects, songs and a stage for ad-hoc performances. Eddy Frankel

The World Is Full of Married MenThe Yard theatre, London, to 1 August The great Yard theatre opens its doors after a huge refurb. Its opening season includes a reimagined King Lear with Ian McKellen as well as this brilliantly bizarre adaptation of Jackie Collins’s racy novel, set amid a series of doll’s houses – and performed by dolls. Miriam Gillinson

Mike Reiss25 July to 6 August; tour starts London As part of The Simpsons’ original writing team – and co-showrunner during the programme’s early 1990s glory years – nobody is better placed to unpick the seminal cartoon’s ingenious comic tapestry than Reiss. This tour sees him spill all his Springfield-related secrets and take audience questions. Rachel Aroesti

Matthew Bourne’s The Car ManSheffield Lyceum, 25 July; Sadler’s Wells, London, 28 July to 29 August One of Bourne’s steamiest dance shows is also one of his best dramas. Loosely based on Bizet’s Carmen, but transported to small-town 50s US, a gang of macho mechanics have their close-knit, closed-minded world interrupted when a stranger comes to town. Tour de France finale, Commonwealth Games and Hungarian GP – follow with us

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 16:06:15 GMT

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

The Commonwealth Games have historically served as a staging post for future stars. While Glasgow’s reduced 10-sport and six para-sport event may not carry the lustre of old, there’s a sense of uplift around this edition, not least due to King Charles’s opening ceremony Tardis scene-stealer. With nine golds up for grabs, Saturday’s highlights include Adam Ramsay-Peaty seeking gold in the 100m breaststroke final (9.04pm). As well as all the fun of the mixed 4x100m freestyle relay (9.11pm), the 18-year-old Filip Nowacki – world junior 100m and 200m breaststroke champion – is looking to become Jersey’s first Commonwealth medallist since 1990. In the artistic gymnastics women’s team final, England are aiming to defend the title they won in 2022. There’s plenty of netball action too, with all four home nations opening their campaigns. Scotland start against New Zealand, who claimed bronze in Birmingham. Will Unwin helms our live blog, with Sean Ingle and Yara El-Shaboury reporting from Glasgow.

Alpe d’Huez hosts a second ⁠straight summit finish on Saturday to conclude ​the Tour de France’s intense Alpine trilogy. The Tour returns to the famous peak for the first time in ⁠four years, when Britain’s Tom Pidcock claimed victory in 2022. On its first appearance in 1952, Fausto Coppi claimed victory but it wasn’t until 24 years later that La Grande Boucle returned. Saturday’s 170.9km route from Bourg-d’Oisans ramps up the difficulty, featuring ‌5,450m of climbing and four categorised ascents. The stage includes a daunting ​approach to Alpe d’Huez via the Col de Sarenne. Tadej Pogacar has a big lead in the race for the yellow jersey, but his team are struggling with a sickness bug. Tom Bassam’s stage 20 rolling blog will capture all the thrills and spills, with Jeremy Whittle reporting.

Ascot is set to stage a truly international renewal of the King George VI and Queen Elizabeth Stakes (3.35pm) with last year’s winner, Calandagan, facing up to eight rivals, including his stablemate Goliath. Jointly owned by an American in John Stewart, Goliath will be ridden by the Belgian Christophe Soumillon, who hopes to avoid a repeat of his Royal Ascot run in the Hardwicke Stakes, when he lost an iron in the closing stages. Aidan O’Brien has a strong hand as he looks to end a 10-year drought in the race since Highland Reel’s 2016 victory. He runs this year’s Irish Derby winner, Benvenuto Cellini, last year’s Derby hero, Lambourn, the Dante runner-up Action and the filly Minnie Hauk, a multiple Group One winner last season. The only UK-trained runner is Andrew Balding’s mare Kalpana, twice a winner at Ascot on Champions Day. Given she gave Calandagan the most to do in this race last year, her track form stands up to scrutiny. Greg Wood helms our live racing blog.

Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton could go into Formula One’s August break on a Hungarian high this weekend while the championship leaders, Mercedes, seek urgent answers to George Russell’s car woes. Russell’s plight, with his car losing chunks of time on the straights, ​has dominated paddock chatter as his 19-year-old Italian teammate Kimi Antonelli goes from strength to strength with six wins in 10 rounds. The Briton is now 50 points adrift of Antonelli after spinning off into the gravel in Belgium last Sunday for his third DNF of the year. That blank let Hamilton back into second place overall, 45 points behind Antonelli, and the ⁠Hungaroring is a favourite for the seven-time world champion, who won six of his titles with Mercedes before moving to Maranello. Philip Cornwall has all the action, lap by thrilling lap.

Another big netball day in Glasgow, and a clash of titans as Australia face England in Pool A. The Diamonds ended England’s defence with a 60-51 semi-final victory at Birmingham NEC four years ago before going on to claim gold. It was sweet revenge for the Aussies, who were denied the title by their old Ashes foes in dramatic fashion in the final second on the Gold Coast in 2018. This may be a group match, but don’t expect either side to dial down the intensity. In Pool B, Wales confront Scotland. There’s more action in the pool, where Australian swimmers are sure to dominate: Olympic and world champion and world record-holder, Cameron McEvoy, goes for gold in the men’s 50m freestyle. In the boxing ring, Scotland’s first female British champion Stephanie Kernachan competes in the women’s bantamweight last 16. Last year she became the first Scottish woman to compete at a boxing world championships. It’s also a day for medals in artist gymnastics and weightlifting. Daniel Harris helms the blog.

Kimi Antonelli has won six of 10 grands prix this season and the 19-year-old Formula One championship leader, in just his second season, heads into Sunday’s Hungarian Grand Prix with a 45-point buffer at the top of the standings. Lewis Hamilton, the man whose seat he filled at Mercedes, is his closest rival, with the Italian’s teammate, George Russell, a further five points back. At the back of the field, the well-funded but hugely disappointing Aston Martin team – with just one point scored this year – have introduced a major upgrade package from their design chief, Adrian Newey. John Brewin hosts our lap-by-lap coverage.

After three weeks of intense action, the big loop lands in Paris for the finale and another cobbled climb of Montmartre, with Tadej Pogacar on the verge of a record-equalling fifth Tour de France, aged only 27. Should he avoid the illness sweeping through his UAE Team Emirates-XRG teammates and win on Sunday, the Slovene would join the greats in the Tour pantheon. The Spaniard Miguel Indurain won the Grande Boucle five times in a row from 1991 to 1995. Eddy Merckx, Jacques Anquetil, Bernard Hinault have also claimed five triumphs. Pogacar has plenty more in the tank and could go on to win several more Tours – an intimidating prospect for the rest of the field. Tom Bassam hosts the final-stage rolling blog.
