Who Are the People Protesting in India?

The New York Times July 25, 2026

India Protests

Advertisement

Supported by

Some of the young demonstrators who forced out the country’s education minister described their deep-seated anger, frustration and desires that drove them into the streets.

By Anupreeta Das and Akansha Bahadur

Reporting from New Delhi

The pent-up hopes and frustrations of India’s young people found a release in a protest movement that gathered steam this past week in the capital, New Delhi, forcing the government to make concessions.

A crowd of thousands was mobilized by a call from the leaders of a youth movement to reform India’s troubled education system and to push for the resignation of the country’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, whom they blamed for a botched college-entrance exam that left millions in the lurch.

On Saturday, Mr. Pradhan submitted his resignation to Mr. Modi, handing the protesters a major win, and organizers called an end to the protests. But the grievances that fueled the protests have united a movement that attracted activists and academics, curious teenagers, blue-collar parents and children from affluent homes, established celebrities and newly minted influencers, atheists, farmers, religious leaders, and even a man wearing a Spiderman mask.

The movement may continue to pose one of the most substantial challenges in years to the leadership of India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, with young people accounting for 40 percent of India’s population.

Here are some of their voices as they attended this week’s protests:

AMAL HAYAT, 20

Amal Hayat, 20, a student of electrical and computer engineering at Delhi’s Jamia Millia Islamia University, is the kind of young person whose ambitions are essential to Mr. Modi’s vision of a “Vikshit Bharat,” or developed India, by 2047.

She is the first woman in her family to go to college — a point of pride — and said she chose engineering because she had a head for math and wanted to pursue a career in artificial intelligence. “Solving problems gives me peace,” she said.

She joined the protests not because of a person, or a political party or movement. “It’s about the issues, the students, it’s about the future of the country,” she said.

And, for her, it’s about fairness. She walked around the protest grounds on Thursday afternoon, holding a large sheet of paper on which she had scrawled in black ink: “Sticks for students, garlands for rapists.”

Ms. Hayat, 20, said she was making a point about impunity. She contrasted the batons used by security forces to hit protesters as they marched toward Parliament on Monday, to the treatment of some Indian politicians who continue to enjoy the perks of public life even as they face criminal cases against them for serious charges, including rape.

“So what kind of justice is this?” she asked.

ANSHU GUDIYA, 13

Anshu Gudiya, an eighth-grader who lives in Faridabad, a city in the greater Delhi area, said she came to the protests to see what the fuss was all about, even if it meant taking a day off from school.

Her father works in a hotel in Delhi, and her mother is a tailor. Her parents allowed her to go by herself, she said, because the scandal that ignited the protest movement — the botched college exam — “also affects my future.”

Science is her favorite subject at school, Anshu said, and she wants to study machine learning and artificial intelligence, two subjects that require government-administered exams to get into top public engineering schools. She has not thought about her future beyond that, but hopes someday to “work at Google.”

Anshu said it took her more than three hours, after multiple train changes and a ride on a rented bike, to reach the protest site, next to the 18th-century Jantar Mantar observatory. She came prepared for Delhi’s merciless sun, with a head scarf and sunscreen.

She had first heard about the protests and the group behind them, the Cockroach Janta Party, on Instagram. “I also wanted to see the protest for myself,” and to understand how people conduct demonstrations against the government, said Anshu.

CHANDAN KUMAR, 28

Chandan Kumar, 28, is a delivery driver, not a student, but the protest movement’s demands resonated with him.

Like millions of India’s young people, he was forced to choose between pursuing school and finding a job. He said he dropped out of high school after his mother fell ill, and the family needed extra income to cover her medical costs. He found work in construction, and eventually gave up his dreams of going back to school.

At one point, he said he learned how to use Excel and interviewed for data entry jobs, but could not type fast enough. In 2018, he found a job as a delivery agent for a popular online food platform. “When a person is left with no options, they have to do whatever comes their way,” Mr. Kumar said.

The work is “decent enough,” Mr. Kumar said, as he sat on his motorbike, taking a break from delivering food that customers had ordered for the protesters, from pizza to vegetable curry.

Mr. Kumar said he supported the protesters’ demand that the education minister resign. He was hopeful that the education system would be fixed so that his child can have a better future. “Compared to where I am, my child will reach a place that is a hundred times better.”

ZAFAR HABIB

Zafar Habib’s future doesn’t directly rest on the outcome of the protest movement. The son of a math professor and an activist mother, Mr. Habib, 22, is a history graduate from a private university, and is headed to Oxford University for further studies.

But although he said he had not faced the same educational challenges, he joined the protests out of solidarity and a sense that the outpouring of anger is a significant moment for the country.

People who had grown up seeing little other than “bigotry, fear-mongering and hatred” under Mr. Modi’s Hindu nationalist government, which has been in power since 2014, were getting the chance to “express a love for each other,” he said. It resonated with him as a Muslim, Mr. Habib said, adding that he had suffered taunts as a child because of his last name.

People were helping each other, handing out free food and water, and joining hands to be heard, he said. The humanity he has witnessed made Mr. Habib hopeful that once people go back to their daily lives, “we will carry this kindness forward.”

Anupreeta Das covers India and South Asia for The Times. She is based in New Delhi.

Saying Farewell to R. E. I.’s Beloved New York City Storefront

The New York Times July 25, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Customers gathered to mourn as the outdoor equipment retailer shuttered its location in the famed Puck building in SoHo, where it had been for 15 years.

By Alisha Haridasani Gupta

Dozens of people stopped at the shrine before sighing and then walking on. One person in a black dress and holding a black umbrella gave a 30-second farewell toast before disappearing into the evening. Another started tearing up as she read the notes on the shrine. Passers-by hugged one another.

It wasn’t a funeral; it was a “celebration of life,” according to the anonymous organizers — for the R. E. I. store. It had occupied a historic building in New York’s SoHo neighborhood for 15 years before closing its doors for good on Thursday night. In another city, perhaps, it might not have been a long run, but in a neighborhood with high business turnover, the company’s sole location in the city became somewhat of a landmark.

“I’ve been living in New York for 20 years now, so I remember the time before R. E. I. and the time after R. E. I.,” said Chaiwen Chou, 43, who had stopped by the store to take some last photos of it and leave a message at the shrine. “It just so happened that when I started getting outdoors more was around the same time that R. E. I. opened,” she said.

“I’m going to miss it,” she added. “It feels like the end of an era.”

Ever since the flagship retailer for outdoor gear moved into three stories of the Puck Building in 2011, it remained an unchanging space amid the rapidly changing downtown neighborhood. Its facade would help orient New Yorkers who emerged from the train station discombobulated, and passers-by found in it an accessible, clean bathroom. It served as a heated oasis on cold days and a cool-down spot to fill up water bottles on hot ones.

The store will also be remembered as a rare doorway to the great outdoors in the middle of an urban jungle, a one-stop shop for hiking boots and tents.

When R. E. I. announced its decision to shutter the SoHo location in October, along with the closure of Boston’s sole storefront and a store in Paramus, N. J., it didn’t provide details. A representative cited a “need to adapt to changing market conditions and customer needs” in an email, but would not elaborate.

After an early pandemic outdoor-gear boom, the company has been clawing its way out of several years of losses. Its new chief executive has focused on cutting overhead costs and halting expansions and R. E. I. posted two profitable quarters last year.

Rising rents in the SoHo neighborhood have led to a revolving door of commercial tenants in recent years. The average retail rent for the neighborhood hovered around $351 per square foot in 2025, up by 9 percent from the year before, according to a report by JLL, a real estate company. Kushner Companies, the building’s landlord, did not respond to requests for comment.

Days before the store’s closure, an anonymous user created an event on the event invitation app Partiful called the SOHO REI funeral.

The invite instructed New Yorkers to gather outside the store, wear black and give it the “send-off she deserves.” There would be speeches and musical performances.

Within hours, hundreds of people said they were going to the party, which would have clogged the triangular convergence of Lafayette and Mulberry Streets. The organizers decided to pivot to an all-day shrine where people could stop by.

On Thursday morning, to the right of the entrance on Lafayette, a placard for farewell messages appeared, with a bag of notecards, marker and tape.

“Once went on a first date here because a guy had to pee,” read one unsigned note.

“Thank you for guiding me when I don’t know if I’m north/east/south/west once I exit the F train,” read a card written by someone who went by Uno.

Katrina Rili, the mourner who teared up reading the notes, went inside and walked out with a new hat.

Dennis Porto, an R. E. I. member who lives down the street, came in with his girlfriend to take it all in one last time.

The R. E. I. era is a relatively new one in the long history of the red-brick, Romanesque-Revival-style Puck Building, which was constructed in the 1880s. Its arched windows and tiara of crenelations predated even Lafayette Street and the underground subway, said Andrew Berman, the executive director of Village Preservation.

From 1887 to 1918, the building housed the country’s first satirical political magazine, Puck, which was named after the Shakespearean fairy, and roughly 30 lithographic printing presses. Two gilded statues of the mischievous character decorate the facade, looking down at the street below while holding a pen, a mirror and a book inscribed with “What Fools These Mortals Be.” Many of the original lithography stones hang in the R. E. I. store’s space.

Over the last roughly 140 years, the building has been through many twists: It was briefly an artist’s cooperative before it was sold to the Kushner family, which still owns it. It was also featured in the popular sitcom “Will and Grace.” In 2013, Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of President Trump, started turning the top two floors and the roof space into luxury penthouses.

In 2022, employees of the SoHo store were the first of the company’s nearly 200 locations to vote to unionize.

“There was some level of hope that R. E. I. would listen because of its image” as a progressive company, Elio Alexander, a worker at the store and a representative of the union’s bargaining committee, said. The company was founded by a group of friends in 1938 as a consumer cooperative owned by millions of its customers and workers who buy memberships.

In the four years since the unionization vote, however, the company and the workers could not agree on a new contract, Alexander, 29, said. The jobs of all 72 workers at the store will be cut. The company has denied that the closures are related to the unionization effort.

During the store’s last few hours of operation, the mood inside was somber. Staff members, who said they were not allowed to talk to the media, expressed disappointment with a company that had otherwise been a fun and fulfilling place to work.

Benji Kalmanowitz, 26, and R. J. Tabachnick, 28, stood outside, dressed in black because they were in mourning. They met while working at the store in 2021 and became roommates, going hiking and biking together. Tabachnick bought his first bike at this store.

The company “represents a movement of getting outside and being active in the world, and having it in New York, one of the biggest cities, is such a statement and has an impact,” Tabachnick said. “The fact that it’s closing kind of takes that away.”

Exactly five seconds before the clock struck 8 p. m., or closing time, on Thursday, Colin Herron, dressed in an olive green vest, grabbed a microphone and started counting down.

“5, 4, 3, 2, 1!” he yelled. Applause and cheers erupted around him.

Herron, who worked there for three years, hugged the rest of the staff members.

After the countdown, just before the doors closed, Porto kissed his girlfriend, laying claim to the last ever kiss to occur at the SoHo R. E. I.

Outside, the shrine was beginning to buckle under the weight of all the notes it had accumulated.

Alisha Haridasani Gupta is a Times reporter covering style and pop culture.

Why Lettuce Is Always Making People Sick

Wired July 22, 2026

Salad is usually synonymous with healthy eating. Except now, as the US grapples with an expanding outbreak of cyclosporiasis that’s sickened more than 7,100 people in Michigan alone, likely caused by iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms.

In fact, leafy greens are frequently implicated in instances of foodborne illness. There was a 2022 multistate E. coli outbreak tied to romaine served on Wendy’s sandwiches and 173 cases of norovirus linked to Illinois eatery D. C. Cobb’s. In 2021, BrightFarms recalled packaged salad greens sold in several states after 31 people got salmonella. And in 2019, a total of 167 people were infected with E. coli after eating romaine harvested from the Salinas Valley region in California. This isn't even the first cyclospora outbreak linked to lettuce: In 2020, Fresh Express salad kits were linked to more than 700 cases of people afflicted with the parasite.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that produce is responsible for almost half of the reported foodborne illness cases, with leafy vegetables topping the list. So what is it that makes lettuce a major source of America’s foodborne tummy troubles?

One big reason is simply because lots of people eat it. Lettuce is the second-most-consumed vegetable in the US behind potatoes. (The latest outbreak ensures potatoes will remain the king of US veggies. Plus, french fries.) Wraps, subs, tacos, you name a fast food sandwich and it’s almost certainly got lettuce on it. Salad-slinging chains are fixtures across the US. Grocery store coolers are stocked with salad kits, on top of the unadorned heads of iceberg lettuce and containers of spinach.

Those ready-to-eat salads and blends of spring mix pose a particularly acute risk because they contain multiple types of leafy greens, which can come from different farms and locations. If one type of lettuce in the mix is contaminated, it can contaminate the whole bag. And because that contaminated lettuce gets packaged into lots and lots of bagged salad, it has the potential to spread germs far and wide.

How lettuce is grown can also expose it to a wide array of pathogens. A 2025 study by researchers at Cornell University who studied E. coli outbreaks in romaine lettuce found that a lot of contamination originates from irrigation with untreated surface water applied through overhead spray irrigation systems. There are ways to lower that risk, including switching to irrigation systems that do not directly touch the leaves, but that would require upgrades and downtime.

Lettuce’s satisfying crunch is also what makes it prone to pesky pathogens. Since it’s eaten raw—really, who wants wilted lettuce?—there’s no opportunity to cook off any lingering contaminants. Like other raw fruit and produce, leafy greens don’t go through what’s known as a “kill step”—heating, pasteurization, or freezing—which is designed to eliminate pathogens during the food manufacturing process.

The texture of lettuce is an additional factor in its ability to spread disease.“Many lettuce types have a lot of crevices and folds,” says Jeanne Marrazzo, CEO of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. “It’s very easy for these tiny pathogens to get in there.”

Even prewashing procedures at manufacturing facilities don’t always remove microbes, which can cling tightly to leaves. In the case of cyclospora, the parasite has thick outer walls, making it highly resistant to most food sanitizers. Experts say vigorous washing that involves scrubbing is the best way to get rid of cyclospora.

“If you don't wash these products well, you're going to end up ingesting whatever is on the lettuce,” says Amira Roess, an epidemiologist at George Mason University.

The White House Is Trying to Figure Out What to Do About Chinese AI

Wired July 22, 2026

The Trump administration is split over how to respond to the rapid rise of China’s leading AI models, according to multiple people familiar with deliberations.

The debate is broadly divided between parts of the White House, which has pushed for stricter controls on Chinese AI that may soon rival the most powerful US models, and the Commerce Department, which has viewed those restrictions as unworkable.

The conundrum has become the latest flash point for the administration over AI, after China’s Moonshot AI lab last week released its Kimi K3 model that rivals the top US models from Anthropic and OpenAI.

In recent days, senior White House officials have discussed possible measures to stop China’s AI labs from developing their models by training them on US models, a practice known as distillation, the people say.

The White House is expected to take some sort of presidential action after Anthropic last month alleged the Chinese tech company Alibaba had carried out the “largest known distillation attack” against it to date. This action is not currently expected to take the form of an executive order, according to one of the people.

A White House spokesperson did not comment on the reporting in this story.

The White House has been taking distillation attacks especially seriously. It announced on Wednesday that Moonshot had developed Kimi K3 by distilling Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 model, and Treasury secretary Scott Bessent told Fox Business that covert distillation could lead to sanctions, describing it as “IP theft.”

While proposals have been making the rounds inside the White House, no formal request for input has been transmitted yet to the Commerce Department, which has its own ideas, according to two people familiar with deliberations.

The Commerce Department has increasingly emerged as an influential part of the intra-administration split over AI, in part because it oversees export controls through the Bureau of Industry and Security.

Lutnick has contemplated ways to create incentives for top US labs to create their own open weight models to counterbalance China, and has spoken with leaders at a number of AI labs in recent weeks, the people add.

Lutnick appears to be straddling a middle ground of regulation—he imposed export controls on Anthropic to bring them to heel—but has been more freewheeling than Cairncross, one of the people said.

Earlier this month, the biggest AI issue for the administration was Anthropic’s Claude Mythos and Fable 5 models, because of their ability to find vulnerabilities in government systems and critical infrastructure.

But policy headaches with AI have only escalated with the rise of so-called open weight models from China—models that have few to no safeguards to prevent hacking government systems and can be downloaded and used by anyone.

The Odyssey’s Success Is Inspiring Unprecedented Levels of Cope

Wired July 22, 2026

For months, Elon Musk and the right-wing cranks he caters to on X have whipped themselves into a raging froth over the supposed desecration of an ancient Greek poem by one of the most successful movie directors alive.

Now that their manufactured backlash has bombed, they’re searching for ways to cope with the reality that they are increasingly divorced from popular opinion.

Christopher Nolan’s artistic crimes in bringing The Odyssey to the screen, according to Musk and others in a furor, were instances of what they called “historical inaccuracy” in a lavish fantasy teeming with monsters, witches, and undead spirits—mainly the casting of Lupita Nyong'o, who is Black, as Helen of Troy, and Elliot Page, who is trans, as Sinon. The grand total of approximately 10 minutes of screen time between these actors in a three-hour saga, combined with the general hysteria over “wokeness” in Hollywood, a rejection of Americanized dialog, and lingering misogyny regarding scholar Emily Wilson’s 2017 translation of Homer’s epic (the first by a woman), resulted in countless teeth-gnashing posts and calls for a boycott that never materialized.

Instead, the mythic drama hauled in a staggering $264 million as it opened this past weekend, sailing toward continued box office dominance and, in all likelihood, a slew of awards. A few conservative commentators, including Ben Shapiro—no fan of DEI or “woke” values—acknowledged it as a landmark achievement. But while some who had predicted its doom knew enough to move on from this battle to other fronts in the culture war, many sank deeper into denial.

“BREAKING,” blared one anonymous X account on Monday. “The Odyssey is FAKING ticket sales by buying up theaters/seats (Fraud) to make the movie look like a success (already $400 million in the hole) moviegoers are reporting having to take terrible seats (because full) but when they show up the theaters are mostly empty.” The post included screenshots of unverifiable anecdotes from Reddit about quiet cinemas and no-show ticket holders.

What Universal Pictures, the studio behind the film, would stand to gain by spending millions beyond a $250 million production budget and $125 million in marketing costs to astroturf a flop was not exactly clear. Then again, these are the same conspiracists who find it suspicious that the critics’ reviews tend to all be published at the same time.

Musk, for his part, seemed to be inspired by an X user who posted three minutes of AI-generated scenes in which characters from The Odyssey are all white and speak in British accents. Commenting on the clip, which at best resembles a montage from a hokey 1970s adaptation, the richest man in the world declared: “Before this year ends, Grok Imagine will make a full-length movie of The Odyssey that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer.”

Those familiar with Musk know that when he vows to reach a milestone by year’s end, it basically never happens. The promise of a Grok-animated Odyssey, though minor compared to most of his ambitions—he even speculated in 2025 that the xAI model might “discover new technologies” within several months—is sure to fall by the wayside as well. Not only is it a tiresome idea with zero appeal to the mainstream moviegoer (who has or will soon see Nolan’s version), it’s also unoriginal: The AI studio Fountain 0 is planning the online release of an artificially generated feature titled Odyssey: The Fall this summer.

Moreover, both ill-conceived projects misunderstand the lesson that the entertainment industry seems to be taking from Nolan’s latest blockbuster. At a moment when executives imagine that AI is the key to cutting costs and turbocharging output, the director has shown once again that the practical craft of filmmaking beats out what he himself has disparaged as “slop.”

So, will this aggrieved little cadre of internet reactionaries ever be able to accept that they don’t understand what audiences want? Or that they have deluded themselves, thanks to skewed algorithms and bogus amplification, into thinking they possess an influence they never had? Please. They’re not capable of conceding a loss. And there’s always another outrage down the road.

China’s Open AI Models Are Challenging Silicon Valley’s Playbook

Wired July 22, 2026

The AI industry is not quite experiencing a DeepSeek 2.0 moment, but it feels very close. The leading Chinese AI labs have been on a roll lately, releasing a series of almost cutting-edge open-source models. Z. ai released GLM 5.2 in June, Moonshot AI released Kimi K3 last week, and Alibaba released Qwen 3.8 this Monday.

Silicon Valley and Washington started talking about the models immediately, especially K3, which is widely seen as the best of the bunch. David Sacks, a venture capitalist and AI adviser to President Donald Trump, called the performance of Moonshot’s model “concerning.” Earlier this week, Commerce Secretary Scott Bessent suggested the US might impose sanctions on Chinese AI companies.

On Wednesday, Michael Kratsios, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, alleged that the Trump administration has “information that Moonshot AI distilled Anthropic’s Fable for the development of its K3 model,” which he said amounted to “stealing proprietary US technology and undermining American research” and was “unacceptable.” (Moonshot AI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)

The new Chinese models have a few things in common: Third-party benchmarks show that they perform nearly as well as the best Western models; they are optimized for agentic coding tasks (the hottest thing in AI this year); and they are or will soon be released with open weights, making them accessible and transparent.

But perhaps the biggest parallel between the current moment and January 2025—when the world was shocked by DeepSeek’s R1 model—is that it reaffirms how American and Chinese AI labs are taking diverging paths when it comes to being open or closed.

When it first burst onto the scene, DeepSeek challenged the premise that only closed-source models built with billions of dollars of investment in compute infrastructure and training could achieve frontier performance. But since then, Western AI labs have continued developing AI the same way, and now American frontier models feel more roped-off than they were a year ago.

Anthropic said for months that its latest Mythos model was so dangerously good at hacking that only approved collaborators could use it. When it was finally released more widely, the White House responded by issuing broad export controls, which forced Anthropic to take Mythos and its less capable sister model, Fable 5, offline temporarily. OpenAI similarly delayed the release of GPT 5.6 after it received a request from the White House.

In China, meanwhile, the situation looks very different. Chinese startups and tech giants have doubled down on open source: Anyone with a good enough computer environment can now download an open-weight model, run it locally, add customizations, and overall enjoy a much greater degree of freedom than OpenAI and Anthropic would ever allow. In many ways, the open versus closed debate is more entangled with the US versus China debate than ever before.

There are a lot of reasons why Chinese labs have chosen a business strategy built atop open-source models. Being the newer, smaller fish in the AI field, making their models free and open can help Chinese firms attract more users, collaborators, and media spotlight. It also puts them in a separate lane of competition from the one that OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, SpaceX, and other deep-pocketed giants are in.

Earlier this year, rumors spread that Alibaba might be considering joining the closed-source race after it rearranged its corporate AI model development teams. But the tech giant announced on Monday that it would again release the latest version of Qwen—its line of open-source models beloved by the global tech community—with open weights, signaling to customers and the public it is not pivoting away yet.

Perhaps the strongest validation of the Chinese approach is the models themselves. Chinese labs have produced what are widely considered the world's best open-source AI models, showing that American companies no longer have an exclusive hold on building the most capable systems.

Arena AI, a crowdsourced model evaluation platform, now ranks K3 as the best model when it comes to web development tasks and number four in agentic tasks, just below Anthropic’s Fable and Opus 4.8, as well as OpenAI’s GPT 5.6. Artificial Analysis, an independent AI benchmarking company, ranks K3 in the third spot in its intelligence index.

Shortly after Moonshot AI released a preview version of K3 on July 16, people around the world began rushing to try it out, consuming so much inference computing resources that the company is temporarily restricting new users from signing up.

As more people start using open-source Chinese models with capabilities nearly on par with that of their Western competitors, some have started questioning whether paying for OpenAI or Anthropic’s offerings is really worth it. The fact that multiple Chinese labs were able to create capable agentic models and were unafraid to release them to the public is poking holes in the popular understanding that OpenAI and Anthropic are miles ahead of the competition.

Just like with DeepSeek, K3 fans are now celebrating it as evidence that Western AI models are overhyped and overprotected. “It is absolutely wild how much love Kimi got,” Rui Ma, founder of the independent research firm Tech Buzz China, said in a social media post, referring to the company’s announcement that demand for K3 had overwhelmed its servers. “Only made possible by the poor comms and decisions from [Silicon Valley] labs in the past year,” she added.

“I think Anthropic has overhyped the risks, or described risks that are coming soon but do not currently proliferate,” says Nathan Lambert, an independent AI researcher in Seattle who recently visited Moonshot AI’s office in China. He admits, though, that just like the rest of the general public, he has little firsthand information about how Mythos really performs. “We rely on a few private companies and a federal government with depleted state capacity to make that judgment call,” he says.

In addition to challenging the mainstream Western narrative about AI, Chinese open-source models are also proving to be a practical commercial replacement for American closed models. They aren’t just talked about on X and benchmarked against other models—they have become a popular and readily usable option for a growing number of Western startups and individual users.

“There's a real shift toward actually using these newest models that started with GLM 5.2,” Lambert says, referring to Z. ai’s model. “​​Even weeks after the GLM 5.2 release, I hear from AI researchers in the Bay Area that they are still using it for a core part of their workflow. Kimi, being a stronger model, will only do more, especially in areas like cybersecurity, where Mythos, Fable, and GPT 5.6 are effectively unusable.”

In fact, this is already happening. On Tuesday, OpenAI disclosed a concerning incident in which its GPT-5.6 Sol model hacked into the production system of Hugging Face, an open-source AI platform. Hugging Face has said it resorted to using the open-source model GLM 5.2 to analyze the cyberattack because other frontier models were refusing to help due to built-in safety guardrails.

Chinese AI models also tend to be cheaper than Western alternatives, but that’s not necessarily their main selling point. While models like K3 charge less for tokens, early tests show that they may require more tokens than Western models to solve the same problems, thus making the cost gap smaller. “In my fairly limited use, [K3] also seemed very token-hungry. It's not obvious to me that this model is actually that cheap to run,” wrote Dean Ball, a former White House AI adviser who recently joined OpenAI as its head of strategic futures, in a social media post in which he also praised K3 as “a very good model.”

Even if they are relatively token-hungry, models like K3 do ultimately challenge a fundamental assumption that has driven OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s strategy for years: that AI labs need infinite funding to scale up their compute capabilities just to make better models. “In the end, open-weight models deter further AI capex,” Ball wrote.

An FDA Panel Just Endorsed These Unproven Peptides

Wired July 23, 2026

Peptides are inching closer to the mainstream.

A panel of experts on Thursday narrowly recommended that the Food and Drug Administration reclassify four popular peptides—including one endorsed by podcaster Joe Rogan—to allow certain pharmacies to legally dispense them.

In an at-times emotionally charged meeting that lasted more than 11 hours, members of an FDA advisory committee heard data presentations from FDA staff on four unapproved peptides—BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, and MOTs-C—as well as testimony from health care practitioners, patients, pharmacies, and clinics.

Members voted eight to six, with one abstention, to add three of the four peptides to the agency’s bulks list, meaning compounding pharmacies can use them to create custom medications for patients. (The fourth peptide—MOTs-C—received a seven-to-five vote in favor, with two abstentions.) The advisory panel, which includes several members tied to peptide-related businesses and telehealth clinics, will consider three more peptides on Friday.

Peptide therapies have been growing in popularity thanks to the endorsement of podcasters, wellness influencers, and Health and Human Services secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has said he’s a “big fan.” Essentially smaller versions of proteins, peptides are being touted for everything from skin rejuvenation and hair growth to gut health and injury recovery despite a lack of scientific evidence to back up these claims.

Many peptides currently exist in an unregulated gray market after the Biden administration banned compounding pharmacies from producing 20 peptides out of safety concerns in 2023. They can be legally sold online for “research use only” and “not for human consumption,” yet their marketing heavily implies otherwise. China and India are major suppliers of peptides, with some crypto-funded fentanyl labs switching gears to produce them.

During the meeting, the FDA’s own scientists recommended against allowing compounding pharmacies to produce any of the seven peptides being considered due to a lack of evidence showing they are safe and effective. Peptide proponents meanwhile testified that US compounding pharmacies should be able to produce them so that patients can access safer, regulated options with a prescription.

“I'm not going to tell you that the evidence for BPC-157 is strong. It isn't, and I won't overclaim it," said Anant Vinjamoori, chief medical officer of telehealth provider Hims & Hers. “What I'd ask is that you not read thin as non-existent.” The company is actively preparing to launch peptide treatments in anticipation of the FDA greenlighting some peptides.

Among the peptides approved, two are particularly popular with podcasters and influencers. BPC-157 and TB-500 are paired as part of a so-called “Wolverine stack” to help improve recovery after injuries. Committee members were asked to evaluate BPC-157, which is thought to promote tissue repair, for ulcerative colitis. The World Anti-Doping Agency says BPC-157 poses a risk to athlete health because it has not been studied extensively in humans.

Some health care providers testified that patients of theirs had turned to the gray market to buy peptides and ended up with products that were laced with illicit substances. But while FDA approval may help reduce some of those risks, other commenters said it could create new ones.

John Hertig, chair of the Collaborative for Evidence-Based Medicines, said allowing compounders to make these peptides sends the message that the FDA is approving them. “That gets very confusing for our patients,” he said, adding that the existence of a gray market isn’t a reason to allow compounders to make these peptides.

He argued that there will still be a gray market even if the FDA allows for compounding of these peptides, citing that patients still seek out gray market GLP-1 drugs despite several FDA-approved drugs on the market.

Adriane Fugh-Berman, a physician and professor at Georgetown University, also challenged the idea that allowing legal versions would eliminate this gray market. “Would the government endorse companies manufacturing heroin because it would be cleaner than what's sold on the street?” she said. “Just because the market is large, doesn’t mean it should be legalized. It means that a product should be studied.”

The experts who voted against adding these four peptides to the bulks list cited a lack of data to support their use.

Elizabeth Rebello, an anesthesiologist at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, was one of the committee members who voted against allowing the four peptides to be compounded, citing unknowns around safety and confusion for the public.

“I'm just concerned that we're entering a Pandora's box here,” she said.

For now, the panel’s recommendations are just that. A formal FDA decision will likely not come for several months.

Meta’s New Feel-Good AI Ad Uses a Song About the World Ending

Wired July 23, 2026

On Thursday morning, Meta published an ad to its official Instagram account with the message that artificial intelligence will not “make us less connected” or “leave us behind.” It was set to the 1972 David Bowie track “Five Years,” which is about, among other things, the end of the world.

“Call us optimists, call us dreamers, call us whatever the hell you want—but we’re betting on people, and we like those odds,” the narrator says, as a toddler plays with a butterfly, two parents laugh with their infant, and Jalen Brunson waves at the Knicks Championship Parade. (The ad also takes special care to highlight use cases for its controversial smart glasses that are not, say, harassing women while surreptitiously recording them.)

The snippet of “Five Years” used in the ad includes the following lyrics:

I heard telephones, opera house, favorite melodies

I saw boys, toys, electric irons and TVs

My brain hurt like a warehouse, it had no room to spare

I had to cram so many things to store everything in there

And all the fat, skinny people

And all the tall, short people

And all the nobody people

And all the somebody people

I never thought I'd need so many people

Perhaps understandably, it skips other parts of the song, including the opening:

News had just come overWe had five years left to cry inNews guy wept and told usEarth was really dying

When reached for comment, Meta spokesperson Francis Brennan said he “would like to highlight what David Bowie himself said about ‘Five Years’ and its meaning: having optimism for the future.” Brennan sent along a 1972 quote about the song that he sourced to BowieBible. com.

“People are so incredibly serious and scared of the future that I would wish to turn the feeling the other way, into a wave of optimism,” reads the quote, which is itself sourced from NME Magazine. “If one can take the micky out of the future, and what it is going to be like … It’s going to be unbelievably technological.”

Nevertheless, BowieBible. com also notes that the song “speaks of a dystopian nightmare in which Earth enters its final five years, for reasons undisclosed, and the ensuing panic, violence, and attempts at redemption.”

BowieBible. com also quotes from a 2018 interview with drummer Mick Woodmansey: “Well, we chatted about it, and we knew it was about the end of the world and pretty depressing,” Woodmansey said of the song. “I remember when we recorded it, he was actually in tears. He was doing the vocal and he was actually crying.”

According to Jeremy D. Larson, the deputy director of Condé Nast sister publication Pitchfork, taking songs out of context for commercials is a time-honored tradition. He points to a Carnival Cruise ad that uses an Iggy Pop song about heroin addiction. (He also says that since Warner Chappell Music owns Bowie’s catalog, they are the ones with discretion over where his songs end up.)

“Meta choosing this specific song where the context for human connection is the apocalypse seems either really ignorant or really insidious,” Larson tells WIRED over Slack. “I don't know, maybe in that context it's genius.”

“Hearing [Bowie’s] work used for AI just feels especially and specifically nonconsensual,” he adds. (CEO Mark Zuckerberg, in a post about the ad, wrote that the company was “focused on giving every person the tools to reach your full potential and making sure the benefits of technology are distributed to everyone.”)

Over the past few years, tech companies have made several heavy-handed attempts to assuage people’s fears about their technology making the world worse. Just a few weeks ago, Anthropic released its own lofty ad, “There’s hope in hard questions.” It opens with a clip of a burning building and asks, “Who’s gonna hit the brakes if we need to?” before flashing over dozens of graves. The tone of the ad gradually shifts toward optimism, and ends with vague questions like, “What if we started to be more human again?” over images of families and a humpback whale.

In 2024, Google released a baffling ad about a father teaching his daughter, an aspiring athlete, how to hurdle. The father decides that he should use Gemini to draft a letter, from the perspective of his daughter, so that she can send it to decorated hurdler Sydney McLaughlin-Levrone. And during the 2022 Super Bowl, FTX aired a now-notorious ad starring Larry David, playing various Larry-esque characters, dismissing useful inventions throughout history—the toilet! the fork! the lightbulb!—before ultimately dismissing FTX.

“Don't be like Larry,” reads the text overlay at the end of the ad. “Don't miss out on crypto, on NFTs, on the next big thing.”

FTX filed for bankruptcy about nine months later.

Of course, it’s understandable that tech companies would use every tool at their disposal to increase goodwill. But the ads also demonstrate that many tech companies are failing to sell products that independently convince people that they are not actively making the world worse.

For Taylor Swift, Madison Square Garden’s Controversial Cameras Briefly Went Dark

Wired July 23, 2026

Madison Square Garden owner James Dolan has insisted that the face-recognition system and array of surveillance cameras deployed at his venues is “very, very useful for security”—a big reason why MSG “is the most secure venue in the country.”

On the night of July 2, security in and around the Garden was particularly intense. Roughly 130 cops were deployed to the area. New York City officials were preparing to shut down the surrounding blocks to both vehicles and pedestrians the next day for a major, major event.

July 2 was, of course, the kickoff to Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s wedding celebration, an approximately 100-person rehearsal dinner at Madison Square Garden’s Infosys Theater. And yet, on that extremely sensitive evening, Dolan’s MSG locked nearly all of its security team out of the network of surveillance cameras inside the arena, according to an internal document reviewed by WIRED. The move functionally prevented MSG security from fully operating the venue’s controversial face-recognition program that evening, two sources familiar with the Garden’s operations say.

While the shutdown order reviewed by WIRED applied only to July 2, those sources add that they were told the lockout was repeated on July 3, Swift and Kelce’s wedding night, which drew roughly 1,000 of the biggest names in media, music, business, and sports.

At every stage of their planning, Swift’s and Kelce’s teams went to extraordinary lengths to keep private what happened inside the Garden. Guests had to sign a nondisclosure agreement before they could receive a digital invitation. Tents were set up for cars to park in, so people could move in and out in relative secrecy (and, presumably, avoid the biometric surveillance gear positioned at the standard entrances). Wedding attendees were told there was a no-phone policy. The only detailed description of the event posted by a wedding night guest was quickly deleted.

According to the internal document, an MSG executive ordered on July 2 a seven-hour lockdown of the Garden’s video management system, made by the security tech company Genetec, “due to a client privacy request.” Security staffers who ordinarily monitor the building’s internal cameras and the accompanying face-recognition software were barred from doing so. The memo states that only a handful of company leaders and engineers were allowed into their Genetec accounts. The rest were “disabled.”

“If you somehow still have access to cameras after 3PM, you will be forcibly logged off,” the document warned MSG security personnel.

Since 2018, Dolan’s company has experimented with biometric surveillance at its venues, which include Radio City Music Hall and the Beacon Theater in New York, as well as the Sphere in Las Vegas. The organization contends that the technology is a security measure, but there are many publicly documented cases where the face-recognition system appears to have been for something else: retribution.

Fans who’ve been critical of Dolan have had their faces captured and then put on watch lists. A lawyer representing a cop was banned in April because his client is suing MSG. A mom trying to take her then 9-year-old Girl Scout to a Christmas show at Radio City Music Hall had her face flagged and was blocked from entering. The reason: She was an attorney, and her firm was in a legal dispute with one Dolan-controlled entity.

Genetec’s software serves as the backbone for MSG’s video security system, monitoring feeds from the various cameras and allowing security personnel to manage the applications that rely on those feeds, including face recognition. Cameras at the guest entrances are tied into a face-recognition system made by eConnect. If someone’s face triggers an alert, Genetec then allows that person to be easily tracked across the camera network. According to a person familiar with the security surveillance setup, “This makes it much easier to track a person, because we can jump from camera to camera in real time and follow them.”

As WIRED previously reported, Garden security used these systems to monitor a transgender woman second-by-second when she was in the arena. The cameras even noted when she went in and out of a bathroom.

Attendees at the Swift-Kelce pre-wedding celebration were spared such prying eyes. Civil libertarians say they understand why the couple might not want Dolan’s surveillance system deployed in full. But those activists see the accommodation as more than a one-off. It’s a preview of “a future where privacy is a luxury for the elite few, and the rest of us are subjected to pervasive surveillance everywhere we go,” says Evan Greer, director of the digital rights group Fight for the Future.

MSG’s venues host private events not infrequently. NBCUniversal takes over Radio City Music Hall every year to preview its shows for the next season; Warner Bros. Discovery goes to other Dolan-owned properties. But those customers did not ask to disable any aspect of the Garden’s security system, according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter. “It has never been done,” the source says, reflecting on their years at MSG, “and the request wouldn’t have been entertained.”

Even when the New York Police Department takes over Madison Square Garden, the cameras have stayed on. The NYPD regularly holds its graduation ceremonies from the Police Academy within the arena. As WIRED previously reported, the MSG face-recognition system contained a photograph apparently taken from one of those events. It shows an officer in his Police Academy dress uniform.

Which would make this celebration an outlier.

There’s the argument that Swift and Kelce, two of the planet’s most famous people, bought some modicum of privacy for themselves and their guests when they spent the estimated $1.2 to $1.6 million to book the Garden. It’s a venue with “some unique advantages,” former NYPD intelligence official John Miller noted for CNN. “The Garden has no windows, is covered by a roof, and access to the venue can be tightly controlled. That limits the ability of paparazzi, helicopters with powerful, long-distance cameras, or drones to capture the kinds of images they have at other celebrity weddings in outdoor venues.” Of course, for that money, they could have reserved any number of islands more private than Manhattan and an event space more discreet than the so-called “World’s Most Famous Arena.”

“People who have their wedding at Madison Square Garden don’t make that choice for privacy,” says a security professional who is deeply familiar with the venue.

Early July was a particularly hectic time. The city was considered to be in a “heightened threat environment” by the New York Police Department because of the America 250 celebrations and ongoing war with Iran. (That threat estimate is presumably one reason why the cameras outside the Garden—which can be accessed by the NYPD—stayed on, according to the memo.) Swift’s presence, of course, amped up the stakes enormously. In May, a man was sentenced to 15 years in prison for planning an attack at her concert in Vienna, Austria.

The Garden’s interior camera network is supposed to help in those situations, and more. What if someone snuck into the ultra-exclusive event? What if that person was a real threat to the people inside? Dolan, in a 2023 interview, told a local news anchor that the combination of surveillance cameras and face recognition did important work to keep such dangerous people out: “Are you someone who is on this list? If you’re a terrorist it’ll say, ‘That’s a terrorist.’”

But the NYPD supplies no such data to the Garden, a department spokesperson previously told WIRED. While some photographs from the FBI’s most-wanted list have been uploaded into the system, a lawsuit from a former MSG security staffer contends that was done to establish “an after-the-fact false narrative” that the face recognition was primarily geared toward stopping hostile actors rather than individuals Dolan perceived to be personal threats.

“Clearly the technology is not that helpful if it wasn’t needed at one of MSG’s highest-profile events of the year,” Michelle Dahl, executive director for the Surveillance Technology Oversight Project, said in a statement.

That said, there are indications that some cameras were rolling during the event. A notice near the Garden’s entrance alerted visitors that there would be “photography and videography” on the premises from June 29 to July 3—the date of the wedding—and that, by entering, guests agreed that their images and voices could be used in “any and all manner, format, and media.”

The Garden has long had a reputation for being the epicenter of global entertainment, a place that attracts the very brightest stars. But the Garden’s handling of its high-profile visitors has come under scrutiny recently, after the hacker collective ShinyHunters posted an internal MSG database of more than 39,000 VIPs. MSG sued WIRED for defamation for its reporting on the database; in the lawsuit, MSG confirmed that the “spreadsheet-like export” was stolen after an employee’s credentials were compromised by a social-engineering attack and that it no longer employed that individual. The lawsuit also confirmed that a small subset of those celebrities were designated some sort of “risk.” Among the 400 or so found by WIRED are the actor and musician Jamie Foxx; former “Real Housewife” Ubah Hassan; Shang-Chi star Simu Liu; Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton; and Achraf Hakimi, the captain of Morocco’s World Cup team.

Sources previously indicated to WIRED that these risk scores could reflect internal assessments of whether the VIPs might say something less than positive about Dolan and the Garden’s management or become involved, even indirectly, with some sort of public relations issue. MSG acknowledged that it maintains a “Threat Management notes field” for VIPs that might address, among other things, “prior incidents at MSG venues, the conduct or intensity of an individual’s fanbase or associates, or identity-verification concerns.” There was “a separate database” for “genuine security risks,” the lawsuit noted.

The celebrity database also included fields for race, gender, and sexual orientation, as MSG confirmed in its suit. The actor Elliot Page and the beauty influencer Emira D’Spain, for instance, were two of the 93 VIPs marked as “LGBTQIA,” as were the singer Avery Wilson and the designer Zac Posen.

“James Dolan has serious questions to answer. First, why is he so obsessed with us?” Tony Simone, an openly gay New York state lawmaker whose district includes midtown Manhattan, posted on July 9.

The company, for its part, states that its “support for the LGBTQIA community is indisputable.” The sexual orientation field, MSG added in its lawsuit against WIRED, was used for “inclusion-oriented outreach, including Pride events, community engagement, sales opportunities, and donations.”

Page, D’Spain, Posen, and Wilson also received a “risk” designation in the Garden database, albeit a “low” one. (In its lawsuit, MSG notes that only 4 percent of the celebrities it “tagged with an orientation of ‘LGBTQIA’” have threat-management notes.) Some of Swift and Kelce’s guests were also given risk scores, including Selena Gomez; her husband, the producer Benny Blanco; the broadcaster and former football player Michael Strahan; the actress Mariska Hargitay; the singer Benson Boone; and the rapper Ice Spice.

Representatives for Swift and Kelce did not respond to requests to comment for this story. In an email, a spokesperson for MSG declined to comment “due to the fact that we are in active litigation with WIRED.”

While face recognition is pervasive at Dolan-owned venues, it is not universal. The iconic Chicago Theater, for example, doesn’t collect biometric data, because private entities are forbidden to do so under an Illinois law that prohibits such surveillance without written consent. In its lawsuit against WIRED, the Garden highlighted at least two statements from current and former lawmakers that discussed WIRED’s reporting along with “existing and proposed biometric-data legislation.” WIRED’s coverage was damaging to the organization, the Garden added, because the public’s reaction to it would increase “the foreseeable regulatory and political consequences to MSG.”

Attempts to rein in MSG’s face-recognition system in New York City and state long predate WIRED’s reporting. A multiyear inquiry by the state liquor authority into the Garden’s use of face recognition ended this week with a “slap on wrist,” in the words of The New York Times. A recent measure in the State Assembly targeting biometric surveillance in public spaces (like MSG) was cosponsored by Simone and Zohran Mamdani, who now serves as New York’s mayor. It’s not hard to imagine why event planners intent on privacy would want to disable the controversial MSG camera system for their ultrahigh-profile clients. “I don’t blame them for turning it off, but let’s be clear,” said Dahl. “Privacy shouldn’t just be afforded to the rich and famous.”

The EU Fines Google $1 Billion for Prioritizing Its Own Services in Search

Wired July 23, 2026

The European Commission has levied a $1 billion penalty against Google over alleged competition law violations.

An EC investigation found that Google had abused its dominance in the European Union’s search and app store markets to funnel people toward its own apps and services, in violation of the EU’s Digital Markets Act.

The body has ordered Google to refrain from giving preferential treatment to its own services—such as shopping, accommodations, transport, and flights—in search rankings. Google must also allow app developers to communicate and transact with users outside the Play Store, where it takes a commission on sales.

“The best products should succeed because they’re better, not because they’re owned by the company running the search engine,” says Teresa Ribera, an executive vice president at the EC. “European consumers have a right to be told by app developers where to sign up to the best offers, even when the app store owner does not get a cut.”

In a statement to WIRED, Google said it would consider appealing the penalty.

“This isn't fair competition; it’s product degradation driven by a small group of self-serving complainants, with European businesses and consumers taking the hit,” says Kent Walker, president of global affairs at Google.

Tech industry trade associations argue that heavy-handed enforcement of the Digital Markets Act is self-defeating. “Reducing the quality of what Europeans have access to is not a positive outcome,” Daniel Friedlaender, senior vice president at trade organization CCIA Europe, tells WIRED.

The EU has brought numerous multi-billion-dollar fines against Google in the last decade over a medley of antitrust violations. In early July, a European court upheld a record $4.1 billion fine brought against Google in 2018 over agreements that required phone makers to install Google Search and the company’s Chrome web browser on their devices.

“Certainly, the stakes are really high for companies. How they are ranked affects their businesses a great deal,” says Kathryn McMahon, an associate professor of law at the University of Warwick. “The way EU competition law looks at it, firms in a dominant position—like Google—have a special responsibility not to distort competition.”

To address the latest complaints, Google has proposed alterations to the way it administers the Play Store and presents its products in search rankings, which the EC has characterized as "progress towards compliance.”

Recently, US president Donald Trump vowed to impose steep new tariffs on European countries that seek to restrict American technology companies. The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

The latest penalty is “quite a strong response, in the context of the transatlantic complaints—the way that Trump can leverage fines,” says McMahon. “It shows the commission is willing to be tough.”

Simply follow the instructions for easy removal. 3M makes clips and different types of hooks, too, for whatever you need to hang. —Brenda Stolyar

Dash

Amazon

Wayfair

The problem with most of our favorite air fryers is that they're all too big for a dorm room. But this little one from Dash should do the trick, and it requires very little space. With a capacity of just 2.6 quarts, it's best for single servings and smaller portions. The basket and removable nonstick base are dishwasher-safe (a nice feature, though you probably won’t make use of it in your dorm room), and the presets include a custom setting so you can easily get back to your favorite mode.

Target

First-aid kits are college-dorm essentials. There are lots of options from Welly that are bright and easy to find. Make sure your kit is always stocked with bandages, antibiotic ointment, antiseptic wipes, over-the-counter pain relief, plus some cold and flu medicine. I also recommend including Tums, Pepto-Bismol, cough drops, and Narcan. It's better to be safe than sickly (and unprepared).

LectroFan

Amazon

This top-recommended sound machine is compact and offers classic fan noise as well as different-colored noises. There may be nights when you're homesick or when you accidentally study-chugged too many energy drinks, and your mind is racing. This little machine may help you relax and get some quality shut-eye.

HoMedics

Homedics

Dorm rooms are notoriously dry and drafty. Putting a small humidifier like this one on your nightstand may help you breathe easier and may even help with dry skin. The humidifier also includes a nightlight, plus a place to add essential oils, if you want to scent the air.

Keurig

Keurig

Amazon

Walmart

For coffee drinkers who prioritize speed in their machine of choice, this pod-style coffee maker is an excellent option, with readily available refills. It has a built-in milk frother, so you can make your own specialty beverages without paying $8 for the same at the local chain coffee spot. The machine is easy to clean, and the water reservoir is large.

Zojirushi

Amazon

Wayfair

Students who want to consume caffeine by the pot rather than by the cup might consider our favorite affordable drip coffee maker. The entire brewing process is automatic with basically zero bells or whistles, but the resulting coffee is flavorful and consistent every time. It also doesn't take up much counter space.

Hatch

Amazon

Hatch

The Hatch Restore 3 is a popular sunrise alarm clock that doubles as a sound machine. Some of the features are paywalled behind a monthly subscription that costs $5 per month or $50 per year, but you don't need to subscribe to get good use out of the device. The alarm can help reinforce positive sleep and wake-up routines, and the Hatch even has fun features (not paywalled) like guided meditation, which stands to help around finals season.

All of us at WIRED have complicated desk setups that make working from home easier. You don't have to go that hard for a dorm room, and you probably only have so much space to spare anyway. See our full work-from-home guide for more options, but these are some of our favorite desk accessories worth considering—plus some more options for around your dorm room.

Aecooly Chic Touch Control Desk Fan: I tested this fan all summer last year for our Best Fans guide, and my friend's son took it to school for his first year at the University of Colorado. It's going to be hot for move-in week, and this fan is not only powerful, but its 8-inch-tall body fits in a suitcase, it’s USB-C rechargeable, and it’s quiet enough (36 decibels on low) that it won’t bother roommates or interfere with studying. —Kat Merck

Ruggable Pamir Ivory Washable Rug: I like this washable rug because it's durable, it looks great, and it's supremely easy to clean. A rug is one of the easiest ways to make a room feel more grown-up, and this one won’t break the bank.

AmazonBasics 3-Tier Utility Cart: I use this utility cart in my kitchen, and I'm about to get another for my bathroom. It's easy to put together and makes good use of vertical storage space. Use it to organize school supplies, toiletries, accessories, or whatever else is taking up space in your half of the dorm room.

BenQ ScreenBar Computer LED Lamp: WIRED editor Julian Chokkattu swears by this desk lamp, which only works if you have an external monitor on your desk. It hangs over the top of the screen and illuminates your workspace. Best of all, it takes up zero space on your desk!

Monoprice Extra Wide Length Microfiber Desk Mat: This mat is soft and doubles as a mouse pad, which is great for students who use a separate keyboard and mouse.

Ikea Skubb Underbed Storage Case: When former WIRED reviewer Medea Giordano lived in a tiny NYC apartment, she stowed four of these storage bins under her bed to hold every item of clothing that her closet couldn't accommodate. The same tack works well for college beds, which generally have ample room underneath. These cases can hold off-season clothing, shoes, or anything else you may need, like party supplies. Amazon has a bunch of similar options.

Dalykate Backpack Laundry Bag: One reality of dorm life is that you may need to hike your dirty laundry down a few flights to the laundry room. This hamper has a pocket to hold your detergent and backpack straps for portability, and it’s not as bulky as a laundry basket. It's what WIRED editor Julian Chokkattu uses to head to his laundromat.

Crocs Classic Clogs: You need a pair of shower shoes. Trust me when I say that you do not want to deal with athlete's foot in a college dorm. These Crocs are my favorite for shared showers—they're not fussy to walk in, easy to slide out of when you're balancing on one leg to wash your feet, and they dry quickly, too. Alternatively, you could go with a dedicated pair of flip-flops or slides. And don’t forget a shower caddy for your toiletries!

Govee RGBIC LED Light Strip: String lights are cute, but this light strip from Govee is much more fun. You can easily adjust the colors and brightness using the smartphone app, and you can trim down the lights to suit the space.

Basic Cleaning Supplies: I didn’t realize how much stuff I was forgetting when I first moved into my dorm. Make sure you remember household essentials, like laundry detergent, paper towels, dish soap, disinfectant wipes, and washcloths. You might also want a little broom and dustpan.
